title: Global Pasture Watch - Grassland sampling design derived by Feature Space Coverage Sampling (FSCS) at 1-km spatial resolution
description: Sampling design used in the production of the global maps of grassland dynamics 2000–2022 at 30 m spatial resolution in the scope of the Global Pasture Wath initiative. The sampling desing was based in Feature Space Coverage Sampling and resulted in 10,000 sample tiles (1x1 km) distributed across the World, which were visual interpreted in Very-High Resolution imagery thorugh the QGIS plugin QGIS Fast Grid Inspection . FSCS steps include: Short vegetation mask that includes all pixels mapped as mosaic, shrubland, grassland, and sparse vegetation in at least one year from 1993 to 2021 according to ESA/CCI global land cover ( gpw_short.veg.mask_esacci.lc_p_1km_s_19920101_20201231_go_epsg.3857_v1.tif ), 87 input raster layers (including vegetation indices, terrain, land temperature, climate and water variable), Principal Components Analysis (PCA) using all input layers, Selection of the 10 first components (explaining 75% of variance), K-Means with 10,000 clusters (targeted number of samples - gpw_grassland_fscs.kmeans.cluster_c_1km_20000101_20221231_go_epsg.3857_v1.tif ) Calculation of euclidean distance (in the principal component space) of all 1-km pixels to the centre of each cluster, Selection of the pixel with the shortest distance for each cluster, Conversion of the selected pixels into sample tiles () The file gpw_grassland_fscs_tile.samples_1km_20000101_20221231_go_epsg.3857_v1.gpkg provides the sample tiles and include the follow collumns: X : Latitude in Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857), Y : Longitude in Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857), cluster_id : K-Means output ranging from 0—9999, cluster_distance : Distance from the selected sample to the centre of the cluster, cluster_size : Number o 1-km pixels inside the K-Means cluster, estimated using Web Mercator projection ( EPSG:3857 ) cluster_size_equal_area : Number o 1-km pixels inside the K-Means cluster, estimated using Goode Homolosine Land projection ( ESRI:54052 ) cluster_size_corr : Correction factor to adjust the area distortion due to Web Mercator projection, estimated by the difference in normalized propotional values of cluster_size and cluster_size_equal_area. rf_n_pred : Number of pixels predicted by a RF model trained to estimate probability to select the pixel closer to the centre of the KMeans cluster. The RF models were trained individually per each cluster using the 10 first components derived by PCA ( gpw_comps_fscs.pca_m_1km_20000101_20221231_go_epsg.3857_v1.tar.gz ). rf_samp_prob : Sampling probability based on RF model ( rf_n_pred / cluster_size ) rf_samp_wei : Sampling weight estimated in Web Mercator projection. rf_samp_wei_coor : Corrected sampling weight estimated in Goode Homolosine Land projection. title: OmniSegger - Figure data files
description: Proliferation dataset: OmniSegger output for phase-contrast images of wild-type MG1655 E. coli grown on a 4% agarose pad. Frame rate: 3min/frame. Morphology dataset: OmniSegger output for phase-contrast images of wild-type MG1655 E. coli treated with 10uM hydroxyurea growing on a 2% agarose pad. Frame rate: 5min/frame. Modality dataset-brightfield under-focused: OmniSegger output for under-focused brightfield and fluorescence images of TB28 attHK022 Plac::zipA-sfGFP bla pal-mCherry cat E. coli growing on a 2% agarose pad. Images chosen from 0.5um below the focal plane. Frame rate: 15min/frame. Modality dataset-brightfield over-focused: OmniSegger output for over-focused brightfield and fluorescence images of TB28 attHK022 Plac::zipA-sfGFP bla pal-mCherry cat E. coli growing on a 2% agarose pad. Images chosen from 0.5um above the focal plane. Frame rate: 15min/frame. Modality dataset-cytoplasmic fluorescence: OmniSegger output for phase-contrast and fluorescence images of lysC-GFP fusion E. coli strain from the ASKA collection growing on a 2% agarose pad. Frame rate: 7min/frame. Fatal errors calculated by Omnipose bact_fluor_omni segmentation on fluorescence images only, files available upon request. Modality dataset-membrane fluorescence: OmniSegger output for phase-contrast and fluorescence images of ygaW-GFP fusion E. coli strain from the ASKA collection growing on a 2% agarose pad. Frame rate: 7min/frame. Fatal errors calculated by Omnipose bact_fluor_omni segmentation on fluorescence images only, files available upon request. Images taken in the Wiggins Lab at UW. Imaging was performed using a Nikon Eclipse Ti-E microscope, through a 60X 1.4 NA CFI oil-immersion Phase objective onto an Andor Neo sCMOS camera.

title: AMBER salmon: A digital river network containing reach-specific habitat variables related to the North-East Atlantic distribution of Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)
description: Summary This dataset was collated through an offshoot of the AMBER project. One of the aims of AMBER was to evaluate the merits of different restoration actions proposed to reconnect Europe’s fragmented and impounded rivers. To this end, an assessment of barrier impacts at pan-European level was desired. We collated this composite digital river network, and associated catchment, lake, and subcatchments geospatial data, to support assessment of impacts of barriers on Atlantic salmon ( Salmo salar ) at a regional scale. The river network may facilitate studies of other aquatic species, particularly diadromous fishes, owing to its hydrologically consistent anabranching topology. Accurately mapped channel planforms are a requirement for quantifying regional and locally-relevant impacts of barriers on the longitudinal connectivity of rivers. To this end, and in contrast to regional-extent digital river networks that have been derived using the D8 flow accumulation method , EU-Hydro was derived from aerial imagery and digital elevation data, and therefore was the chosen foundation for the composite river network. However, the amount of detail and spatial extent of EU-Hydro was insufficient to capture some North-East Atlantic salmon populations, so hydrography90 , CCM2 and OpenStreetMap data were included where necessary. Topological adjustments of the composite river network were necessary to facilitate hydrologic routing from source to sea. Adjustments included dissolving pseudo-nodes, splitting polylines at lake polygon perimeters, disconnection of incorrectly joined reaches between neighbouring catchments (i.e., inaccurate topological bifurcations/diffluences), and reversal of flow directions in cases of topological loops. Following this preparation using graph-based methods, we were able to generate lookup fields for network tracing and aggregation of upstream/downstream information. To facilitate estimation of barrier-attributable losses of Atlantic salmon habitat in terms of wetted area, we added data fields containing reach specific hydraulic geometries. To do so, we used downscaling and hydrologic routing of gridded runoff data (using hydrostreamer ) followed by a catchment character-aware statistical model relating aerial imagery-derived channel width to discharge, and further approximated depth using Burek et al.’s (2014) Manning’s equation derived method, adjusting for channel gradient (using elevatr and exactextractr ) and a estimated hydraulic roughness. To estimate general suitability of habitat to Atlantic salmon based on water temperature, and potential losses of habitat due to poor water quality (e.g., quantified by WFD ecological quality scores ), we spatially interpolated DynWat and DynQual gridded model outputs onto river segments using a topological adjustment to approximate monthly average temperatures at the reach scale. All geospatial data in this repository follow a naming convention that links river segments to lake flowlines and associated catchment and segment-specific subcatchment polygons, enabling various table join operations and efficient data extraction. To facilitate efficient extraction/ queries, data are provided here in parquet format, including pre-calculated concatenated lists of all upstream and downstream segment ids and shortest downstream paths per segment each stored as a list column . Note – An ongoing project within the ICES working group WGTRUTTA ( Working Group to Develop and Test Assessment Methods for Sea Trout (Salmo Trutta) Populations ) is currently using the river network and national-level river obstacle data to map the available habitat for sea trout (anadromous Salmo trutta ). It is intended to publish the results of that project following an interactive web based GIS validation coordinated through WGTRUTTA and the ICES Data Centre, which will identify the first barrier encountered by anadromous trout migrating upstream from the tidal limit. Limitations We acknowledge that the digital representations of the river systems included in this repository are likely inaccurate in comparison to many national level higher-resolution products. These inaccuracies include, but are not limited to, geometric planform oversimplification, incorrectly mapped anabranches and diffluences, and modelled hydraulic geometries. Moreover, river geometries vary in detail among countries, even within a single product (e.g., EU-Hydro for Scotland is more detailed (or "segment-dense") than for Ireland). With many known and potential limitations in mind, users should carefully inspect their chosen areas of interest for errors and compare the data in this repository to other products to assess suitability for their study before using these data. Note - These data are released under the version 0.9.0, as it is expected that errors will require correction before submission of a manuscript describing the full methods including code and validation (e.g., hydraulic geometry/channel width model, downscaled water temperatures vs. observations etc.) for publication in a data/geospatial data journal and ascension to version 1.0.0. Licences and redistribution of modified open-licensed geospatial data Licences The digital river network and associated geospatial data in this repository are composed of raw, modified, and derived geospatial data from publicly available (open data) sources. Among the licences for these datasets, there were conflicting redistribution terms that dictated how we have packaged the data in this repository. The original authors presented their terms for redistribution as described below: EU-Hydro Copernicus Land Monitoring Service Dataset: "The Copernicus land monitoring products and services are made available on a principle of full, open and free access, as established by the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1159/2013 of 12 July 2013." (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32013R1159) CCM2: "Data are provided free of charge for non-commercial use ." We interpreted this statement as compatible with CC BY NC 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). Hydrography90: " the dataset is protected by the Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial 4.0 International License CC-BY-NC 4.0 " (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) OpenStreetMap: " You are free to copy, distribute, transmit and adapt our data, as long as you credit OpenStreetMap and its contributors. If you alter or build upon our data, you may distribute the result only under the same license "; ODbL v1 (https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/) Modifications and file contents The geometries of the EU-Hydro and OSM river networks were edited to fix broken connections and adjust topology for hydrologic routing. The geometries of the CCM2 river network were edited to ensure hydrologically consistent connectivity with EU-Hydro at EEA boundaries. All river network geometries were edited to split river lines at lake polygon perimeters where splits were not already present. Owing to the incompatibility between CC BY 4.0, CC-BY-NC 4.0, and ODbL v1, geospatial river networks, lakes, and derivative catchments and subcatchments were necessarily written to separate parquet files, thus this repository constitutes a Collective Database (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Collective_Database_Guideline). NOTE - Users should be aware that querying the collection from multiple DRN river line or subcatchment parquet files simultaneously should be seamless (e.g., using the arrow package in R to query a single river system "river_group"), and therefore not require any further geometry operations to restore topological connectivity. Derivative catchment polygons are stored in separate parquet files; however, as the EU-Hydro licence is permissive, catchment polygons that cross EU-Hydro and CCM2 boundaries are retained unbroken within a single parquet file. This aggregation of data was considered appropriate because it avoids users having to dissolve catchment polygons in cases where river systems crossed the borders between CCM2 and EU-Hydro spatial extents. As a result, catchment polygons are stored in three files, reflecting three licenses: (i) CC-BY-NC v4.0, for hydrography90 catchments and those that cross CCM2 and EU-Hydro boundaries; (ii) CC-BY 4.0, consistent with EU-Hydro for catchments that fall entirely within EU-Hydro's spatial extent, and (iii) ODbL, consistent with OSM for all catchments within Isle of Man, Orkney, Shetland and Faroe Islands. Lakes were collated from four sources, (i) CCM2, for which we deemed license redistribution terms to be are consistent with CC-BY NC 4.0, (ii) EU-Hydro and HydroLAKES, which we deemed consistent with CC-BY 4.0, and (iii) OpenStreetMap, which is licensed under ODbL v1. Following the same approach to that used above for the enveloping catchments, we split the data into three files. The files are licensed as follows: Digital river network (linestrings) and subcatchments (polygons; where subcatchment polygons are associated with individual river segments) amber_drn_eu_hydro_rivers & amber_subcatchments_eu_hydro_rivers (CC BY 4.0) amber_drn_ccm2 & amber_subcatchments_ccm2 (CC BY NC 4.0) amber_drn_hydrography90 & amber_subcatchments_hydrography90 (CC BY NC 4.0) amber_drn_osm_waterways & amber_subcatchments_osm_waterways (ODbL) Catchments (polygons enveloping complete river systems) amber_h1_catchments_eu_hydro_ccm2_hydrography90 (CC BY NC 4.0) amber_h1_catchments_eu_hydro (CC BY 4.0) amber_h1_catchments_osm (ODbL) Lakes (polygons) amber_lakes_eu_hydro_ccm2_hydrography90 (CC BY NC 4.0) amber_lakes_eu_hydro (CC BY 4.0) amber_lakes_osm (ODbL) River obstacles (points) amber_post_glacial_analysis (ODbL) OSM countries (polygons) countries_osm_admin_levels_2_and_4 (ODbL) Computation regions (polygons) amber_salmon_regions_eu_hydro (CC BY 4.0) amber_salmon_regions_eu_hydro_ccm2_hydrography90 (CC BY NC 4.0) amber_salmon_regions_osm (ODbL) Example R code to read geospatial data from multiple parquet files # ------------------------------------------------------ # # READ DRN FOR BARENTS SEA # ------------------------------------------------------ # arrow_ds "C:\\PATHTO\\zenodo_drn_files\\" )) |> dplyr::filter(.data$sea_region == "Barents Sea") |> dplyr::select(c("riverID","geom")) con duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "riv_table", arrow_ds) DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSTALL spatial;") DBI::dbExecute(con, "LOAD spatial;") rivdb dplyr::mutate("geom" = ST_GeomFromWKB(.data$geom)) drn dplyr::collect() |> dplyr::mutate("geom" = sf::st_as_sfc(.data$geom)) |> sf::st_as_sf() |> sf::st_set_crs("EPSG:3035") drn |> ggplot2::ggplot()+ ggplot2::geom_sf(ggplot2::aes(geometry = geom)) # ------------------------------------------------------ # References Amatulli, G., Garcia Marquez, J., Sethi, T., Kiesel, J., Grigoropoulou, A., Üblacker, M. title: Global tree percent cover and impervious surfaces (urban) cover based on GLC_FCS30D for years 1985 and 2022 at 30 m spatial resolution
description: Global tree percent cover and impervious surfaces (urban) cover for years 1985 and 2022 at 30 m spatial resolution based on the GLC_FCS30D data set produced by the State Key Laboratory of Remote Sensing, Aerospace Information Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing. The tree cover has been estimated using the 37 class legend ( GLC_FCS30D_legend.csv ) and is only an approximation of might have been the actual tree cover. Note : the GLC_FCS30D data set is probably over-estimating tree-based vegetation types in arid and semi-arid areas so this would need to be corrected; in addition, several artifacts due to the tiling system / locally fitted classification are visible in the GLC_FCS30D maps. The GLC_FCS30D data set is available for viewing from https://OpenLandMap.org and is explained in detail in: Zhang, X., Liu, L., Chen, X., Gao, Y., Xie, S., and Mi, J. (2021): GLC_FCS30: global land-cover product with fine classification system at 30 m using time-series Landsat imagery, Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 13, 2753–2776, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-13-2753-2021 It is estimated that world has lost 1/3rd of original pre-industrial forest areas, however, many current forest areas also have a thinner tree cover than before. title: TCSIF_005: A Temporally Consistent Global SIF Dataset with 0.05° Spatial Resolution (1995–2023)
description: This dataset provides a temporally consistent global solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) product spanning from 1995 to 2023 . The dataset was generated by harmonizing SIF observations from multiple satellite sensors, including GOME, SCIAMACHY, GOME-2, and OCO-2 , using a cross-sensor moment-matching approach. Temporal corrections and downscaling via a light use efficiency (LUE) model were applied to achieve a fine spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° .
producing_institution: Zou, Chu; Liu, Liangyun; Du, Shanshan

title: Crocus-ERA-Interim daily snow product over the Northern Hemisphere at 0.5° resolution
description: The Crocus-ERA-Interim daily snow product is derived from the complex snow scheme Crocus coupled to the ISBA (Interactions between Soil–Biosphere–Atmosphere) land surface model ( Brun et al., 2013 ) and embedded into the SURFEX numerical platform ( https://www.umr-cnrm.fr/surfex/ ). The model is driven by a meteorological forcing (temperature, precipitation, humidity, winds, etc) derived from the ERA-Interim global atmospheric reanalysis ( https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/dataset/ecmwf-reanalysis-interim ). This product only concerns open field snowpack, i.e. only low vegetation is modeled (no forest). It covers the entire Northern Hemisphere at 0.5° resolution over the 1979-07-01 to 2019-06-30 period. Snow depth and snow water equivalent (i.e. the snow mass) are available at a dailly frequency. The simulated snow depth, snow water equivalent, and density over open fields were validated against local observations from over 1000 monitoring sites in Northern Eurasian, available either once a day or three times per month ( Brun et al., 2013 ). This product was used by the NOAA Artic Report Card from 2017 to 2020 for the annual survey of the Terrestrial Snow Cover anomalies over the Northern Hemisphere. This product was also used in several research studies (e.g. Mudryk et al., 2015 ; Mortimer et al., 2020 ; Kouki et al., 2023 ). The successor of this product based on ERA5 at 0.25° resolution over 1950 to 2023 can be found in Decharme (2024b) .

title: MeanDRS River Width Sampling: Data products corresponding to "Intrinsic spatial scales of river stores and fluxes and their relative contributions to the global water cycle"
description: Corresponding peer-reviewed publication This dataset corresponds to all input and output files that were used in the study reported in: Wade, J., David, C.H., Collins, E.L., Denbina, M., Cerbelaud, A., Tom, M., Reager, J.T., Frasson, R.P.M., Famiglietti, J.S., Lee, T., Gierach, M.M. (In Review), Intrinsic spatial scales of river stores and fluxes and their relative contributions to the global water cycle. When making use of any of the files in this dataset, please cite both the aforementioned article and the dataset herein. Summary The Earth’s rivers vary in size across several orders of magnitude. Yet, the relative significance of small upstream reaches compared to large downstream rivers in the global water cycle remains unclear, challenging the determination of adequate spatial resolution for observations. Using monthly simulations of river stores and fluxes from the MeanDRS river routing dataset, we sample global rivers by a range of estimated river width thresholds to investigate the intrinsic spatial scales of the global river water cycle. We frame these scale-dependent river dynamics in terms of observational capabilities, assessing how the size of rivers that can be resolved influences our ability to capture key global hydrologic stores and fluxes. We aim to answer two questions: 1. What is the intrinsic spatial resolution of global river dynamics? 2. How can the spatial scale of river processes be used to inform efficient monitoring and modeling strategies of global river stores and fluxes? title: Supplementary Data for "Progressively smaller outbursts despite worldwide growth of glacier lakes"
description: This respository contains the source data for the study for Progressively smaller outbursts despite worldwide growth of glacier lakes by Georg Veh and co-authors. We investigate trends in the size of glacier lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in 13 mountain regions on 4 continents between 1990 and 2023. We distinguish between moraine-and bedrock-dammed lakes on the one hand, and ice-dammed and supraglacial lakes on the other hand. We use Bayesian hierarchical models, implemented in the package brms in in the statistical programming software R to model temporal trends in the lake area prior to failure on different geographical levels. More information on these data, including detailed scripts to process them, are available at https://github.com/geveh/GLOFsize. We provide the following data: 1 The GLOF database glofdatabase_2024_10_21.ods: OpenOffice table with all reported GLOFs. Compiliation as of Oct 21, 2024. all_glofs_tibble.RDS: R-object of all reported GLOFs in the global GLOF database; data are not trimmed to the period 1990-2023. la_sf.RDS: R-object containing all GLOFs with mapped lake areas before the outburst in the period 1990-2023. reported_GLOFs.rds: R-object containing a table of reported GLOFs in the period 1990-2023 with machine readable names of glaciers and lakes. reported_GLOFs_with_geometry.rds: R-object containing a simple features (sf) object of reported GLOFs in the period 1990-2023 with machine readable names of glaciers and lakes. For a description of the parameters in these tables and R-objects, please visit: Lützow, N., Veh, G., & Korup, O. (2023). A global database of historic glacier lake outburst floods. Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 15, 2983–3000, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-2983-2023 The GLOF database, V4.1 is also available at: http://glofs.geoecology.uni-potsdam.de/ 2 Regional extents of study regions rgiO2_dissolved_outlines.shp : Merged outlines of the RGI O2 according to the 13 study regions in ESRI shapefile format glacier_buffers_split_by_O2_no_fid_correct_FULLNAME_2.gpkg: Regional 5-km buffers around glaciers with overlapping buffers removed in geopackage format. 3 Estimated glacier thickness data RGI-wide_composites_stats_GV.txt: Textfile of estimated glacier thickness for every glacier in the Randolph Glacier Inventory V6.0. Data were made available from Daniel Farinotti (personal communication). reg_invs_bind.rds: A table of all glaciers in the 13 study region that had an estimate of average ice thickness. 4 Glacier lake data We do not share raw data from previously lake inventories because they might be subject to different licenses. Please contact the authors directly if you would like to access these data. Here we share Glacier_lakes_global.ods: OpenOffice spreadsheet of previously published glacier lake inventories, including reference to the underlying study, year, and satellite image used to map glacier lakes. lakes_gt_1km.gpkg: A geopackage of all lakes >1km² as of 2015 or later, manually labelled with descriptors of their geometric properties obtained from interpreting high-resolution satellite images.

title: Transformation Rate Maps of Dissolved Organic Carbon in the Contiguous U.S.
description: We develop two new maps of the dissolved organic carbon (DOC) transformation rate (\(P_r\)) over the contiguous United States. Those maps are derived by combining the USGS riverine DOC observations, soil organic carbon (SOC) data from two sources—HWSD v1.2 and SoilGrids 2.0, and the watershed characteristics from two existing datasets medium-resolution NHDplus and ScienceBase, and state-of-the-art machine learning techniques.

title: Long-term Continuous SIF-informed Photosynthesis Proxy reconstructed with calibrated AVHRR surface reflectance (LCSPP-AVHRR), 1982-2000
description: Usage Notes : This is the updated LCSPP dataset (v3.2), reconstructed using the AVHRR record from 1982–2023. Due to Zenodo’s size constraints, LCSPP-AVHRR is divided into two separate repositories. Previously referred to as "LCSIF," the dataset was renamed to emphasize its role as a SIF-informed long-term photosynthesis proxy derived from surface reflectance and to avoid confusion with directly measured SIF signals. Key updates in version 3.2 include: Improved Calibration : Enhanced consistency in calibration methods, addressing technical limitations in version 3.1 including applying more stringent quality filtering and snow masks. We also Quality Flags : New quality flag layer enables users to identify whether a pixel is derived from observed surface reflectance (QA=0), high-quality gap-filled values (QA=1), lower-quality gap-filled based on the mean seasonal cycle (QA=2), or missing entirely (QA=3). We advice the user to rely only on observed and high-quality gap-filled values for their analyses. Extension to include observations from the year of 2023. Other LCSPP repositories can be accessed via the following links: LCSPP-AVHRR v3.2 (2001-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11906675 LCSPP-MODIS v3.2(2001-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11658088 The user can choose between LCSPP-AVHRR and LCSPP-MODIS for the overlapping period from 2001-2023. The two datasets are generally consistent during this overlapping period, although LCSPP-MODIS shows a stronger greening trend between 2001-2023. For studies exploring the long-term vegetation dynamics, the user can either use only LCSPP-AVHRR or use a blend dataset of LCSPP-AVHRR and LCSPP-MODIS as a sensitivity test. In addition, the updated long-term continuous reflectance datasets (LCREF), used for the production of LCSPP, can be accessed using the following links: LCREF-AVHRR v3.1 (1982-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11905959 LCREF-MODIS v3.1 (2001-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11657458 A manuscript describing the technical details is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.14987 , while detailed the uses and limitations of the dataset. In particular, we note that LCSPP is a reconstruction of SIF-informed photosynthesis proxy and should not be treated as SIF measurements . Although LCSPP has demonstrated skill in tracking the dynamics of GPP and PAR absorbed by canopy chlorophyll (APARchl), it is not suitable for estimating fluorescence quantum yield. All data outputs from this study are available at 0.05° spatial resolution and biweekly temporal resolution in NetCDF format. Each month is divided into two files, with the first file “a” representative of the 1 st day to the 15 th day of a month, and the second file “b” representative of the 16 th day to the last day of a month. Abstract: Satellite-observed solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is a powerful proxy for the photosynthetic characteristics of terrestrial ecosystems. Direct SIF observations are primarily limited to the recent decade, impeding their application in detecting long-term dynamics of ecosystem function. In this study, we leverage two surface reflectance bands available both from Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR, 1982-2023) and MODerate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS, 2001-2023). Importantly, we calibrate and orbit-correct the AVHRR bands against their MODIS counterparts during their overlapping period. Using the long-term bias-corrected reflectance data from AVHRR and MODIS, a neural network is trained to produce a Long-term Continuous SIF-informed Photosynthesis Proxy (LCSPP) by emulating Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 SIF, mapping it globally over the 1982-2023 period. Compared with previous SIF-informed photosynthesis proxies, LCSPP has similar skill but can be advantageously extended to the AVHRR period. Further comparison with three widely used vegetation indices (NDVI, kNDVI, NIRv) shows a higher or comparable correlation of LCSPP with satellite SIF and site-level GPP estimates across vegetation types, ensuring a greater capacity for representing long-term photosynthetic activity.

title: geoSABINA: Environmental variables
description: This dataset provides environmental variables from Spain, selected for their relevance in modeling the distribution of plant species. However, they can also be applied to other species and purposes. It includes a total of 103 raster layers in tif format at 250-meter resolution. The detailed list of layers available is provided in data_table_env_variables.csv, which includes information on the category, dataset, description, resolution, time period, and path. This dataset includes: Climatic variables : 19 bioclimatic variables under current (1990-2010) and 4 future (2071-2100) climate scenarios. Climatic variables were sourced from the climatologies for the Earth’s Land Surface Areas (CHELSA) and downscaled to 250 m in https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.07328. The future scenarios were generated according two global climate models [the latest Institute Pierre Simon Laplace climate model (IPSL_CM6A_LR) and the Meteorological Research Institute Earth System Model version 2.0 (MRI_ESM2)] and two socio-economic pathways: an optimistic low greenhouse gas emissions scenario (SSP126) and a pessimistic high emissions scenario (SSP585). The climatic variables of each scenario are compressed within a zip file. Edaphic variables : Four soil characteristics (pH, nitrogen, sand content, organic carbon) at 0 to 5 cm depth sourced from SoilGrids. The four edaphic variables are compressed within a zip file. Hydrologic variables : Three hydrologic variables (distance to rivers, flow accumulation, and topographic index) derived from the digital elevation model DAT-193-en (Copernicus Land Cover Service) in https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.07328. Solar radiation : Annual solar exposure values calculated from the digital elevation model DAT-193-en in https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.07328. title: Long-term Continuous Red and Near-infrared Channel Reflectance from AVHRR, 1982-2023 (LCREF-AVHRR)
description: Usage Notes : This is the updated LCREF dataset (v3.2) consists of calibrated AVHRR surface reflectance record for the red and near-infrared channel. Key updates in version 3.2 include: Improved Calibration : Enhanced consistency in calibration methods, addressing technical limitations in version 3.1 including applying more stringent quality filtering and snow masks. Quality Flags : New quality flag layer enables users to identify whether a pixel is derived from observed surface reflectance (QA=0), high-quality gap-filled values (QA=1), lower-quality gap-filled based on the mean seasonal cycle (QA=2), or missing entirely (QA=3). We advice the user to rely only on observed and high-quality gap-filled values for their analyses. Extension to include observations from the year of 2023. The user can choose between LCREF-AVHRR and LCREF-MODIS for the overlapping period from 2001-2023. The two datasets are generally consistent during this overlapping period, although LCREF-MODIS shows a stronger greening trend between 2001-2023. For studies exploring the long-term vegetation dynamics, the user can either use only LCREF-AVHRR or use a blend dataset of LCREF-AVHRR and LCREF-MODIS as a sensitivity test. The LCREF-MODIS v3.2 (2001-2023) is available at 10.5281/zenodo.11657458 . The LCREF-AVHRR dataset was used as the input to generate LCSPP-AVHRR (previously known as LCSIF-AVHRR), and it can also be used to derive temporally consistant records of NDVI, NIRv, kNDVI, and other vegetation indices based on red and NIR surface reflectance variables. The user can access LCSPP products at: LCSPP-AVHRR v3.2 (1982-2000): 10.5281/zenodo.7916850 LCSPP-AVHRR v3.2 (2001-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11906675 LCSPP-MODIS v3.2(2001-2023): 10.5281/zenodo.11658088 A manuscript describing the technical details is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.14987 , which detailed the uses and limitations of the dataset. All data outputs from this study are available at 0.05° spatial resolution and biweekly temporal resolution in NetCDF format. Each month is divided into two files, with the first file “a” representative of the 1 st day to the 15 th day of a month, and the second file “b” representative of the 16 th day to the last day of a month. Abstract: Satellite-observed solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is a powerful proxy for the photosynthetic characteristics of terrestrial ecosystems. Direct SIF observations are primarily limited to the recent decade, impeding their application in detecting long-term dynamics of ecosystem function. In this study, we leverage two surface reflectance bands available both from Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR, 1982-2023) and MODerate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS, 2001-2023). Importantly, we calibrate and orbit-correct the AVHRR bands against their MODIS counterparts during their overlapping period. Using the long-term bias-corrected reflectance data from AVHRR and MODIS, a neural network is trained to produce a Long-term Continuous SIF-informed Photosynthesis Proxy (LCSPP) by emulating Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 SIF, mapping it globally over the 1982-2023 period. Compared with previous SIF-informed photosynthesis proxies, LCSPP has similar skill but can be advantageously extended to the AVHRR period. Further comparison with three widely used vegetation indices (NDVI, kNDVI, NIRv) shows a higher or comparable correlation of LCSPP with satellite SIF and site-level GPP estimates across vegetation types, ensuring a greater capacity for representing long-term photosynthetic activity.

title: High-spatial-resolution (0.0083° × 0.0083°) and long-term (1982 to 2010) monthly gridded wetland CH4 flux product for the Southeastern United States
description: This dataset presents monthly gridded methane emissions from subtropical freshwater wetlands across the Southeastern United States spanning from 1982 to 2010, measured in nmol m-2 s-1. Each grid cell's methane flux prediction was adjusted based on the fractional wetland extent within that cell, utilizing data from the National Wetland Inventory (NWI) and the Wetland Area and Dynamics for Methane Modeling (WAD2M) product. The dataset includes mean monthly fluxes with no adjustment for wetland area (i.e., fluxes assuming hypothetical 100% wetland cover), as well as mean monthly fluxes adjusted for wetland area based on NWI or WAD2M, along with their respective standard deviations of the daily emissions for each month. Data are provided in NetCDF4 format. title: Potential U.S. Production of Liquid Hydrocarbons from Biomass with Addition of Massive External Heat and Hydrogen Inputs Supplementary Dataset
description: This dataset provides a detailed assessment of U.S. biomass production potential and their potential for conversion into liquid hydrocarbon fuels under various market scenarios. It builds on the dataset from the U.S. Department of Energy and U.S. Department of Agriculture's Billion Ton Report 2023 (BTR2023), by incorporating additional sources of carbon: adjusting BTR2023 assumptions and considering more speculative biomass resources. The dataset is organized in the following columns, each resource is assessed based on its abundance within the corresponding market case: Class / Sub-Class / Resource: Categorises biomass resources into classes and sub-classes, based on those found in the BTR2023, with speculative additions appended. Dry Feedstock Mass: On a resource-by-resource basis, quantifies biomass production across five market scenarios, ranging from current production to speculative upper-bound estimates. It includes contributions from agriculture, forestry, and waste sectors, with additional speculative sources from practices such as double cropping, reclaimed land, and macroalgae cultivation. (million dry tons per year) Energy from Burning: Presents the maximum recoverable energy from burning the dry biomass resources. (quadrillion BTU per year) Dry Feedstock Mass Carbon: Presents the percentage carbon content of each biomass resource. (%) Dry Mass Carbon: Presents the (theoretical maximum) absolute carbon content of each resource (available for conversion into liquid hydrocarbons). (billion kg per year) Mass Diesel: Presents the equivalent mass of produced liquid hydrocarbons of diesel, according to the IEA standard. (billion kg) Mol Carbon: Presents the annual available amount of biomass-derived carbon. (mol C per year) Equivalent Diesel Energy Estimate: Estimates the amount of diesel-equivalent fuel that could be produced from available biomass under the assumption of ideal conversion process, and external, low-carbon hydrogen and heat inputs. (million barrel per year & quadrillion BTU per year) Hydrogen Demand: Provides annual hydrogen requirements for each scenario, reflecting the role of hydrogen in removing oxygen from biomass during conversion processes. (billion kg per year) This dataset supports a systematic evaluation of how U.S. biomass resources, when paired with massive external heat and hydrogen inputs, could meet a significant portion of national liquid hydrocarbon demand while achieving net-negative carbon emissions. It is intended for policymakers, researchers, and industry stakeholders to explore sustainable pathways for decarbonizing the transportation and chemical sectors.

title: Global Carbon Budget 2024, surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux of individual global ocean biogeochemical models and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products
description: v2 update: update to data in UoEX-UEPFFNU fCO2-product fix of lat-lon issue in Jena-MLS fCO2-product minor fixes to metadata in fCO2-products The v2 data is used for the final published version of the Global Carbon Budget 2024. ----------------- Surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs) and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products). There are three types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series, (2) one file per GOBM with gridded fields, and (3) one file with the regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2024 (https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2024-519), are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2024 spreadsheet. The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2024 paper (https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2024-519), the river flux adjustment needs to be added to the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2024 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. What is in the files? (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields, for simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. title: Pemanfaatan Media Canva Dalam Pemeblajaran Fisika Untuk Meningkatkan Pengalaman Belajar Peserta Didik Di Kelas XI SMA Negeri 2 Kabupaten Pulau Morotai
description: This research aims to determine how the use of Canva media in physics learning can enhance the learning experience of students in the 11th grade at SMA Negeri 2 Pulau Morotai and to assess the effectiveness of Canva media in improving the learning experience of students in the 11th grade at SMA Negeri 2 Pulau Morotai. The formulation of the research problem is as follows: (1) How is the utilization of Canva media in physics learning to enhance students' learning experiences, (2) How effective is the utilization of Canva media in physics learning to improve students' learning experiences in the XI grade at SMA Negeri 2 Kabupaten Pulau Morotai. The research method used in this study is the qualitative method. The subjects of this research are all students and a physics teacher in the 11th grade at SMA Negeri 2 Pulau Morotai. The research instruments used in this study include observation, interviews, questionnaires, and documentation. The data is then analyzed using percentage formulas and triangulation. From the research results, the observation of students showed 72.20% in the very good category, the observation of teachers showed 100% in the very good category, the teacher questionnaire showed 92.5% in the very feasible category, and the student questionnaire showed 67% in the very good/feasible category. Thus, it can be concluded that the use of the Canva application as an electronic-based learning media is very effective in enhancing the learning experience of students in the XI grade at SMA Negeri 2, Morotai Island Regency

title: Global urban tree LAI/SAI dataset for urban climate modeling
description: This dataset is the first global urban tree LAI/SAI product at a 500-meter resolution, specifically designed for urban climate modeling to simulate the tree's effects in urban environments. It covers the period from 2000 to 2022 and was developed by using a reprocessed MODIS LAI product with a Random Forest model, demonstrating high accuracy. The original product is a netCDF4 file that has been compressed into three tar.gz files: global_15s.tar.gz, global_0.05.tar.gz, and global_0.5.tar.gz, with resolutions of 500 m, 0.05°, and 0.5°, respectively. Each netCDF4 file in the compressed archive is named Global_UrbanTree_LAI_XX_YYYY.nc, where XX represents the resolution and YYYY represents the year. Each file contains monthly LAI/SAI data for that year, with data dimensions of mon x lat x lon. For version 3 of the LAI data, we replaced the meteorological data from WorldClim v2 with WorldClim v2.1 during model training. This version of the dataset has undergone peer review.

title: GLEAM4
description: The Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) is a set of algorithms that separately estimate the different components of terrestrial evaporation (i.e. 'evapotranspiration') based on satellite observations: transpiration (Et), interception loss (Ei), bare-soil evaporation (Eb), snow sublimation (Es) and open-water evaporation (Ew). Intermediate outputs of the model include potential evaporation (Ep), root-zone soil moisture (SMrz), surface soil moisture (SMs), evaporative stress (S), and surface sensible heat flux (H). The rationale of the method is to maximize the recovery of information about evaporation contained in the available data stack of climatic and environmental observations from space.Compared to previous GLEAM versions, GLEAM4 includes the following updates: Hybrid learning of evaporative stress from eddy-covariance and sapflow data Improved representation of interception, including short vegetation Potential evaporation based on Penman's instead of Priestley and Taylor's equation Explicit consideration of plant access to groundwater Higher spatial resolution (0.1°) and longer record (1980–2023) GLEAM4.2a data are accesible via www.gleam.eu .

title: WORCC-PMOD/WRC quality assured aerosol optical depth and Ångström exponent for Ny-Ålesund GAW-PFR station (2002- 2023)
description: Aerosol optical depth (AOD) measurements have been performed within the frame of Global Atmospheric Watch Precision Filter Radiometer (GAW-PFR) network in Ny-Ålesund (79N, 11E) since 2002. The measurements are performed from March to October, with PFR (PrecisionFilterRadiometer) instruments provided by Physikalisch-Meteorologisches Observatorium Davos, World Radiation Center (PMOD/WRC). The solar tracker and infrastructure are provided by provided by NILU (Norsk institutt for luftforskning) in collaboration with the Norwegian Polar Institute. PFR manufactured by PMOD/WRC is a temperature stabilized instrument at 20 o C equipped with four narrow band interference filters with nominal centroid wavelengths 368 nm, 412 nm, 500 nm and 862 nm and bandpass (fullwidth half maximum) 4 nm for 368 nm channel and 5 nm for the rest. The instrument is calibrated on a yearly basis against the WMO-AOD reference (GAWPFR-TRIAD) at PMOD/WRC during the polar winter. The operation is done remotely by PMOD/WRC with the installation and onsite maintenance (cleaning, alignment adjustments) done by personnel of Norwegian Polar Institute and NILU in collaboration with PMOD/WRC. The processing and quality assurance of the data is done following the protocols of World Optical depth Research and Calibration Center (WORCC, PMOD/WRC) (Kazadzis, et. al., 2018), and the data are submitted to the WDCA database (EBAS-NILU) as hourly mean AOD and AE values. This dataset contains high-resolution data (1 min) and daily mean values cloud screened and quality assured since 2002. The provided Ångström exponent is retrieved from the 4 wavelengths. zenodo version 1 (02-May-2002 - 30-Sep-2023), format: mat zenodo version 2 (02-May-2002 - 30-Sep-2023), format: mat and csv Contributions: KN: Calibration, operation, and processing since 2014, WORCC quality assurance protocols, quality assurance of the presented dataset WC: calibration, operation, and processing 2002- 2014 KS: consulting on WORCC quality assurance protocols SK: principal investigator of hosting institute NILU NS: operation and processing 2005- 2012 Acknowledgement: Special thanks to the personnel of the Norwegian Polar Institute at Ny-Ålesund for all the valuable technical support.

PFR manufactured by PMOD/WRC is a temperature stabilized instrument at 20 o C equipped with four narrow band interference filters with nominal centroid wavelengths 368 nm, 412 nm, 500 nm and 862 nm and bandpass (fullwidth half maximum) 4 nm for 368 nm channel and 5 nm for the rest. The instruments are calibrated in yearly bases against the WMO-AOD reference (GAWPFR-TRIAD) at PMOD/WRC during the polar winter. The operation is done remotely by FMI and PMOD/WRC with the installation and onsite maintenance (cleaning, alignment adjustments) done by personnel of FMI and SMN. The processing and quality assurance of the data is done following the protocols of World Optical depth Research and Calibration Center (WORCC, PMOD/WRC) (Kazadzis et al., 2018) and are submitted to the WDCA database (EBAS-NILU) as hourly mean AOD and AE values. This dataset contains high-resolution data (1 min) and daily mean values of cloud screened and quality assured since 2005. description: This record consists of the shorelines and their derived products, elevation transects and environmental data used for the Cryosphere preprint: Multiple modes of shoreline change along the Alaskan Beaufort Sea observed using ICESat-2 altimetry and satellite imagery . It also includes cross-shore transects used to project ICESat-2-derived changes into the local shoreline-perpindicular direction. Planet_shorelines contains shorelines drived from 3m multispectral imagery from Planet Labs (Planet Team, 2024) as well as their derivatiev products. description: These datasets were created using a machine learning algorithm that reduces noise and artifacts in the original noisy satellite data product, solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) from the Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment 2 (GOME-2) instruments on the European operational Meteorological Satellites A and B (METOP-A and METOP-B). Noise reduction is important because SIF retrievals are typically noisy, and the noise limits their ability to be used for diagnosing plant health and productivity. Our results show substantial improvement in SIF retrievals that may lead to new applications. However, users should be aware that there could be some biases with respect to the original data sets so the data should be used with caution. These data sets were not designed to be used in trend studies as the calibration could contain errors.

title: Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland
description: Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - " Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland" Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186 Methods - CEA energy demand model setup To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems. The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al. [24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al. [24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters. Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al. [24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand: dE/dt = Q Sun + Q Heat + Q Lamp - Q Vent - Q Latent - Q Con – Q FIR – Q cool (J m -2 s -1 = W m -2 ) dMW/dt = W Trans + W Evap + W Hum - W Cond - W Vent - W Dehum (kg {water vapor} m -2 s -1 ) dE/dt = net change of energy Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space dMW/dt = net change of water mass W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]: Energy Use lights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * η lights *10 -6 (MJ m -2 day -1 ) η lights = electrical efficacy The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m -2 day -1 ). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m -2 s -1 ) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m -2 day -1 . The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m -2 day -1 ) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*1 6 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m -2 day -1 ) for each month of 2020. While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al. [24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg -1 ) for each crop and CEA system. The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems. CEA energy demand simulation inputs The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m 2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al. [24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day -1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included. A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J -1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4). ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m -2 ), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg -1 ) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg -1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2. Global crop area, yield, and production We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km -2 ) and crop harvest area (ha km -2 ) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha -1 ) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha -1 ), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4. PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km -2 ) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell. To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m -2 ) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4. For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7. This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9. Yield gap analysis The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset. CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered . Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process. Electricity grid constraints The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10. Aridity Index The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al. (52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11. Model assumption sensitivity A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%. For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands. Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges. title: Global Pasture Watch - Annual maps of potential land for livestock production at 1-km for 2000–2022 (including production systems)
description: Maps produced by per-pixel integration of cultivated and natural/semi-natural grassland ( Parente et al., 2024 ) and cropland extent ( Potapov, et al., 2022 ) considering fractions of land use inside 1 km2 grid cell. The annual time series (2000-2022) of integrated maps provided 1 km spatial resolution ranging from 1–100%, with potential land used for livestock production. title: Distribution and Characteristics of Lightning-Ignited Wildfires in Boreal Forests - the BoLtFire database
description: This repository holds a dataset of lightning-ignited wildfires across the boreal biome. The BoLtFire dataset covers the period 2012 to 2022 and encompasses 6,902 fires - 4,201 in Eurasia and 2,701 in North America. The layers included in this dataset are: FireID, StartDate, EndDate, FireYdear, AreaHa (burned area), ClassSize, BiomeName, EcoBiome, EcoName, EcoID, Realm, LCDN (Land cover number), LCName (land cover name), Country, Continent, HoldoverD (days), HoldoverRD (holdover rounded), IgnLat (Ignition location Latitude), IgnLong (Ignition Location Longitude), DisPol (Distance of the ignition location to the fire perimeter if it is located outside the polygon), and PerCheck (designates if the ignition location is within the fire perimeter or oustide the perimeter). The datasets are available per continent (North America, Europe, and Asia) as shapefiles. The spatial reference system is Global LANd Cover mapping and Estimation (GLANCE) Grids - Version 01 CRS. *Please note: Versions 1 and 2 are missing LIW from Canada between 2021-2022.

De-trending has been applied to all parameters.
