title: Pre-event composite of the EarthDEM Strips for the 2026-08-26 Rasuwa (Langtang Lirung) ice-rock avalanche, Nepal
description: This record provides pre-event digital elevation model (DEM) composites for the area affected by the 2026-08-26 ice-rock avalanche on the north flank of Langtang Lirung, Rasuwa District, Nepal, and its downstream flood along the Chhochen Khola, Lhende Khola, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The composites are the pre-event reference surface for the post-event DEMs of this event (Shean, 2026a; Shean and Bhushan, 2026a, 2026b). The composites combine 109 EarthDEM strip DEMs, version 4.1 (Porter et al., 2024), from WorldView-1/2/3 and GeoEye-1 in-track stereo images acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. Each strip was co-registered by translation on stable ground, and the co-registered stack was tied to ICESat-2. Two sets are provided. The 2 m set is clipped to the affected corridor and has 1032 km2 of valid data. The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source, runout and upper corridor, with 1721 km2 of valid data. Both sets include median and weighted-mean DEMs, per-pixel strip count and normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD), hillshades, an ordered temporal layer set and a strip footprint index. The ordered layers are earliest- and latest-strip-on-top DEMs with source-strip and acquisition-date maps, their elevation difference and the apparent rate. No individual strip DEMs and no source imagery are distributed. All products are cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs in EPSG:32645 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 45N) with heights above the WGS 84 ellipsoid. License: CC BY-NC 4.0. DEMs provided by the Polar Geospatial Center under NSF-OPP awards 1043681, 1559691, 1542736, 1810976, and 2129685. Original Level-1B Imagery © 2009-2024 Vantor. 1. Products Nodata is -9999 in elevation, date, change, NMAD and count layers, 0 in hillshade layers and -1 in index layers. NMAD layers are nodata where fewer than two strips overlap. 00_*.png files are quick-look figures. 1.1 Corridor 2 m composite ( earthdem_corridor_2m.zip : earthdem_corridor_2m_ _v1.0.tif ) The 2 m set is clipped to the affected-corridor polygon plus a 500 m buffer, and the strips were clipped before compositing. The 88 contributing strips were acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. The median of date_median is about 2016.7, and the median of date_wmean is about 2017.5. layer description wmean weighted-mean composite DEM (edge-distance weights) -- recommended surface for relief and as a co-registration reference median per-pixel median DEM count , nmad per-pixel strip count and NMAD (m) wmean_hs , median_hs multidirectional hillshades first , last earliest- and latest-strip-on-top DEMs, with first_hs , last_hs index_first , index_last index of the strip supplying each first / last pixel, into earthdem_corridor_2m_strip_order_v1.0.csv (0 = oldest) date_first , date_last , dt_yr acquisition date (decimal year) of the first / last pixel, and dt_yr = date_last minus date_first (decimal years) date_median , date_wmean acquisition date of the strip nearest the median value, and the weight-averaged acquisition date of the wmean dh_m elevation difference last minus first (m), where the two dates differ dhdt_myr apparent rate dh_m / dt_yr (m/yr), only where dt_yr is at least 2 years Also in the zip: earthdem_corridor_2m_strip_order_v1.0.csv : the strips in the product, oldest first. earthdem_strip_index_v1.geojson : footprints, acquisition dates and co-registration shifts of the 224 strips considered. in_mosaic marks the 208 strips in the co-registered stack. The shifts exclude the common tie to ICESat-2 (dE +0.07 m, dN -2.44 m, dU -0.10 m) that was applied to every strip. earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_stats_v1.0.json : coverage and stable-ground statistics of dh_m and dhdt_myr . 00_earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_qa_v1.0.png : quick-look figure of the ordered layers. 1.2 Source-rectangle 8 m composite ( earthdem_source_8m.zip : earthdem_source_8m_ _v1.0.tif ) The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source area, runout and upper corridor, and is not clipped to the corridor. The rectangle is the same as in the companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c). The 8 m composite combines 66 co-registered strips acquired 2012-01-15 to 2023-12-02. The median of date_median is about 2016.0, and the median of date_wmean is about 2016.5. The layers and sidecar files are the same as in the 2 m set (section 1.1). In this set the wmean has smoother relief across strip boundaries, and the median has a slightly lower NMAD against ICESat-2 (0.90 m vs 0.94 m). 1.3 Validation ( validation_v1.0.zip ) The validation zip holds the ICESat-2 comparison for each DEM: a summary table, and a figure and a statistics file per product (section 3). 2. Methods Each strip was co-registered by translation in three passes. The first pass used the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM (European Space Agency and Airbus, 2022), converted to ellipsoid heights, as the reference. The second and third passes used the median of the aligned stack. Each pass solved the horizontal offset with the method of Nuth and Kääb (2011) on exposed stable ground with slopes of 1-45 degrees. Stable ground is the ESA WorldCover 2021 bare, grass, shrub, moss and cropland classes, excluding Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) 6.0 glaciers with a 100 m buffer. Before each solve, differences more than 100 m from the median difference and outliers beyond 3 NMAD were removed. The vertical offset is the median residual on stable ground. A refit was accepted only where it reduced the residual aspect signature. The strips were composited with the NASA Ames Stereo Pipeline dem_mosaic tool (Beyer et al., 2018). SETSM (Noh and Howat, 2015) is the EarthDEM stereo software. The 2 m composites use only stereo-matched pixels. Pixels that SETSM interpolated were masked along with the strip bitmask, and they are about 2 % of the valid strip area. The 8 m composites apply the bitmask only. GLO-30 was used only as the first-pass registration reference. No GLO-30 values enter any product, and voids are left as nodata. Before compositing, obvious blunders of up to hundreds of meters were removed from the strips over the source area. The 2019 Pléiades DEM (Berthier, 2026) and other independent DEMs served as the reference there. Coordinates are ITRF2020 at epoch 2022.27, the median date of the ICESat-2 data. The composite surfaces mostly date from about 2016, and plate motion of about 4 cm/yr toward the northeast moves the area about 0.25 m between 2016 and 2022. The 2015-04-25 Gorkha earthquake displaced the area by about 1.5 m horizontally, partway through the strip archive. Each strip was co-registered separately, so strips from before and after the earthquake are aligned to the same stack median. 3. Accuracy The ICESat-2 reference elevations are 10 m segment fits to all ATL03 photons, limited to exposed stable terrain. Against these segments, the four DEMs have median differences of -0.02 to +0.02 m and NMAD of 0.81 to 0.94 m. The 2 m DEMs overlap 43,031 segments and the 8 m DEMs overlap 72,773. Per-product statistics and figures are in validation_v1.0.zip . The figures include a diagnostic Nuth and Kääb (2011) horizontal fit. 4. Known issues The DEMs have voids on snow, shadow and glacier surfaces. median and wmean combine strips acquired 2009-2024, so on glacier, snow and vegetated surfaces they do not represent a single date; date_median and date_wmean give the approximate date of each pixel. first and last take each pixel from a single strip, identified in index_first / index_last and dated in date_first / date_last . The first and last mosaics can have larger errors and more blunders than median and wmean . The latest strip is from 2024-01-05. Along the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi, differences against post-event DEMs include changes from the separate 2025-07-08 Lhende Khola flood as well as the 2026-08-26 event. Blunders were removed only over the source area, inside the 2019 Pléiades footprint (section 2). Elsewhere, isolated blunders can remain where few strips overlap. Check the count and nmad layers before interpreting a large elevation change. The companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c) is co-registered to the same frame; the 8 m medians of the two records agree on stable ground to 0.8 m NMAD. 5. title: AquaEdge
description: Raw and processed sensor, weather, and satellite datasets, plus trained model weights, from the AquaEdge project — estimating root-zone soil moisture/temperature at four depths (S1T-S4T) for agricultural fields in Morocco by fusing Pycno in-situ soil probes, Open-Meteo/ERA5 weather, Sentinel-1/2 satellite imagery, and SoilGrids soil texture. Companion code, notebooks, and pipelines are at the linked GitHub repository.

title: Spatial counterfactual geometry shapes coal-mine impact assessments: research data and analysis code
description: Research data and analysis code supporting the manuscript: “Spatial counterfactual geometry shapes coal-mine impact assessments” This repository contains the derived mine-level datasets, matching outputs, satellite extraction outputs, footprint-geometry sensitivity analyses, formal geometry tests, biomass analyses, recovery-chronology analyses, Earth Engine scripts, statistical analysis code, data dictionaries and provenance documentation used to produce the reported results. The study evaluates how spatial counterfactual geometry affects satellite-derived environmental contrasts between matched surface and underground coal mines. The primary outcomes are land-surface temperature (LST), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and woody above-ground biomass (AGB). The repository includes the complete reproducibility archive corresponding to version 1.0.0 of the analysis. Source datasets are third-party resources and remain subject to their original provider terms. These include the Global Coal Mine Tracker, Landsat Collection 2, GLC_FCS30D and the ESA Climate Change Initiative Biomass product. This repository is intended to support reproducibility, peer review and subsequent reuse of the derived analysis materials.

title: AquaEdge
description: Raw and processed sensor, weather, and satellite datasets, plus trained model weights, from the AquaEdge project — estimating root-zone soil moisture/temperature at four depths (S1T-S4T) for agricultural fields in Morocco by fusing Pycno in-situ soil probes, Open-Meteo/ERA5 weather, Sentinel-1/2 satellite imagery, and SoilGrids soil texture. title: Pléiades (CNES) DEMs and elevation change map for the 5 August 2025 Dharali disaster
description: =========================== Introduction On 5 August 2025, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Dharali and Harshil valleys of Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, India We provide here pre-event and post-even Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of this area from Pléiades stereo-pairs acquired on the 7 October 2017 and 15 October 2025. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and the CIEST² initiative from CNES/Formaterre (https://www.poleterresolide.fr/ciest-2-nouvelle-generation-2/). We share here the Pléiades DEMs and the elevation change maps derived from these images. The collection includes: A pre-event DEM and a preview 2017-10-07_SGM_4m_align.tif A post-event DEM and a preview 2025-10-15_SGM_4m_align.tif One grid of elevation change from 2017 to 2025 and a preview 2025-10-15_SGM_4m_align-2017-10-07_SGM_4m_align_dh_after_correction.tif =========================== Methods The Pléiades stereo-images were processed using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding a DEM in 4x4 m GSD. The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then interpolated using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020) DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean’s dem_align implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). The elevation change grid is calculated using the method of the Pléiades Glacier Observatory (Berthier et al., 2024) Berthier, E., Lebreton, J., Fontannaz, D., Hosford, S., Belart, J. title: Unprecedented warming and increased herbivory drive collapse of Japan's kelp forests
description: Kelp forests underpin entire ecosystems and provide key services for human society, yet are threatened by anthropogenic stressors, most notably ocean warming and overgrazing. While Japanese kelp forests have substantial historical and cultural value, responses to recent environmental change remain poorly resolved. Here, we assessed how recent Kuroshio-associated warming and increased herbivory were linked to kelp forest collapse across approximately 200 km of the Izu Peninsula (central-eastern Japan). We combined 40 years of in situ kelp biomass (1980–2024) and 12–14 years of canopy-cover records (2009–2025) with satellite-derived sea-surface temperature and marine heatwave metrics. Herbivorous fish assemblages and bite rates were surveyed monthly (2021–2022) across reefs spanning healthy, mosaic, and barren states. Laboratory experiments quantified lethal and sub-lethal thermal thresholds of juvenile Ecklonia cava using temperature-ramping (20–33 °C) and growth trials (22 vs 28 °C). Spatial analyses compared thermal-threshold exceedance and seasonal grazing-window expansion with observed canopy loss, evaluating whether warming and herbivory were consistent with the spatial extent of decline. Warming along the Izu coast intensified during the recent Kuroshio Large Meander, increasing from 0.15 °C decade-1 (1982–2016) to 2.98 °C decade -1 (2017–2024), with cumulative marine heatwave intensity rising from 2.34 to 63.22 °C·day decade -1 . Over the same period, canopy-forming E. cava cover fell from ~75% to zero, and peak biomass declined from 2.37 kg DW.m⁻² to zero, indicating local extirpation and likely regional functional loss. Laboratory assays showed rapid physiological decline above 29.5 °C and mortality at 32–33 °C; temperatures exceeded during summer 2023/2024. The grazing season by warm-adapted herbivorous fishes expanded by up to 86 days, amplifying kelp loss across heat-stressed reefs. Together, extreme thermal stress and expanded herbivory were strongly associated with a shift from kelp forests to barren reefs, highlighting how physiological stress and trophic processes can contribute to rapid kelp loss in warming boundary-current systems.

title: Uranium comminution ages and denudation rates for quartz-poor Sumatran catchments, with global ¹⁰Be comparison
description: This dataset contains the supporting tables for the manuscript: "Uranium Comminution Ages as a Denudation Chronometer in Tectonically Active Orogens" It contains: 1. Supplementary Note S1 – Methodology Detailed description of the sequential leaching protocol for detrital uranium isolation, total digestion and uranium purification, MC‑ICP‑MS measurement procedures, determination of the α‑recoil loss fraction (fα), and construction of the flux‑weighted effective initial ratio (A0), including piecewise‑linear integration and Excel implementation. 2. Supplementary Note S2 – Supporting tables Contains two tables: Table 1 Sample details, comminution ages, and denudation rates for detrital sediments from the Asahan and Batang Toru rivers (Sumatra). Comminution ages were calculated under the conventional secular-equilibrium assumption ( A ₀ = 1) and with the flux-weighted effective initial ratio ( A ₀ᵉᶠᶠ). Denudation rates were derived via the steady-state relation ε = h / t com using SoilGrids regolith thicknesses. Table 2 Global comparison of uranium-series comminution-age-derived denudation rates with independent in-situ ¹⁰Be denudation rates. For each catchment, the comminution age is calculated first under the conventional A ₀ = 1 assumption, and then with a representative non-equilibrium A ₀ (0.98–0.99), consistent with the bedrock ²³⁴U depletion observed in active orogens. The ¹⁰Be denudation rate serves as the independent reference.

title: CitiesGOER: Globally Observed Environmental Data for 52,602 Cities with a Population ≥ 5000
description: CitiesGOER is a database that provides environmental data for 52,602 cities and 48 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 2 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927 . Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species . Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914 . CitiesGOER was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023 ) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. The identities and coordinates of cities were sourced from a data set with information for cities with a population size larger than 1000 that was created by Opendatasoft and made available from https://public.opendatasoft.com/explore/dataset/geonames-all-cities-with-a-population-1000/table/?disjunctive.cou_name_en&sort=name . The data was downloaded on 22-JULY-2023 and afterwards filtered for cities with a population of 5000 or above. Cities where information on the country was missing were removed. The coordinates of cities were used to extract the environmental data via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.6-47) in the R 4.2.1 environment . Version 2023.08 provided median values from 23 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 and from 18 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0, both for the 2050s (2041-2060). Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1 ). Version 2023.09 used similar methods as for previous versions to provide median values from 13 GCMs for the 2090s (2081-2100) for SSP 5-8.5. The locations of the 52,602 cities are mapped in one of the series available from the TreeGOER Global Zones atlas that can be obtained from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8252756 . Version 2024.10 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Holdridge Life Zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1920), contemporary (1979-2013) and future (2061-2080; separately for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) climates inferred from global raster layers that are available for download from DRYAD and were created for the following article: Elsen et al. 2022. Accelerated shifts in terrestrial life zones under rapid climate change. Global Change Biology , 28, 918–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15962 . Version 2024.10 further includes Holdridge Life Zones for the climates that were available from the previous versions, calculating biotemperatures and life zones with similar methods as used by Holdridge ( 1947 ; 1967 ) and Elsen et al. ( 2022 ) (for future climates, median values were determined first for monthly maximum and minimum temperatures across GCMs ). The distributions of the 48,129 species documented in TreeGOER across the Holdridge Life Zones are given in this Zenodo archive: https://zenodo.org/records/14020914 . Version 2024.11 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Köppen-Geiger climate zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1930, 1931-1960, 1961-1990) and future (2041-2070 and 2071-2099) climates, with for the future climates seven scenarios each (SSP 1-1.9, SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 3-7.0, SSP 4-3.4, SSP 4-6.0 and SSP 5-8.5). This data set was created from 30 arc-second raster layers available via: Beck, H.E., McVicar, T.R., Vergopolan, N. et al. High-resolution (1 km) Köppen-Geiger maps for 1901–2099 based on constrained CMIP6 projections. Sci Data 10, 724 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02549-6 Version 2025.03 includes extra columns for the baseline, 2050s and 2090s datasets that partially correspond to climate zones used in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database. One of these zones are the Whittaker biome types , available as a polygon from the plotbiomes package (see also here ). Whittaker biome types were extracted with similar R scripts as described by Kindt 2025 (these were also used to calculate environmental ranges of TreeGOER species, as archived here ). Version 2025.03 further includes information for the baseline climate on the steady state water table depth, obtained from a 30 arc-seconds raster layer calculated by the GLOBGM v1.0 model (Verkaik et al. 2024 ). Also included was the elevation, obtained from the same WorldClim 2.1 raster layer used to prepare TreeGOER. Version 2026.04 includes a new Excel workbook that provides the nearest urban centre centroid from the Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database ( UCDB R2024A, reference epoch 2025 , World Mollweide, EPSG:54009, 1km; https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/datasets.php ; Melchiori et al. 2024 ). Different searches were done for the nearest urban centre centroid, searching among all centres, among all centres with a 2025 population size ≥ 100,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 500,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 1 million, among all centres with a population size ≥ 5 million and among all centres with a population size ≥ 10 million. Distances between city locations from CitiesGOER and urban centre centroids were calculated in R via geosphere::distGeo (version 1.5-20; Hijmans 2024 ). Version 2026.09 includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_GAIPED) that provide the locations of cities in Climatic Moisture Index zones ( https://zenodo.org/records/21808912 ) calculated via the Potential Evapotranspiration ( ET 0 ) obtained from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database (GAIPED; Zomer et al. 2022 ). Version 2026.09 also includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_Global Climate Zones_Audebert) that provides the locations of cities in Global Climate Zones derived via the Mean Annual Biotemperature and the Inverted Aridity Index ( https://zenodo.org/records/21901225 ), using the decision framework developed by Audebert et al. ( 2026 ). As an alternative to CitiesGOER, the ClimateForecasts database ( https://zenodo.org/records/10776414 ) documents the environmental conditions at the locations of 15,504 weather stations. ClimateForecasts was integrated in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (see Kindt et al. 2023 ). When using CitiesGOER in your work, cite this depository and the following: Fick, S. E., & Hijmans, R. J. (2017). WorldClim 2: New 1‐km spatial resolution climate surfaces for global land areas. title: Data and code for "Physiological costs of drought resistance shape vegetation recovery"
description: This Zenodo record contains the analysis-ready data and Python scripts supporting the manuscript "Physiological costs of drought resistance shape vegetation recovery". The study examines the relationships between the physiological costs of drought resistance and vegetation recovery using satellite observations, meteorological datasets, and FLUXNET measurements during 2018-2023. The deposited data include event-level and model-ready tables for the main analysis, the alternative-meteorology analysis, and the FLUXNET site-level evaluation. The deposited code contains the Python scripts used for the analyses and figure generation reported in the manuscript. The original TROPOSIF, MODIS LAI, ERA5-Land, GLEAM, MERRA-2, and FLUXNET datasets are not redistributed in this record and should be obtained from the original providers identified in the manuscript’s Data availability statement.

title: ClimateForecasts: Globally Observed Environmental Data for 15,504 Weather Station Locations
description: ClimateForecasts is a database that provides environmental data for 15,504 weather station locations and 49 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 3 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927 . Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species . Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914 . A similar extraction process was used for the CitiesGOER database that is also available from Zenodo via https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.8175429 . ClimateForecasts (as the CitiesGOER) was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023 ) or EcoregionsTreeFinder (Kindt & Pedercini 2025 ) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. One example of combining data from these different sets in the R statistical environment is available from this Rpub: https://rpubs.com/Roeland-KINDT/1114902 . The identities including the geographical coordinates of weather stations were sourced from Meteostat , specifically by downloading (17-FEB-2024) the ‘lite dump’ data set with information for active weather stations only. Two weather stations where the country could not be determined from the ISO 3166-1 code of ‘XA’ were removed. If weather stations had the same name, but occurred in different ISO 3166-2 regions, this region code was added to the name of the weather station between square brackets. Afterwards duplicates (weather stations of the same name and region) were manually removed. Bioclimatic variables for future climates correspond to the median values from 24 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 for the 2050s (2041-2060), from 21 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0 for the 2050s and from 13 GCMs for SSP 5-8.5 for the 2090s. Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1 ). Maps were added in version 2024.03 where locations of weather stations were shown on a map of the Climatic Moisture Index (CMI). These maps were created by a similar process as in the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas from the environmental raster layers used to create the TreeGOER via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.7-46) in the R 4.2.1 environment . Added country boundaries were obtained from Natural Earth as Admin 0 – countries vector layers (version 5.1.1). Also added after obtaining them from Natural Earth were Admin 0 – Breakaway, Disputed areas (version 5.1.0, coloured yellow in the atlas) and Roads (version 5.0.0, coloured red in the atlas). For countries where the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database included subnational levels, boundaries were added and depicted as dot-dash lines. These subnational levels correspond to level 3 boundaries in the World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions. These were obtained from https://github.com/tdwg/wgsrpd . Check Brummit 2001 for details such as the maps shown at the end of this document. Maps for version 2024.07 modified the dimensions of the sheets to those used in version 2024.06 of the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas . Another modification was the inclusion of Natural Earth boundaries for Lakes (version 5.0.0, coloured darkblue in the atlas). Version 2024.10 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Holdridge Life Zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1920), contemporary (1979-2013) and future (2061-2080; separately for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) that are available for download from DRYAD and were created for the following article: Elsen et al. 2022. Accelerated shifts in terrestrial life zones under rapid climate change. Global Change Biology , 28, 918–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15962 . Version 2024.10 further includes Holdridge Life Zones for the climates available from the previously included climates, calculating biotemperatures and life zones with similar methods as used by Holdridge ( 1947 ; 1967 ) and Elsen et al. ( 2022 ) (for future climates, median values were determined first for monthly maximum and minimum temperatures across GCMs ). The distributions of the 48,129 species documented in TreeGOER across the Holdridge Life Zones are given in this Zenodo archive: https://zenodo.org/records/14020914 . Version 2024.11 includes a new data set that documents the location of the weather stations in Köppen-Geiger climate zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1930, 1931-1960, 1961-1990) and future (2041-2070 and 2071-2099) climates, with for the future climates seven scenarios each (SSP 1-1.9, SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 3-7.0, SSP 4-3.4, SSP 4-6.0 and SSP 5-8.5). This data set was created from raster layers available via: Beck, H.E., McVicar, T.R., Vergopolan, N. et al. High-resolution (1 km) Köppen-Geiger maps for 1901–2099 based on constrained CMIP6 projections. Sci Data 10, 724 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02549-6 . Version 2025.03 includes extra columns for the baseline, 2050s and 2090s datasets that partially correspond to climate zones used in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database. One of these zones are the Whittaker biome types , available as a polygon from the plotbiomes package (see also here ). Whittaker biome types were extracted with similar R scripts as described by Kindt 2025 (these were also used to calculate environmental ranges of TreeGOER species, as archived here ). Version 2025.03 further includes information for the baseline climate on the steady state water table depth, obtained from a 30 arc-seconds raster layer calculated by the GLOBGM v1.0 model (Verkaik et al. 2024 ). Version 2026.04 includes a new Excel workbook that provides the nearest urban centre centroid from the Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database ( UCDB R2024A, reference epoch 2025 , World Mollweide, EPSG:54009, 1km; https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/datasets.php ; Melchiori et al. 2024 ). Different searches were done for the nearest urban centre centroid, searching among all centres, among all centres with a 2025 population size ≥ 100,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 500,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 1 million, among all centres with a population size ≥ 5 million and among all centres with a population size ≥ 10 million. This distance was calculated in R via geosphere::distGeo (version 1.5-20; Hijmans 2024 ). Version 2026.09 includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_GAIPED) that provide the locations of cities in Climatic Moisture Index zones ( https://zenodo.org/records/21808912 ) calculated via the Potential Evapotranspiration ( ET 0 ) obtained from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database (GAIPED; Zomer et al. 2022 ). Version 2026.09 also includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_Global Climate Zones_Audebert) that provides the locations of cities in Global Climate Zones derived via the Mean Annual Biotemperature and the Inverted Aridity Index ( https://zenodo.org/records/21901225 ), using the decision framework developed by Audebert et al. title: Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset
description: The Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset provides estimates of annual sediment volume and reservoir sedimentation rate (RSR) for 34,372 reservoirs worldwide. The dataset was developed using the Integrated Reservoir Sedimentation Prediction (IRSP) framework, which integrates machine learning with climatic, geomorphic, hydrological, and reservoir-specific predictors. For each reservoir, the dataset provides the predicted annual sediment volume, its prediction variability quantified by the standard deviation (SD) across spatial cross-validation folds, and the RSR, defined as the ratio of annual sediment volume to initial reservoir storage capacity. Each reservoir is linked to the Global Dam Watch (GDW) v1.0 dataset through its corresponding GDW identifier.

title: Dataset and Analysis Code Supporting "Asymmetric Impacts of Supply- and Demand-Driven Flash Droughts on Leaf Senescence"
description: README This repository contains the processed datasets and R scripts supporting the manuscript entitled “Asymmetric impacts of supply- and demand-driven flash droughts on leaf senescence.” The study investigates the asymmetric effects of supply-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with precipitation deficits, and demand-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with enhanced atmospheric evaporative demand, on vegetation leaf senescence across the Northern Hemisphere during 2001–2024. The repository contains the processed datasets supporting the analyses and visualizations. Owing to repository file-size constraints, some processed datasets are provided as ZIP archives. Compression does not alter the data content, and the files should be extracted before use. Phenology_North_poly.csv contains annual satellite-derived vegetation phenological metrics for each grid cell across the Northern Hemisphere and was used for phenological quality control and anomaly calculation. all_GS_FD_years.csv contains the grid-year combinations with at least one FD overlapping the growing season and was used to identify non-FD years for calculating the phenological baseline. dEOS_poly.csv contains the resulting LSD anomalies derived from the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). The term “EOS” used in the file name and scripts denotes the end-of-season phenological metric and corresponds to the leaf senescence date (LSD) used in the manuscript. phenology_poly_pentad.csv records the long-term mean timing of the start, peak, and end of the growing season, expressed as the corresponding 8-day periods for each grid cell. SMrz_drought_events.csv contains the flash drought events identified from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles using 01_FD_detection.R , including the original P1–P4 event timing indices, minimum soil-moisture percentile, onset rate, and cumulative severity. SMrz_drought_events_mean_environment_anomaly.csv contains flash drought events overlapping the growing season and their mean environmental anomalies calculated over the complete, untruncated P1–P4 event periods. These variables were used to characterize the hydroclimatic conditions of the events and as inputs for their subsequent classification into supply- and demand-driven flash droughts. final_FD_events.csv is the final analytical dataset and contains 1,141,551 event records. It retains the original, untruncated P1–P4 indices and was constructed by (1) retaining FD events that overlapped the growing season, (2) retaining phenological observations within the grid-specific median ± 2.5 median absolute deviations and grid cells with an interannual LSD standard deviation below 30 days, (3) retaining only grid-year combinations with a single FD overlapping the growing season, and (4) excluding non-target land-cover and biome classes, including croplands, and records with predictor values outside their respective 1st–99th percentile ranges. This dataset was used in the subsequent LSD-response, structural equation modeling, random forest, SHAP, and model-improvement analyses. Meanenv_EarlyGS_anomaly.csv and Meanenv_LateGS_anomaly.csv contain environmental anomalies during the early and late growing seasons, respectively, while Additional_data.csv provides the additional background and vegetation variables used to construct the predictor set for the RF, SHAP, and related analyses. The background spatial datasets include MODIS_IGBP0.1deg_type.csv , which contains MODIS International Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land-cover classifications at a spatial resolution of 0.1°; phe_poly_biome.csv , which contains biome classifications based on the World Wildlife Fund terrestrial ecoregions; and Background_MAP.csv and Background_MAT.csv , which contain mean annual precipitation and mean annual temperature, respectively. worldmap.zip contains the world map and national boundary files used for spatial visualization. The datasets supporting the response and modeling analyses include dEOSsig_supply_poly.csv and dEOSsig_demand_poly.csv , which contain the statistical significance of LSD responses to supply- and demand-driven flash droughts, respectively. RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_EVI.csv and RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_SIF.csv contain the random forest model outputs used to evaluate and compare the simulated LSD responses based on EVI and SIF. FD_ET_series.csv contains the time series of evapotranspiration anomalies before and after flash drought onset. The SHAP outputs from the random forest models are provided in shap_mat_EVI_demand.rds , shap_mat_SIF_demand.rds , shap_mat_EVI_supply.rds , and shap_mat_SIF_supply.rds . These files contain the SHAP values used to quantify and visualize the contributions of climatic, biological, and flash-drought-related variables to the modeled LSD responses under the two flash drought types. The accompanying R scripts perform the principal data processing, statistical analyses, and visualization procedures used in the study. 01_FD_detection.R identifies flash drought events from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles, calculates their characteristics, and applies the prescribed duration criterion of 4–12 consecutive 8-day periods. 02_phenology_extraction.R extracts vegetation phenological metrics from satellite-derived EVI and SIF time series. 03_FD_environment_anomaly.R retains FD events that overlap the growing season without modifying their original P1–P4 indices and calculates environmental anomalies over their complete event periods. 04_phenology_anomaly_nonFD_baseline.R calculates phenological anomalies relative to years without growing-season FDs and applies the grid-specific phenological quality-control and single-event grid-year criteria. 05_final_FD_event_filtering.R generates the final analytical dataset from the records processed in the preceding steps and applies the land-cover, biome, and predictor percentile filters. 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R conducts random forest modeling and SHAP analysis to identify the climatic and biotic controls of leaf senescence responses. 07_SEM_analysis.R performs structural equation modeling to examine the pathways through which the two flash drought types regulate leaf senescence. 08_phenology_response_significance.R evaluates the significance of phenological responses to flash droughts. 09_visualization_analysis.R generates the principal figures and statistical visualizations, and 10_visualization_SHAP_analysis.R produces the SHAP importance and dependence plots. The original satellite, reanalysis, and ancillary datasets are not redistributed in this repository, except for the processed background and boundary data used for visualization. The original root-zone soil-moisture percentile series and processed LAI time series are not redistributed because of their large file sizes; their data sources and processing procedures are documented in the manuscript and accompanying code. The original datasets are publicly available from their respective data providers, as documented in the associated manuscript. The deposited processed datasets and scripts provide the materials needed to evaluate the reported results and reproduce the principal analyses and visualizations. Code execution and software environment All scripts were developed and tested using R version 4.5.2 in RStudio under Windows. No GPU or other non-standard hardware is required for most analyses. Before running the scripts, users should replace the placeholder input, output, and figure paths at the beginning of each script with valid local paths. The scripts can then be executed directly in RStudio. The scripts are numbered according to their recommended execution order. Scripts 01_FD_detection.R – 05_final_FD_event_filtering.R perform FD detection, phenological extraction, anomaly calculation, and construction of the final analytical dataset. Scripts 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R – 08_phenology_response_significance.R perform the RF–SHAP, SEM, and significance analyses, respectively. The final visualization scripts generate the figures reported in the manuscript. The deposited processed datasets allow the principal statistical analyses and figures to be reproduced without rerunning the complete processing chain from the original satellite and reanalysis data. Using the prepared input datasets, all scripts except 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R typically complete within several minutes, although runtime depends on computer performance and data-transfer speed. The complete random forest and SHAP workflow in 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R was run on a multicore server and required approximately four days. This script calculates one response–FD-type SHAP combination per run and should be executed for the four combinations of EVI/SIF and supply-/demand-driven FDs to regenerate all deposited SHAP objects. title: Dataset for "Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan, Atmos. Environ."
description: This dataset is for “Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan” by Wei et al. in Atmospheric Environment. The contents are described in the sheet “Readme” of the Excel file named “Dataset_cw260904.xlsx”. The dataset contains the data used in the manuscript, including average fluorescence spectra, fluorescence indices, atmospheric fluorescence volumes, normalized fluorescence volumes, and PARAFAC components of water-soluble organic matter (WSOM) in atmospheric aerosol samples collected at forest, remote, and urban sites in Japan. The dataset also includes the correlations of the atmospheric fluorescence volumes of the PARAFAC components with the concentrations of water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) and meteorological parameters. The dataset further provides fluorescence indices and atmospheric fluorescence volumes for three subfractions of WSOM obtained from aerosol and rainwater samples collected in Nagoya. The excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectra of WSOM in aqueous extracts were measured using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (FP-6600, JASCO) with a 1-cm path length quartz cell. The ranges of the excitation and emission wavelengths were 235-500 nm and 300-600 nm, respectively. The drEEM toolbox for MATLAB was used to preprocess the EEMs and to perform parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis. The concentrations of WSOC and water-soluble inorganic ions were measured using a total organic carbon analyzer and ion chromatography, respectively. The dataset was obtained in the study conducted under JSPS KAKENHI (JP26281007, JP23H00515, and JP19KK0265); ArCS II (JPMXD1420318865); and ERDF from ERCA (JPMEERF20232001). Other acknowledgments are provided in the associated manuscript.

title: Analysis-derived datasets for: "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins"
description: Derived datasets underlying Ismail and Yamashiki, "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins", submitted to Earth Systems and Environment. The study assesses fluvial flood hazard and population exposure across Pakistan's five major drainage basins (872,782 km², 99% of national territory) from the 50-year to the 500-year return period, combining Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) inundation mapping with GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge, Generalised Extreme Value flood frequency analysis, and hydraulic-geometry depth estimation. A first-order sensitivity decomposition attributes total exposure uncertainty to four sources: rating curve parameters, DEM resolution, GEV parameter uncertainty and population data uncertainty. Every number reported in the paper can be checked directly against these files. NOT INCLUDED Input rasters and gauge records are third-party data distributed under their own terms and are not redistributed here. Their sources and versions are listed in the paper's Data Availability statement: GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge v4.0 (Copernicus Climate Change Service); SRTM 30 m and 90 m (NASA Earthdata, USGS EarthExplorer); GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT-S R2023A epoch 2025 (European Commission JRC); HydroBASINS Level 4 (HydroSHEDS); Sentinel-1 GRD (Copernicus, via Google Earth Engine); Global Flood Database 2010 extent. Gauge records are available from the Global Runoff Data Centre, Koblenz, on request under their data-sharing policy and are not redistributable. Analysis code is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. CHANGES FROM VERSION 1.0 Version 1.0 (April 2026) accompanied the originally submitted manuscript. The sensitivity decomposition has been recomputed: the population uncertainty term now uses the full width of the symmetric ±30% bound on gridded population counts, as set out in Section 3.7 of the revised paper. Shape-parameter confidence intervals, design depths, Southern Basin dual-resolution exposure and the full set of published tables have been added.

title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height : Surface elevation wnd100m : Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth : Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness : Surface roughness length influx_toa : Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo : Surface albedo temperature : Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature : Soil temperature at level 4 runoff : Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct : Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse : Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude : Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth : Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN . Source: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Terms of Use These cutouts contain processed meteorological data derived from ERA5, provided by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), and SARAH-3, provided by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 Contains modified EUMETSAT CM SAF SARAH-3 data (2026). Copyright © 2026 EUMETSAT. All intellectual property rights to the original CM SAF products belong to EUMETSAT. These products are made available free of charge under the applicable EUMETSAT data policy. Users must acknowledge EUMETSAT when using or redistributing the data and are requested to cite the original SARAH-3 dataset: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Licensing and Attribution The cutouts are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, subject to the attribution requirements associated with the original data sources. Users of these cutouts should acknowledge the original ERA5 and SARAH-3 datasets and cite their corresponding sources in scientific publications and derived products.

title: Soil Organic Carbon Threshold and Historical-baseline Datasets Underlying a Soil Degradation Boundary Assessment for India
description: Overview This record contains the full dataset (data/) supporting the Research Paper titled Integrating functionally-based soil organic carbon threshold models with reconstructed historical baselines to evaluate a soil degradation boundary in India and every raw/reconstructed geospatial input, every pixel- and ecoregion-level analysis-ready table, and every precomputed intermediate result (threshold-fit curves, sensitivity and resilience classifications) used to generate the Research paper results using the code accessible openly as Jupyter-notebook analysis code on https://github.com/sirtiza34/SOC_Functional_Thresholds_India_Analysis and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22806576 . Together they allow full reproduction of the Research Paper's quantitative results. All the dataset files are distributed only through this Zenodo record and the code repositories document this and points here. Spatial and temporal scope The dataset covers the soilscapes delimited by the territorial extents of India. Contemporary layers are at 250 m pixel resolution (50.48 million pixels) and temporal snapshot of 2019 developed from the SOC concentration data available at https://soilgrids.org/ . The historical baseline is sourced from the Sanderman et al. (2017)’s paleo-SOC reconstructions available at https://github.com/whrc/Soil-Carbon-Debt . The baseline is reconstructed on a coarser (~10 km) grid. All analyses are synthesized to 49 terrestrial ecoregions (World Wildlife Federation) covering the territory of India, and further stratified into 1,156 ecoregion × soil-order × land-use Environmental Context Units (ECUs) for threshold assignment. Contents, by category Pixel-level analysis-ready tables (the three large files) master_analysis_database.parquet — the master contemporary pixel database, 50.48 million rows, carrying assigned functional thresholds and derived metrics for every 250 m pixel in India. step6_functional_state_sample.csv — a spatially block-declustered sample of 395,750 pixels carrying per-pixel probability of being below threshold, P(SOC step4_distance_sample.csv — a pixel sample used to compute distance-to-functional-transition. Geospatial layers (rasters and vectors) ecoregion_id.tif, accel_class_map.tif, step10_feature_stack.tif, step13_soc_stack.tif — raster layers used in mapping and feature construction. step11_map_c_class_raster.npy / step14_boundary_raster.npy (with matching *_meta.pkl files) — precomputed classification and boundary-classification rasters plus their georeferencing metadata. india_boundary.geojson — national boundary vector used for map masking/plotting. Ecoregion-level and threshold tables About 30 CSV files cover, among others, the common analytical framework and state variables per ecoregion, tiered threshold assignment and tier-usage area shares, national and per-ecoregion threshold estimates and their uncertainty, historical-depletion/functional-risk correlation by response domain, degradation-boundary classification per ecoregion, area-weighted vs. unit-weighted synthesis, directional consistency and cross-domain overlap, resilience-opportunity and continued-loss-risk groupings, degradation hotspot lists, and area-weighting tables. Precomputed model curves step12_curves.pkl, step13_curves.pkl — fitted threshold-response curve objects. Data provenance Historical SOC baseline: depth-integrated (0–30 cm) reconstruction following the global SOC-debt method of Sanderman, Hengl & Fiske (2017, PNAS). Contemporary soil properties: SoilGrids v2.0 (Poggio et al., 2021, SOIL). Ecoregion boundaries: WWF terrestrial ecoregions. File formats GeoTIFF (.tif), NumPy array (.npy) with pickled metadata (.pkl), GeoJSON (.geojson), Apache Parquet (.parquet), and CSV — all openly readable with standard open-source GIS/Python tooling (rasterio, pyarrow, pandas, geopandas).

title: Global 0.05° 8-day Gridded TROPOMI Solar-Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence (dcSIF) from ANN-based Retrievals, May 2018 – July 2025
description: This dataset provides global gridded solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) derived from TROPOMI (Sentinel-5P) observations at 0.05° spatial resolution and 8-day temporal resolution, covering the period from 1 May 2018 to 31 July 2025. The input data are ungridded (Level-2) SIF soundings retrieved using the artificial neural network (ANN) approach developed by Li et al.( 10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987 ), which are publicly available on Zenodo ( https://zenodo.org/records/16537343 ). These soundings were aggregated onto a regular grid following the oversampling approach of Frankenberg et al., as implemented in SatelliteGridding.jl ( https://github.com/cfranken/SatelliteGridding ). The variable dcSIF denotes daily-corrected SIF, obtained by applying the day-length correction factor following Köhler et al.( https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GL079031 ), which scales instantaneous SIF to daily average values. Data are provided as one NetCDF file per year. Citation: If you use this dataset, please cite the original SIF retrieval paper by Li et al. (2025; 10.1016/j.rse.2025.114987 ), as well as the methodological references listed above where appropriate.

title: A Global Soil Spectral Library and Soil Organic Carbon Estimation Dataset Based on Geographical Stratification
description: This dataset comprises 784 topsoil samples selected from the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), including soil organic carbon content, geographic coordinates, and visible–near-infrared spectral data covering 400–2400 nm at a standardized 10 nm interval. The dataset also integrates ten environmental covariates: clay content, silt content, cation exchange capacity, soil pH, elevation, slope, annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, NDVI, and land-cover type. Based on these covariates, the samples were classified into five geographical environmental zones using a Gaussian mixture model. The dataset supports comparisons between global and geographically stratified models for soil organic carbon estimation and facilitates the regional application of global soil spectral libraries.

title: Urban Morphology and Land Surface Temperature: A 30-Meter Pixel-Level Dataset for Guadalajara, Mexico
description: This dataset contains pixel-level urban morphology and Landsat-derived land surface temperature data for the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area, Mexico. The dataset was constructed by integrating geospatial data from multiple sources: the USGS Earth Explorer (Landsat imagery), Visor Urbano Guadalajara (urban tree inventory), SITE Jalisco (green areas and water bodies), and Catastro Municipal de Guadalajara (building footprints, roads, and sidewalks).

title: EcoTwin Model Input Data Collection in Uniform Format
description: Lake-Specific ERA5, ISIMIP3b and ESA CCI Lakes Datasets Overview : This repository contains lake-specific climate and lake-observation datasets extracted and processed from three established data products: - ERA5 meteorological data - ISIMIP3b climate forcing data - ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1 The datasets were extracted for four study lakes: - Lake Balaton - Lake Iseo - Lake Mälaren - Lake Wylerbergmeer The processing workflow identifies the source-data grid cells intersecting each lake, extracts the corresponding time series, and produces lake-specific NetCDF datasets suitable for subsequent analysis. **Important:** The files in this repository are derived/extracted products. They do not replace the original ERA5, ISIMIP3b, or ESA CCI Lakes datasets. Users should consult and cite the original data providers and comply with the terms and licences of the original datasets. Study lakes : | Lake | ERA5 grid cells | ISIMIP3b grid cells | ESA CCI Lakes | | Balaton | 7 | 4 | Available (ID 310) | | Iseo | 1 | 2 | Available (ID 300014185) | | Mälaren | 17 | 9 | Available (ID 163) | | Wylerbergmeer | 1 | 1 | Not available | The lake polygons for Balaton, Iseo and Mälaren were obtained from HydroLAKES. A custom shapefile was used for Wylerbergmeer. 1. ERA5 meteorological data 1.1 Grid-cell identification The ERA5 workflow identifies the ERA5 0.25° × 0.25° grid cells that intersect each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - The lake bounding box is calculated. - A regular 0.25° latitude–longitude ERA5 grid is generated over the bounding box. - Square polygons representing the ERA5 grid cells are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection is used to identify all grid cells intersecting the lake polygon. - The coordinates of the selected grid-cell centres are extracted. 1.2 ERA5 data extraction Hourly ERA5 single-level meteorological data are downloaded for each selected grid cell using the Copernicus Climate Data Store and the ecmwfr R package. The extraction period is: 1980-01-01 to 2026-05-31 The following variables are included: | Variable | ERA5 short name | Units | | 2 m air temperature | t2m | K | | 2 m dew point temperature | d2m | K | | Surface pressure | sp | Pa | | Surface solar radiation downwards | ssrd | J m⁻² | | Surface thermal radiation downwards | strd | J m⁻² | | Total precipitation | tp | m | | 10 m zonal wind component | u10 | m s⁻¹ | | 10 m meridional wind component | v10 | m s⁻¹ | | Total cloud cover | tcc | fraction (0–1) | 1.3 ERA5 merging The individual ERA5 grid-cell NetCDF files are merged into one multi-station NetCDF file per lake. The merged datasets contain: - A common time dimension (valid_time) - Station identifiers corresponding to ERA5 grid cells - Latitude and longitude for each grid cell - Meteorological variables stored as time × station arrays; - Selected metadata copied from the original ERA5 files, including units, long names and standard names. Final files: - lake_balaton_era5.nc - lake_iseo_era5.nc - lake_mälaren_era5.nc - lake_wylerbergmeer_era5.nc 2. ESA CCI Lakes products 2.1 Data source and extraction Daily ESA CCI Lakes Level-3S merged products, version 2.1, are downloaded from the CEDA THREDDS server for 1992–2022. A unique ESA CCI Lakes ID is used to isolate each lake from the static lake mask. | Lake | ESA CCI Lakes ID | | Mälaren | 163 | | Balaton | 310 | | Iseo | 300014185 | | Wylerbergmeer | Not available | Wylerbergmeer is therefore excluded from the ESA CCI Lakes dataset. 2.2 Spatial processing The static CCI_lakeid mask is used to: - Identify all grid cells belonging to the selected lake ID - Calculate a bounding box around the selected pixels, with a one-pixel buffer - Extract a reduced spatial subset from the global dataset After subsetting, all variables are masked so that only pixels belonging to the selected lake ID remain valid. Other pixels are assigned _FillValue. 2.3 Variables The extracted ESA CCI Lakes variables are: | Variable | Name | Units | | Lake surface water temperature | lake_surface_water_temperature | K | | LSWT uncertainty | lswt_uncertainty | K | | Chlorophyll-a concentration | chla_mean | mg m⁻³ | | Chlorophyll-a uncertainty | chla_uncertainty | % | | Turbidity | turbidity_mean | NTU | | Turbidity uncertainty | turbidity_uncertainty | % | | Lake ice cover class | lake_ice_cover_class | categorical | | Lake surface water extent | lake_surface_water_extent | km² | | Water surface height above reference datum | water_surface_height_above_reference_datum | m | Associated quality-control variables include: lswt_quality_level, lwlr_quality_flag, lwe_quality_flag and lwl_quality_flag. 2.4 Quality control LSWT LSWT and its uncertainty are retained only for: lswt_quality_level = 4 or 5 Values equal to the specified fill value are removed, and invalid pixels are set to NA. Chlorophyll-a chla_mean and chla_uncertainty are filtered using lwlr_quality_flag. Pixels for which the relevant poor/low-consistency quality bits are set are removed. Turbidity Turbidity and its uncertainty use the same lwlr_quality_flag filtering approach as chlorophyll-a. Ice cover Only the following classes are retained: 1 = water and 2 = ice. All other values are assigned NA. Lake surface water extent Only lwe_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwe_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. Water level Only lwl_quality_flag = 0 (good) and lwl_quality_flag = 1 (medium) are retained. 2.5 Final CCI Lakes datasets After filtering, daily files are merged along a new time dimension. The final NetCDF datasets have dimensions: lat × lon × time Final files: - lake_mälaren_cci_lakes.nc - lake_balaton_cci_lakes.nc - lake_iseo_cci_lakes.nc 3. ISIMIP3b climate data 3.1 Grid-cell identification The ISIMIP3b workflow identifies the 0.5° × 0.5° grid cells intersecting each study lake. For each lake: - The lake polygon is read from HydroLAKES or the custom Wylerbergmeer shapefile. - A regular 0.5° latitude–longitude grid is generated. - Grid-cell polygons are created around each grid-cell centre. - Spatial intersection identifies the grid cells intersecting the lake. - The selected grid-cell centre coordinates are stored. 3.2 Climate models The ISIMIP3b data include the following GCMs: - GFDL-ESM4 - IPSL-CM6A-LR - MPI-ESM1-2-HR - MRI-ESM2-0 - UKESM1-0-LL 3.3 Scenarios The following scenarios are included: | Simulation | Period | | Historical | 1850–2014 | | SSP126 | 2015–2100 | | SSP370 | 2015–2100 | | SSP585 | 2015–2100 | 3.4 Variables | Variable | ISIMIP3b short name | Units | | Near-surface air temperature | tas | K | | Daily maximum air temperature | tasmax | K | | Daily minimum air temperature | tasmin | K | | Near-surface relative humidity | hurs | % | | Near-surface specific humidity | huss | kg kg⁻¹ | | Surface air pressure | ps | Pa | | Precipitation | pr | kg m⁻² s⁻¹ | | Surface downwelling shortwave radiation | rsds | W m⁻² | | Surface downwelling longwave radiation | `rlds` | W m⁻² | | Near-surface wind speed | sfcWind | m s⁻¹ | 3.5 Extraction and merging The global ISIMIP3b NetCDF files are opened and the grid cells identified for each lake are extracted. The extracted 10-year chunks are concatenated to reconstruct continuous time series for: - historical: 1850–2014 - SSP126: 2015–2100 - SSP370: 2015–2100 - SSP585: 2015–2100 The time axis is reconstructed using the same time origin across the complete period. Latitude and longitude are retained for each grid cell, and variables are assembled into time × station arrays. Selected metadata, including units, long names, standard names and selected global attributes, are copied from the original ISIMIP3b files. The final output is one multi-station NetCDF file per lake, GCM and scenario. title: The Global Carbon Budget (GCB) Allocation Debate in Post-Paris Climate Politics: New Insights for Current Discussions-Database Construction
description: The deposit contains three tables. gcb_panel.csv is a country–year panel with 13,327 rows covering 1990–2050: greenhouse gas emissions in CO₂e with and without LULUCF, population observed to 2019 and projected thereafter, and GDP at current and at constant 2015 prices. gcb_indicators.csv holds one row per country with every allocation indicator, the components of the re-specified ECPC, and the descriptive weights. gcb_national_budgets.csv converts each share into an allocation in GtCO₂e, into years of 2019 emissions, and into the constant annual reduction rate that exhausts it by 2050, for every combination of criterion and budget scenario. codebook.md defines every variable with its unit, time window and source, and is regenerated from the configuration file on every run, so it cannot drift from the calculation. MANIFEST.json records the SHA-256 checksum of each of the 12 source files and of each output, together with the versions of Python and of every library used. A single command, run_all.py, rebuilds everything from the frozen sources and exits with a non-zero status if the replication of the published tables fails.

title: Code and trained model weights for "GRBD: A Global-Scale Multiple-Type River Barrier Annotation Database for Global River Barrier Mapping with Deep Learning"
description: This Zenodo record contains code and analysis data supporting a study on deep-learning-based mapping and evaluation of river barriers. The materials cover annotation-format conversion, dataset preparation, model training and inference, detection-performance evaluation, approximate barrier-size classification, and cross-basin barrier-density analysis. The repository includes scripts for converting LabelMe annotations to YOLO and COCO formats, randomly splitting a COCO dataset into training, validation, and test subsets using an 8:1:1 ratio, training YOLO11 and RT-DETRv2 models, conducting batch inference with RT-DETRv2, and evaluating predictions against manually interpreted ground-truth annotations using intersection over union (IoU). An additional script estimates approximate barrier lengths from annotated coordinates and classifies barriers into three size classes (≤30 m, 30–100 m, and >100 m). The record also includes analysis data for 58 selected sub-basins used to compare barrier counts and densities derived from three sources: manual visual interpretation, deep-learning predictions, and Global Dam Watch (GDW). These data were used for the statistical analyses reported in the associated study. The object-detection workflow includes six river-barrier classes: weir, dam, sluice, tide, earth, and lock. Some scripts retain environment-specific file paths and therefore require users to modify input/output paths before execution. RT-DETRv2 and YOLO scripts also depend on their respective external frameworks, configuration files, and model weights. Further details are provided in the accompanying README. RT-DETRv2-x-bestpt.zip contains the trained weights of the best-performing RT-DETRv2-X model used in this study. The model was selected for subsequent cross-basin generalization testing and river-barrier detection analyses.

title: 13 October 2019 Pléiades (CNES) pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli catastrophic flood
description: Updated version of the 2 m merged Pléiades DEM where a ~10 m horizontal shift was corrected. =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal (Rasuwa) and Tibet : (see e.g. https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/) We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades tri-stereo acquired on the 13 October 2019, 7 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The updated collection includes one DEM : 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The three Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Shean et al., 2016, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total nine DEMs in 2x2m, 4x4m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean's demcoreg (https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/72886193) implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). Then, for each GSD (20m, 4m and 2m), the three DEMs are mosaicked using the median value. 2019-10-13_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the three above DEMs retaining the highest resolution (2 m)where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. Deschamps-Berger, C., Gascoin, S., Berthier, E., Deems, J., Gutmann, E., Dehecq, A., Shean, D., and Dumont, M.: Snow depth mapping from stereo satellite imagery in mountainous terrain: evaluation using airborne laser-scanning data, The Cryosphere, 14, 2925–2940, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-14-2925-2020, 2020. Nuth, C. and Kääb, A.: Co-registration and bias corrections of satellite elevation data sets for quantifying glacier thickness change, The Cryosphere, 5, 271–290, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-5-271-2011, 2011. title: GLCD250-MOD: Global Lakes Chlorophyll-a Daily 250 m based on MODIS — Part 1 of 3 (Lake IDs 1–50)
description: GLCD250-MOD is a global dataset of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentrations for inland lakes. It provides daily Chl-a estimates at a nominal spatial resolution of 250 m over the period 2000–2024. Chl-a concentration is estimated by a trained transformer-based hierarchical deep learning model based on MODIS satellite observations. With its high-resolution Chl-a estimates, GLCD250-MOD improves data availability for small lakes compared to the MODIS Terra Level-3 product (4.6 km spatial resolution, daily). GLCD250-MOD covers 465,966 lakes selected from the HydroLAKES database. The dataset is expected to support analysis of algal bloom dynamics, enabling monitoring of spatiotemporal bloom patterns and detection of long-term changes in inland lake ecosystems. GLCD250-MOD provides the variable ' chlor_a ', representing chlorophyll-a concentration in mg m⁻³. Each NetCDF file includes daily time coordinates, MODIS sinusoidal X and Y coordinates in metres, and metadata describing the lake identifier, temporal coverage, and model provenance. Missing predictions are represented by the fill value −999. The complete dataset is distributed across three Zenodo records using independently extractable Zstandard-compressed TAR archives (.tar.zst). This record contains Part 1, covering Lake IDs 1–50, with 74 NetCDF files for 50 lakes. The total compressed size is approximately 43.300 GB . Caspian Sea (Hylak_id: 1). Given its substantial data volume, the Caspian Sea is divided into two independently extractable archives by year: 0000001_2000-2011.tar.zst , containing 12 annual NetCDF files for 2000–2011, and 0000001_2012-2024.tar.zst , containing 13 annual NetCDF files for 2012–2024. Together, these archives provide the complete 25-year period from 2000 to 2024 (e.g., GLCD250-MOD_0000001_2000.nc and GLCD250-MOD_0000001_2012.nc ). Lakes with Hylak_id: 2–50. These lakes are distributed across two independently extractable archives: 0000002-0000010.tar.zst , containing 9 NetCDF files for Lake IDs 2–10, and 0000011-0000050.tar.zst , containing 40 NetCDF files for Lake IDs 11–50. Each lake is represented by one NetCDF file (e.g., GLCD250-MOD_0000002.nc and GLCD250-MOD_0000011.nc ), covering the period from 24 February 2000 to 31 December 2024, with predictions available where valid satellite inputs exist. Each archive contains a top-level directory matching its filename without the .tar.zst extension. Lake-ID ranges in archive filenames include both endpoints. Lake 1 intentionally occurs in two archives with disjoint year ranges , whereas all other lakes in Part 1 occur in exactly one archive. Every NetCDF file occurs exactly once. The remaining data are available in Part 2 (Lake IDs 51–2,000) and Part 3 (Lake IDs 2,001–1,427,688) . This dataset is developed and maintained by the Water Environmental Management Lab at the University of Seoul. For inquiries or technical support, please contact YoonKyung Cha ( ykcha@uos.ac.kr ). The dataset is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. For further methodological details and background, users are encouraged to consult the following reference: Yang S., Lee H., Lee G., Gu T., Park T., Park J., Shin J., Kim T., Cha Y. (2026). GLCD250-MOD: Global Daily 250 m Chlorophyll-a Dataset for Inland Lakes based on MODIS. Earth System Science Data [In review].
