title: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change
description: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change 1. Overview This archive contains the processed data, Python scripts, reproduced figure outputs, and per-figure statistics used for the manuscript "Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change" . The original daily meteorological forcing data and high-resolution process-based model outputs for 1,427,688 lakes are too large to include here. The archive instead provides processed lake-level, gridded, validation, and figure-source datasets sufficient to reproduce the main quantitative results and figures included in this package. 2. Getting Started and System Requirements 2.1 Zenodo Archives and Extraction The repository is distributed as standard ZIP archives and approximately 1 GB file parts so that large downloads can be transferred reliably: README.md : documentation for archive extraction, software setup, data contents, and reproduction. lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip : script/ and requirements.txt . lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip : demo data, external geospatial data, and processed data (including lake_qc_exclusions.csv ) other than the two largest NPZ files. lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part007 : parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/daily_nonoverlap_results.npz . lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part011 : parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/background_results.npz . lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip : 26 reference PDF/JPG files for 13 manuscript figures and 13 per-figure statistics CSV files, regenerated in the latest test run. Demo outputs are generated separately by script/demo.py . The README, scripts, core data archive, and every part of both large data archives are required to rerun every analysis. The results archive is optional and provides reference outputs for comparison. Download all required files into one directory. Individual .partNNN files cannot be extracted directly; they must first be joined in numerical order. On macOS, open Terminal in the download directory and run: cat lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip cat lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip mkdir -p lake_thermal_structure cp README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure cd lake_thermal_structure On Windows 11, open PowerShell in the download directory. Paste and run the entire function definition below before running the two Join-FileParts commands. Each command reports the part being joined and the completed ZIP path. Joining several gigabytes may take a few minutes. function Join-FileParts($Pattern, $OutputFile, [int]$ExpectedParts) { $directory = (Get-Location).ProviderPath $parts = @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $directory -Filter $Pattern -File | Sort-Object Name) if ($parts.Count -ne $ExpectedParts) { throw "Expected $ExpectedParts parts in $directory; found $($parts.Count)." } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $ExpectedParts; $i++) { $expected = $OutputFile + ('.part{0:D3}' -f $i) if ($parts[$i].Name -ne $expected) { throw "Missing or incorrectly named part: $expected" } } $outputPath = Join-Path $directory $OutputFile $temporaryPath = $outputPath + '.joining' $outputStream = [System.IO.File]::Create($temporaryPath) try { foreach ($part in $parts) { Write-Host "Joining $($part.Name)..." $partStream = [System.IO.File]::OpenRead($part.FullName) try { $partStream.CopyTo($outputStream) } finally { $partStream.Dispose() } } } finally { $outputStream.Dispose() } $expectedSize = ($parts | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum if ((Get-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath).Length -ne $expectedSize) { throw "Joined file size does not match the total part size." } Move-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath -Destination $outputPath -Force Write-Host "Completed: $outputPath" } Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip" 8 Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip" 12 New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force lake_thermal_structure | Out-Null Copy-Item README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure Set-Location lake_thermal_structure The commands use built-in macOS and Windows 11 tools. If the optional results ZIP was not downloaded, omit its tar -xf command. Extracting the archives into the same destination reconstructs this layout: lake_thermal_structure/ ├── README.md ├── requirements.txt ├── script/ ├── data/ └── results/ 2.2 Hardware A standard desktop or laptop computer can run the scripts, but the full data workflow is memory intensive. We recommend: RAM: at least 64 GB for the full datasets included here. Storage: at least 25 GB for the extracted repository and generated outputs. Allow at least 65 GB of free space while joining and extracting all downloaded archive parts; the downloaded parts and reconstructed ZIP files can be deleted after successful extraction. GPU: not required. Non-standard hardware: not required. The lightweight Poyang Lake demo dataset requires substantially less memory than the full figure workflows. 2.3 Software Setup and First Run The scripts were developed and tested with Python 3.13.5 on Windows 11. Required Python packages are listed in requirements.txt . Install them and run the lightweight demo from the reconstructed repository root: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python script/demo.py The demo writes its outputs to results/demo/ . Full manuscript figures can be regenerated with the commands in Section 6. Generating each figure takes approximately 10 minutes. Figure 4 may take longer time for its large amount of data input. The generated figures were further edited in Adobe Illustrator for publication. title: Developing a dynamic semi-distributed hydrological model considering interactions between soil moisture and evapotranspiration: application of bulk transfer method
description: Empirically-derived relationships are mainly used to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) in water balance models. Due to a lack of effective factors and correct conceptual relationships, the resulting ET may be inaccurate. Therefore, a hydrological model was developed by combining water balance and bulk transfer theory, called semi-distributed coupled water balance and bulk transfer (SD-CWBT). According to it, a dynamic interrelationship between ET and soil moisture was correctly established to estimate ET via physical concepts. Global gridded ET retrievals, which provide the spatiotemporal distribution of ET at a global scale, including ECMWF Reanalysis v5-Land (ERA5-Land), TERRA, Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and Operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop), were employed to evaluate the model. The results indicated the SD-CWBT, with Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of [0.6, 0.95], [0.68, 0.96], and [12.61, 0.99] for the streamflow and groundwater level simulation, respectively, had better performance compared to the alternatives. Furthermore, the estimated spatiotemporal distributions of ET agreed well with the climatic-vegetation conditions.

title: Data and code supporting concurrent burned-area detections and persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon
description: This release supports the study “Concurrent burned-area detections are associated with persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon”. Version 1.1.0 adds Supplementary_Data_1_Active_Fire_Analysis.zip, containing the complementary historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS analysis, the fixed protocol, input data, derived matching results, scripts, environment requirements, provenance, checksums, tests and independent verification results. Download and extract this ZIP without changing its folder structure, then open 08_VALIDACION_FUEGO_ACTIVO/START_HERE_REVIEWERS.md. The ZIP is 17,955,692 bytes and contains 59 files. The original cohort archive fire_loss_conversion_peruvian_amazon_v1.0.0.zip and its separate companion files are preserved unchanged. Those historical companions retain the original title, DOI, version and figure numbering. For this release, read START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md and use CITATION_VERSION_1_1_0.cff. The original release remains available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21881539. The study uses a retrospective spatial cohort sampled on a systematic 0.01° lattice in stable forests of the Peruvian Amazon. Hansen Global Forest Change defines first loss during 2014–2021; MapBiomas Peru Collection 3 defines baseline and subsequent land cover; MapBiomas Fire and GABAM define concurrent burned-area detection categories. Persistent conversion requires anthropogenic cover in each of three consecutive post-loss years. The original archive reproduces analyses from derived panels, not the raster-to-panel extraction. The estimates are associational. Thermal observations corroborate nearby combustion but do not validate individual 30 m burned pixels or subsequent land use. No field photographs or field campaign data are included. This dataset release does not publish the manuscript or confidential review correspondence. Author-owned material is covered by the record-level CC BY 4.0 licence. Software in the preserved original code folder retains its included additional MIT licence. NASA data and other third-party materials retain their original terms, attribution and disclaimers and are not relicensed by this deposit. See START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md for details. title: SCOPE / NCEO: Monthly global Marine Phytoplankton Primary Production, between 1998-2025 at 9 km resolution (derived from the Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative v6.0)
description: This dataset contains global, monthly marine phytoplankton primary production products (in mg C m-2 d-1) for the period of 1998 to 2025 at 9 km spatial resolution. Data are provided in NetCDF format. Primary production by marine phytoplankton was modelled using ocean-colour remote sensing products and a spectrally-resolved primary production model that incorporates the vertical structure of phytoplankton and simulates changes in photosynthesis as a function of irradiance using a two-parameter photosynthesis versus irradiance (P-I) function (see Kulk et al. 2020, Sathyendranath et al. 2020a, and references therein for details). Chlorophyll-a products were obtained from the European Space Agency (ESA) Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI v6 dataet). Photosynthetic Active Radiation (PAR) products were obtained from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and were corrected for inter-sensor bias in products. In situ datasets of chlorophyll-a profile parameters and P-I parameters were incorporated as described in Kulk et al. (2020). The primary production products were generated as part of the European Space Agency (ESA) project 'Satellite-based observations of Carbon in the Ocean: Pools, fluxes and Exchanges' (SCOPE). Support from the National Centre of Earth Observation (NCEO) is also acknowledged. References: Kulk, G.; Platt, T.; Dingle, J.; Jackson, T.; Jönsson, B.F.; Bouman, H.A.; Babin, M.; Brewin, R.J.W.; Doblin, M.; Estrada, M.; et al. Primary Production, an Index of Climate Change in the Ocean: Satellite-Based Estimates over Two Decades. title: Global ensemble of land cover indicators at 100 m (2000-2003): Terra firma short vegetation cover (part 1 of 7)
description: This dataset provides a global time series of land cover indicators at 100 m spatial resolution for the period 2000–2024. It is part of a global ensemble of eight land cover indicators derived from two global land cover products, namely GLAD GLCLUC and GLC_FCS30D . The dataset was generated by combining the source land cover products through temporal interpolation, weighted averaging, and class overwriting. The native resolution of the source products is 30 m. The resulting data were resampled to 100 m using average resampling and are provided as COGs. The eight land cover indicators included in the overall dataset are: tfshortveg, tftrees, wtshortveg, wttrees, water, cropland, snowice, builtup Further details on the methodology, source datasets, processing workflow, and data structure are available in the associated GitHub repository . This Zenodo record contains the terra firma short vegetation cover (tfshortveg) indicator. The indicator represents cover of short vegetation on dry ground, from true desert (~3%) to dense short vegetation (100%). Value type: Percentage (0-100%) Years covered: 2000-2003

title: Satellite-derived evaluation of thermal and non-thermal controls on seawater CO2 fugacity along the Nordic Seas during spring - Data availability
description: We present the dataset (in .csv) of sea surface temperature (SST, in °C), sea surface salinity (SSS), chlorophyll- a (Chl- a , in mg m³) and sea surface CO 2 fugacity ( f CO 2 , in µatm) used for the development of the f CO 2 model. Recalculated measurements of f CO 2 were extracted from cruises with quality control flags A and B in the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas version 2025 (SOCAT v2025, https://doi.org/10.25921/648f-fv35). SST and SSS data were extracted from the L4 product Multi Observation Global Ocean ARMOR3D (https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00052) matching the in situ f CO 2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 0.25°. Satellite-derived Chl-a data was extracted from daily images from the ESA Ocean Color Climate Change Initiative 6.0 database (https://www.oceancolour.org/) matching the in situ f CO 2 measurements in a spatial resolution of 1 km. We also present the recalculated spatial fields (in .nc) of SST (in °C), SSS, Chl- a (in mg m³), f CO 2 (in µatm) and calculated uncertainty (in µatm) for March, April and May between 2010 and 2025, with a spatial resolution of 0.125°.

title: Geospatial Dataset of Forest Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization in La Malinche, Mexico: 2019 Random Forest–Derived Canopy-Height and Structural Products and Structural Products Derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map
description: La Malinche Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization (LMCHSR) is a public geospatial dataset of forest canopy height and structural regionalization for an area of interest encompassing the La Montaña Malinche o Matlalcuéyatl Federal Protected Natural Area, Mexico, and the adjacent peripheral area included in the analysis. The 2019 canopy-height raster was produced by integrating three Random Forest models corresponding to Sentinel-2 Level-2A acquisitions on 22 January, 28 March, and 12 April 2019. Each model used the red (B4), red-edge (B5), and shortwave-infrared (B12) bands, together with elevation and slope, as predictors. Canopy heights from CHMv2 (Brandt et al., 2026) served as the response reference after spatial harmonization to the 10 m modeling grid. The date-specific predictions were integrated into a multitemporal canopy-height surface. Structural products were derived from this RF surface on a 20 m analytical grid. They include structural objects, aggregated regions, five canopy-height classes (S01–S05), and connected class patches. An independent set of 20 m structural products was derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map of Lang et al. (2023), with separately determined objects, regions, and five classes (E01–E05). The harmonized source ETH canopy-height raster is not redistributed. The release contains 18 geospatial assets: one area-of-interest boundary, the 2019 RF canopy-height raster (RF 2019), eight RF-derived structural products, and eight ETH2020-derived structural products. Raster and vector files are supplied as GeoTIFF and GeoPackage files, respectively, using the WGS 84 / UTM zone 14N coordinate reference system (CRS; EPSG:32614). The release also includes metadata, dictionaries, a class legend, and Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksums. The two structural classifications were generated independently; matching class codes do not imply identical class definitions or direct temporal forest change.

title: Pantropical calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) of cropland and grassland at 30 m (2020-2024)
description: This dataset provides annual calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) for cropland and grassland at 30 m spatial resolution for the pantropical belt (48°S-36°N) for the years 2020-2024 , and the rate of change of GPP for both land-cover classes. The calibrated GPP is derived from the Global Pasture Watch uncalibrated GPP (uGPP) product (Isik et al., 2025) , which uses a uniform light-use efficiency (LUE) of 1 gC m-2 d-1 MJ-1 across all land cover types. Here, uGPP is multiplied, pixel by pixel and year by year, by a land-cover-specific LUE factor taken from the Global Harmonized Land Cover (Moreno et al., 2026) map of the same year. The result is then masked to the cropland and grassland classes of that year. Layers Layer Value Unit Data type NoData Annual GPP (cropland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m -2 yr -1 UInt16 65535 Annual GPP (grassland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m -2 yr -1 UInt16 65535 Rate of change 2020-2024 (cropland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m -2 yr -1 per year Float32 -9999 Rate of change 2020-2024 (grassland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m -2 yr -1 per year Float32 -9999 Methods Input alignment. The annual uGPP and GHLC land cover maps for 2020-2024 were placed on one common grid (0.00025°, EPSG:4326) using virtual rasters (VRT). Both products share the same pixel grid, so no resampling was applied. Calibration. For every pixel and year: GPP = uGPP × LUE(land-cover class of the same year) , using the LUE factors below. uGPP values ≥ 65000 and land-cover nodata (255) are treated as nodata. Values are rounded to 1 gC m -2 yr -1 . Masking. The annual GPP was retained only where the land cover for that year belongs to the cropland (classes 2-9) or grassland (classes 10-11) group; all other pixels are nodata. Rate of change. Computed from the masked annual GPP as rate = [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 , i.e. the difference between the late and the early two-year means, divided by the 2020-2024 period length (4 years). A pixel has a rate only if it belongs to the group in all four years used (2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) and has valid, non-capped GPP in all of them. Processing and quality control. Processing was done in 1° × 1° tiles in parallel. Each tile is tagged with the input version and a fingerprint of the LUE table. After processing, all tiles were scanned for block-shaped gaps caused by failed data transfers (areas missing in one year but valid in all other years); affected tiles were recomputed. title: Reshuihe watershed, Liangshan (China): online household survey, fire-prevention burden and greening — data and code
description: De-identified data, analysis code and analysis outputs for a study of ecological restoration ("greening"), wildfire and fire-prevention duties in the Reshuihe watershed (174.7 km²), Xide County, Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, China. Survey. 815 questionnaires submitted online (Tencent Questionnaire) between 26 April and 3 May 2026, with the link forwarded by local government staff, who asked that their office and channels not be named; respondents answered on their own phones and staff had no access to the answers. Convenience sample; 84 submissions came from IP addresses in Liangshan Prefecture, 17 from elsewhere in Sichuan and 714 from outside Sichuan (released as a three-level variable). 73 coded variables, including five three-item Likert constructs (hazard concern, fire-duty burden, project participation, project dependence, perceived welfare) and four post hoc data-quality flags. Bilingual codebook and questionnaire text included. Code and outputs. Structural equation models with robustness checks, measurement-invariance and equivalence tests, and heterogeneity by IP location (R, lavaan); a Google Earth Engine pipeline for Landsat-only NDVI 2000–2025, a 200-basin donor pool, MODIS MCD64A1 burned area, FIRMS active fire, GLC_FCS30D land cover and CHIRPS/ERA5-Land climate; Python scripts for pixel-wise trends with FDR control, synthetic control / synthetic difference-in-differences with placebo inference, and fire activity relative to donor basins. Remote-sensing results. Growing-season NDVI rose across the watershed (median Sen's slope +0.0058 per year, 2000–2025), but no more than in 104 comparable basins: synthetic difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of the 2008 works −0.028 (95% CI −0.068 to 0.012, placebo p = 0.17). Version 2 corrects the description of how the survey data were collected, releases all 815 responses with collection date, completion time and IP-location group, replaces the version 1 remote-sensing files with the exports and outputs of a new Landsat-only pipeline, and corrects two specification issues of the version 1 SEM analysis. See CHANGELOG.md.

title: Mapping crown length and canopy depth across global forests at 1 km from multi-platform lidar and satellite data
description: Crown length (CL) describes the vertical extent of an individual tree's live crown. Canopy depth (CD) describes the vertical extent of the canopy within a forest stand. Both inform fire behaviour, vegetation and habitat models, yet their global distributions remain poorly resolved. We present global maps of mean CL and CD at 1 km resolution for 2020. We first retrieved CL for individual trees segmented from lidar point clouds, as tree height minus crown-base height. Within each of 1147 reference records on six continents, mean CL was the average of the tree values and CD was the 95th-percentile tree height minus the lowest crown base. Both were related to satellite and environmental predictors using random forest models. Tree-level CL agreed with field measurements and manual annotations with R² = 0.62 and RMSE = 2.63 m. Across 46 validation plots, RMSE was 1.90 m for mean CL and 2.09 m for CD. In the 30 % hold-out set, the mapping models achieved R² = 0.64 for CL and 0.72 for CD, with RMSE of 2.15 m and 2.98 m. Global mean CL and CD were 7.0 m and 14.2 m. Long crowns and deep canopies occurred in equatorial rain forests and humid temperate forests. Savannas, Mediterranean woodlands and dry forests had the smallest values. These maps give the first globally consistent view of the crown layer beneath the canopy top. They can constrain crown geometry in vegetation models, canopy fuel depth in fire models and vertical habitat structure in biodiversity studies.

title: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance"
description: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance" (Yiran Li), revision 1 (R1) of the manuscript under review at the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies. This version supersedes version 1, which accompanied the original submission. The package contains the analysis code, the derived data tables and the figures underlying the paper, which presents a global source–receptor accounting of cross-border delta sediment starvation. Local sediment production is routed along the HydroBASINS river network; each dam's trapping is computed from its Brune efficiency and regulated-flow share; large natural lakes retain sediment with and without dams; natural loads are anchored to observed pre-dam values (39 rivers) or to the pristine loads of the Nienhuis et al. (2020) delta inventory; and each delta's dam-induced deficit is split into a domestic and a cross-border part and attributed to the upstream countries responsible. Key results (R1): dams withhold about 5,100 Mt yr⁻¹ of sediment from the world's inventoried deltas, of which about 1,130 Mt yr⁻¹ (22.1%) is withheld by dams in another country; 46 countries are net downstream bearers (25 of them bearing at least 1 Mt yr⁻¹); about 156 million people live on national delta parts that have lost at least a tenth of their sediment supply, mostly to foreign dams, 87% of them in Bangladesh and Egypt. Leading upstream sources: India, the United States, China, Ethiopia and Brazil. Contents: the analysis scripts (sediment_routing.py and the revision scripts run by run_all_r1.sh), the builders of the manuscript, Supplementary Material and response letter (build_all.sh), all derived CSV and JSON tables, Figures 1–5 and the graphical abstract. README_R1.md documents the input data, the run order, the method and all changes from version 1. A clean-room run from the public raw inputs (HydroBASINS, BasinATLAS, Global Dam Watch, the GlobalDeltaData of Nienhuis et al., the delta extents of Edmonds et al., the WorldPop 2020 grid, Natural Earth and World Bank GDP) reproduces every derived table byte for byte. The reviewer reports are confidential and are not included. No generative-AI tools were used to produce any figure or graphical artwork; all figures are data plots generated by the included code.

title: SOCOMv2: Experiment 2 (GOBM subsampling experiment) full experimental dataset
description: Dataset Information Current Version: v2 (changelog at end of repository Contacts: Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk) and Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) The Surface Ocean CO2 Mapping program entered its second phase (SOCOMv2) with a range of experiments which provides a coordinated, community-driven framework to evaluate surface ocean fugacity of CO2 in seawater (sfCO2) reconstructions and derived air–sea CO2 fluxes under present-day observational constraints. This repository holds the dataset used within a Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model (GOBM) subsampling experiment designated Experiment 2, where nine fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) reconstruction methodologies reconstructed five GOBMs from the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (and one from 2024). title: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes
description: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes This dataset maps potential habitat within populated, human-used landscapes on a ~1 km² hexagonal discrete global grid (ISEA3H, resolution 16; 1.18491 km² cells). Spatial domain: all files cover the 114,791,301 land cells whose centroid lies at or north of 60°S. Antarctica and other land south of 60°S are not included. For each cell, the dataset provides: the cell centroid; country (FAO GAUL 2024, with de facto assignment for disputed areas); counts of 10 m land-cover pixels: Dynamic World 2024, ESA WorldCover 2021, Global Pasture Watch and the Spatial Database of Planted Trees v2.0; land area, habitat area and habitat fraction of land; population: WorldPop R2025A, 2024, 100 m; classification into 'Populated' and 'Shared' Landscapes. 'Populated Landscapes' are cells where more than 1% of land is non-habitat (crop, built-up, pasture or tree crops) and population density is at least 1 person per km² of land. 'Shared Landscapes' are Populated Landscapes in which at least 20% of land is habitat. Globally: Populated Landscapes cover 26.14 million km² (20.5% of land); Shared Landscapes cover 18.87 million km² (14.8% of land; 72.2% of Populated Landscapes); 37.75% of the population lives in Shared Landscapes. Files dgg_isea3h16_land_shapefiles.zip : the land grid as 377 zipped shapefiles (10° tiles). Cells touch Natural Earth 10m or OpenStreetMap land, with a 200 m buffer. dgg_cells_shared_landscapes_dataset.csv.gz : per-cell results: centroid, country assignment, pixel counts, population, land and habitat areas and fractions, and landscape classes (gzip CSV, 33 columns). dataset_summaries.zip : global_summary.csv and country_summary.csv , with areas, fractions and the fraction of population in Shared Landscapes. DATA_DICTIONARY.md : definitions of every column and file format. Code: https://github.com/njdepsky/SharedLandscapes (MIT). The grid script accepts any bounding box, for example a global grid. Article: Ellis et al., Data in Brief (2026). Licence and attribution: Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0. The grid is derived from OpenStreetMap data, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Dynamic World: "This dataset is produced for the Dynamic World Project by Google in partnership with National Geographic Society and the World Resources Institute." The inputs (Dynamic World, ESA WorldCover, Global Pasture Watch, SDPT v2.0, FAO GAUL 2024, WorldPop, Natural Earth) are used under their respective licences.

title: California Wildfire Perimeters with Environmental and WUI Attributes
description: This dataset contains processed fire perimeter records from four wildfire datasets: the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CalFire; 1990–2025), Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS; 1990–2024), the Global Fire Atlas (Atlas; 2001–2025), and the FIREDpy-based country-level dataset (FIRED; 2000–2024). Atlas and FIRED are derived from MODIS imagery. CalFire records are limited to fire events larger than 1 km². All four shapefiles include fire identifiers, ignition date, year and decade, burned area (size_km2), Northern/Southern California flags, and WUI classification attributes from intersecting fire perimeters with WUI boundaries (FireType: WUI vs Wildland; reachWUI; reachUrban). CalFire further includes containment date, ignition cause, climate and terrain variables (temperature, vapor pressure deficit, precipitation, wind, elevation, slope, NDVI, and land cover), ignition-based WUI classes derived by matching Global Fire Atlas ignition points to CalFire perimeters (IgnWUI; IgnType: WUIIgnite, WUISpread, or Wildland), the within-perimeter WUI burned-area fraction (WUIfrac), 4-day mean Canadian Fire Weather Index moisture codes (FFMC_4d, DMC_4d, DC_4d), Santa Ana wind occurrence flags for Southern California fires (SAW), and within-perimeter land-cover fractions from MCD12Q1 FAO-LCCS1 2020 (fracFor, fracGrass, fracShrub, fracSG). A full field list is provided in CalFire_added_fields.txt. The four perimeter datasets are provided as compressed Shapefiles. These data are intended to support research on fire size distribution, fire behavior, land-fire interactions, and WUI risk assessment.

title: Code and derived results: river-size association of Palaeolithic findspots in the Wainganga-Wardha basin, Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India
description: R code, unit tests, saved summary tables and figure-source tables for a spatial analysis of 197 Palaeolithic findspots (59 source references) in Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India (Wainganga-Wardha basin). The primary analysis estimates how site intensity varies with distance to drainage of increasing river size (WRIS stream order >= k, k = 3 to 9), using a down-weighted Poisson point-process likelihood with a ridge prior, spatial cluster-bootstrap inference, spatial cross-validation, a lineament-distance negative control and a robustness matrix. The analysis design was frozen and checksummed before the site-water models were fitted; the manifest is included. The primary hypothesis (intensity falls with distance to larger rivers) was not supported; the association depends on site classification, and exploratory analyses are labelled as such. Contents: scripts S01-S19, tests, saved result tables, figure-source tables, PDF figures, renv lockfile (R 4.5.2). Not included: exact site coordinates, the 1 km coarsened site table, and raw third-party data layers (WRIS, HydroRIVERS, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap, Global Dam Watch), which must be obtained from their providers. Limitations: modern water bodies are a proxy for Pleistocene water; legacy survey bias; mixed coordinate quality; undated typology; no field validation.

title: Data and code for Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification
description: This archive contains the R code, dataset provenance, input-file fingerprints, summary data, validation outputs and reference figures supporting the study “Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification”. The analysis covers 2000–2020 at a 0.05-degree working grid and distinguishes five temporally stable vegetation classes. Ecosystem-stratified generalised additive models include site random intercepts and AR(1) errors. The primary model includes a spherical spatial smooth and CO2; a matched 2 × 2 design tests sensitivity to these two terms. Trend inference uses Newey–West standard errors and global Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Global and ecosystem summaries use actual pixel area, with spatial-block bootstrap intervals and spatial-block cross-validation. The archive includes pooled out-of-fold level, trend and sign diagnostics, area-representative held-out trend shares, five CO2 spatial-support scenarios, and machine-readable CSV versions of all 30 parts of Supplementary Tables 1–9. The environment–CO2 baseline and unexplained-residual shares are descriptive co-directional trend components. Their association with composite human pressure is exploratory and does not identify causal effects of human activity. Raw third-party datasets, high-resolution derived rasters, site-level source and prediction tables, and model objects are excluded where redistribution rights are unclear. Users must acquire source data from the official providers and follow the documented reconstruction workflow. The included Natural Earth coastline is public domain.

title: AZ-Hydro — Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use: Software, Input Data, Models, Raster and Well Package Predictions, and Validation at 2 km Resolution (1896–2099)

The standalone copies of these files in this deposit are the current versions. How to unpack the .7z files The archives use LZMA2 with solid-block compression, which macOS Archive Utility cannot open. Use one of: macOS : Keka or The Unarchiver Windows : 7-Zip , WinRAR , or Bandizip Linux : p7zip (for example apt install p7zip-full , then 7z x az-hydro-data.7z ) What’s new in v1.2 Post-2026 Colorado River shortage. The central projection now uses the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines (U.S. Department of the Interior, August 2026), which reduce Arizona’s Colorado River apportionment by 760 kAF yr⁻¹ (CAP delivery factor 0.49, groundwater boost 7.5). The guidelines cover 2027–2028; 2029–2099 hold that latest official condition as a stand-in for continued shortage, not as a forecast. v1.0–v1.1 held the Tier 1 cut (512 kAF yr⁻¹) through 2099. Projected 2027–2099 groundwater withdrawal is 5.5 % higher and surface-water withdrawal 5.5 % lower than in v1.1; total withdrawal and all 1896–2026 predictions are unchanged. CAP scenario sweep. It adds 1.30 MAF of groundwater pumping over 2027–2060 and 3.15 MAF over 2027–2099. The other scenarios are unchanged. Uncertainty ensemble. The ensemble members now apply the same dynamic CAP caps and floors as the central partition (a missing import had disabled them). σ for the groundwater and surface-water categories changes in every year; σ for total withdrawal does not. The scenario sweep keeps its full-delivery counterfactual. ADWR partner CSVs ( Outputs/.../ADWR/ ). In v1.1, 14 of the 16 CSVs listed every basin-year twice, because the export also picked up the all-basin aggregate files. Each row now appears once, and Total_Predicted is built from the same per-basin series as the other categories, so Total_GW + Total_SW = Total_Predicted holds row by row. Basin totals count boundary pixels in every basin they touch, so summing basins exceeds the statewide total by about 2–3 %; statewide totals are in Annual_Summaries/ . Headline archive now also includes the out-of-distribution probability rasters ( OOD_Rasters/ , 68 MB). GEE assets for the AZ-Hydro Explorer moved to projects/azhydro/assets/az-wu-v1-2/ . Methods overview AZ-Hydro is a physics-constrained machine learning pipeline: XGBRF prediction of total annual withdrawal depth per 2 km pixel, trained on ADWR metered pumping records (1984–2024) with 22 predictors (actual and reference ET, precipitation, effective precipitation, temperature, land-cover fractions and densities, irrigated and groundwater-irrigation fractions, soil properties, water-table depth, well, surface-water-rights and canal densities, watershed streamflow, and pixel coordinates). Climate, ET, and land-cover inputs from different eras are joined into continuous 1896–2099 series by overlap-period bias correction. Density-ratio partition of the total into irrigation and non-irrigation withdrawals from groundwater and surface water, with consumptive use derived as CU = irrigation efficiency × irrigation withdrawal. The few free partition parameters were tuned to statewide USGS and ADWR records (USGS OFR 94-476, 1915–1990; USGS Circulars, 1950–2015; ADWR Annual Report totals and the 2019 ADWR shares); the machine learning totals are never adjusted. Six-component uncertainty quantification : σ_MACA (5 GCMs), σ_model (10 XGBRF seeds), σ_irr (irrigated-area input), σ_LULC (4 USGS land-use scenarios), σ_GW (5 recent well-registry snapshots), and σ_USBR (5 Upper Colorado River streamflow members), combined in quadrature and propagated to consumptive use (σ_CU). Stream capture index combining connectivity (exponential decay with water-table depth) and nearby surface-water availability, with pumping and connectivity uncertainty propagated to the capture volumes. Key validations Statewide agency reconciliation (calibration adequacy, not an independent test): 2017 ADWR total withdrawal 6.81 vs 7.00 MAF (−2.7 %); 2015 USGS groundwater withdrawal 2.96 vs 3.09 MAF (−4.1 %); 2019 ADWR irrigation share 74.2 % vs 72 %; 1955 and 1980 pumping peaks under-predicted by 6–11 %, with every reported total inside the model’s 95 % σ_total interval. Independent comparisons against USGS NHM withdrawals and consumptive use, USGS Reitz irrigation rasters, the USGS public-supply reanalysis, and CAP and SRP delivery records (statewide surface water within 0.8 % of the 1985–2024 CAP + SRP mean). WestWater Research (2026) CAP shortage anchor : Basic Coordination cumulative additional groundwater pumping 7.24 MAF over 2027–2060 vs 8.0 MAF (−9.5 %); Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF vs 8.7 MAF (the gap reflects AZ-Hydro’s no-regulatory-ceiling framing). CAP delivery shortage scenario sweep Nine scenarios (the no-cut Baseline_900kAF; DCP Tiers 0, 1, 2a, 2b, and 3; the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines; WestWater Basic Coordination; Extreme Shortage) re-partitioned over 2026–2099. Cumulative additional groundwater pumping over 2027–2060: Operating Guidelines 1.30 MAF, DCP Tier 1 4.05 MAF, DCP Tier 3 10.69 MAF, Basic Coordination 7.24 MAF, Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF. Basin and per-pixel maps, cumulative σ, and signal-to-noise figures are included for the 2027–2060 and 2027–2099 windows. External datasets required to reproduce the pipeline (not redistributed here) The pipeline reads four USGS ScienceBase data products that must be downloaded separately: USGS NHM withdrawals ( Haynes et al. 2023 ): irrigation withdrawals and efficiency by HUC12, 2000–2020 USGS NHM consumptive use reanalysis ( Martin et al. 2023 ; Martin et al. 2025 ): irrigation consumptive use by HUC12 USGS public-supply reanalysis ( Luukkonen et al. 2023 ; Alzraiee et al. 2024 ): public-supply withdrawals by HUC12 USGS Reitz historical ET ( Reitz et al. 2023 ; Reitz, Sanford & Saxe 2023 ): 800 m gridded ET Bundled here directly: ADWR Well Registry and metered pumping records, GW basin / AMA-INA / CAP / SRP / streamflow / USBR vectors, HarDWR water rights (Lisk et al. 2024) , GRAIN canal network (Suresh et al. 2026) , and the Ma et al. (2026) water-table depth . See Data/README.md inside each .7z for the exact file names and folders. title: Global gridded canopy height and height distributions from GEDI and ICESat-2 for EDv3 initialization at 0.01° resolution
description: This dataset provides gridded forest canopy structure inputs developed for the lidar-based initialization of the Ecosystem Demography model (ED v3.0), as described in Ma et al. (2023). It includes mean canopy height and canopy height histograms derived from NASA GEDI and ICESat-2 observations, together with tree canopy cover from the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS), at a spatial resolution of 0.01°. These products characterize spatial variation in canopy height and the distribution of observed canopy heights within each grid cell. They were developed to connect satellite observations of forest structure with mechanistic ecosystem modeling and can support initialization and evaluation of other forest and vegetation models. Data contents The repository contains five GeoTIFF files: Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_avg.tif : Mean canopy height, in meters, calculated from filtered GEDI L2A version 002 RH100 observations. Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_hist_count.tif : GEDI canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_avg.tif : Mean canopy height, in meters, derived from filtered ICESat-2 ATL08 version 005 observations. Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_hist_count.tif : ICESat-2 canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell. CGLS_forest_percent_2019_001deg.tif : Tree canopy cover percentage for 2019, aggregated from the native 100 m CGLS product to 0.01°. Source observations and processing The study used GEDI observations acquired from March 2019 through August 2021 and ICESat-2 observations acquired from October 2018 through October 2021. GEDI observations cover approximately 51°S–51°N, while ICESat-2 provides observations beyond this latitude range. Observations were quality filtered and assigned to 0.01° grid cells. The filtering criteria documented in the paper were: GEDI: quality_flag = 1 , sensitivity > 0.95 , and RH100 > 5 m . ICESat-2: dem_removal_flag = 0 , canopy_flag = 1 , cloud_flag_atm , and h_canopy > 5 m . Canopy height histograms contain 90 bins spanning 5–50 m at 0.5 m intervals. Each histogram layer records sample counts rather than normalized probabilities. Mean canopy height summarizes the retained observations within each grid cell. The products pool observations across the acquisition periods and do not represent annual time series. Use in model initialization In the associated study, canopy height histograms were used to index height-based lookup tables generated by ED v3.0. Model states associated with each height bin were weighted by the observed sample counts, preserving variation in canopy height within a grid cell. Tree canopy cover was then used to scale forest estimates to the whole grid cell. The histograms describe the distribution of sampled canopy heights across footprints or segments within a grid cell; they are not vertical foliage profiles or distributions of individual tree heights. Spatial coverage and sampling density vary because both lidar missions collect observations along orbital tracks. Cells without retained observations should not be interpreted as having zero canopy height. Associated publication Ma, L., et al. (2023). Spatial heterogeneity of global forest aboveground carbon stocks and fluxes constrained by spaceborne lidar data and mechanistic modeling. Global Change Biology , 29, 3378–3394. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16682 Please cite this dataset and the associated publication when using these products.

title: Ocean acidification and aragonite saturation, compounding anthropogenic stressors on marine life
description: Analysis scripts and derived data products behind the figures and numerical claims of Dryden & Duncan, "Ocean acidification, compounding anthropogenic stressors and marine water chemistry: evidence, regime-shift risk and implications for marine life". Contents: the winter aragonite threshold classification for all three zonation schemes; the same pipeline restricted to the polar and subpolar zone; the MODIS-Aqua equatorial Atlantic chlorophyll trend test; the figure build scripts; the derived 1-degree winter saturation and trend grids; the PyCO2SYS recomputation of aragonite saturation at the study sites with its per-point uncertainty; and the independent verification block. Each script run against the original file reproduces the published values exactly. Expected outputs are tabulated in README.md so that any discrepancy is immediately visible. The polar-zone script deliberately reports the measured present state and no projection; the reason, a coverage artefact caused by seasonal ice in the trend mask, is documented in both the script header and the paper's Methods. Version 7 (October 2026) adds GOES_R1_graded_threshold_package.zip, the material behind the revised manuscript (revision R1 for BMC Marine Science): the graded ecological reference threshold (Omega 3.3 equatorward of 10 degrees to 1.6 poleward of 60 degrees), the winter aragonite saturation grids for 1982 to 2024 with the per-cell trend and the mask, the 1-degree block-mean MODIS-Aqua weights (net primary production, calcite and chlorophyll, 2019 to 2021) used to weight the water below its threshold, the month-by-month version of that weighting, the Monte Carlo, block-bootstrap and structural uncertainty with projections counted from 2023, the sea-surface-temperature variant of the threshold, and the scripts for Figures 1 to 3, S1 and S2 of the revised paper. Every script was re-run from the package before deposit: the numerical scripts reproduce the deposited results to rounding (two of them, run against the raw OceanSODA-ETHZ file, reproduce the deposited grids and JSON exactly), and the figure scripts reproduce the deposited PNG files byte for byte. title: GRedSIF: the first long-term harmonized global red solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from the GOME-2 satellite series for 2007-2025
description: GRedSIF is a global monthly terrestrial red solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (RSIF) dataset derived from observations by GOME-2A, GOME-2B, and GOME-2C. It covers April 2007–December 2025 at a spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°. RSIF values represent fluorescence at 683 nm and are expressed in mW m⁻² sr⁻¹ nm⁻¹. The dataset was generated through instrument degradation correction, robust principal component analysis (RPCA)-based radiance spectral denoising, singular value decomposition (SVD)-based RSIF retrieval, and zero-level bias correction. Cross-satellite differences were reduced using cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching, with GOME-2B serving as the reference. GRedSIF provides a harmonized, long-term RSIF record to support studies of vegetation photosynthetic activity, seasonal dynamics, interannual variability, and joint analyses of red and far-red SIF.
producing_institution: Aerospace Information Research Institute; University of Valencia

title: TROFSIF: A global full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from TROPOMI enabled by radiance-spectrum denoising (Part 1: May 2018–October 2022)
description: This repository provides Part 1 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering May 2018 to October 2022. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 1 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 2, covering November 2022 to July 2026, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23585026).

title: 202609 - Vessel detections from Sentinel 2
description: Vessel detections with Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from 2019 to 14 days ago. Multiyear detection of vessels with respective length, speed and orientation estimates based on deep-learning models applied to electro-optical imagery (RGB and near-infrared) at 10-m resolution covering most exclusive economic zones and marine protected areas across the ocean. Sentinel-2 detections are based on electro-optical imagery at 10-m resolution. Compared with our published Sentinel-1 detections based on SAR imagery at 20-m resolution, Sentinel-2 allows detecting smaller vessels with all types of vessel materials, in contrast with the weakness of SAR imagery on revealing vessels made of wood and fiberglass. Sentinel-2 also images the wakes of moving vessels, which further increase the detectability of small vessels and allow us to infer the vessels’ speed and orientation.The rich information contained in the optical imagery can be used to map not only vessel presence, but also vessel activities such as vessel encounters and bottom trawling. Sentinel-2 also covers more area of the ocean than Sentinel-1, and the novel neural-net detection approach does not require the exclusion of near-shore regions (as opposed to the CFAR approach), allowing detection of vessels in highly-packed areas all the way to the shoreline where most human activity is concentrated. Overall, with Sentinel-2 imagery we are able to detect about 3 times more vessels, “see” a broader range of vessel lengths and types, and infer more information of vessel activities than in our previous mapping using Sentinel-1 imagery.

title: WorldCereal crop calendars
description: This dataset contains the global crop calendar training and validation data used in the manuscript “Enhancing WorldCereal crop calendars with land surface phenology and machine learning” ( Moletto-Lobos et al., 2026 ). It includes harmonized reference crop calendar points derived from GEOGLAM Crop Monitor, USDA-FAS, JRC ASAP, and FAO sources, together with phenology-based samples retrieved from MODIS Aqua NDVI Land Surface Phenology (LSP) time series and ERA5-Land climate variables. The dataset is organized into two main seasonal groups that follow the nomenclature used in the manuscript: S1 = Winter crops (equivalent to winter cereals in the paper) Includes reference and LSP-derived Start of Season (SOS) and End of Season (EOS) dates, including explicitly modeled dormancy periods. S2 = Summer crops (equivalent to summer cropping systems in the paper) Includes SOS and EOS samples for rainfed and monsoon-driven summer crops, corresponding to the “summer season” definition of the study.
producing_institution: Universitat de València; Universitat de Valencia

title: ISOP synthetic ocean temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific, 2015
description: Daily ISOP (Improved Synthetic Ocean Profile) synthetic temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific (99°E–170°E, 20°S–66°N) for 1 January–31 December 2015. The product was developed by the authors following the methodology of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (Helber et al., 2013), with minor modifications. As described in the accompanying manuscript (Dan et al.), ISOP employs a three-layer vertical structure model (mixed layer, thermocline layer and deep quiescent layer) and uses a variational method combined with historical profile EOF statistics to project satellite sea surface observations onto the subsurface, generating three-dimensional temperature and salinity fields. Its satellite inputs are OISSTv2.1 daily 1/4° sea surface temperature, AVISO/DUACS global 1/8° multi-satellite merged sea surface height anomaly, and the Copernicus 1/8° sea surface salinity merged product. The product extends to a maximum depth of 1000 m (47 levels) at 1/4° horizontal resolution. Observational validation shows that its temperature and salinity errors are comparable to those of the HYCOM and GLORYS12V1 reanalyses, with grid-point temporal and daily spatial correlation coefficients of steric sea surface height with AVISO SLA of 0.874 and 0.897, respectively. The archive contains 365 daily NetCDF files named YYYYMMDD_isop.nc (20150101–20151231); temperature is in degrees Celsius and salinity in PSU, with missing values masked. Data are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Contact: Bo Dan (danb1991@163.com).
producing_institution: National Marine Data and Information Service

title: Reproducibility package for: Systematic biases in global site-frequency proxies limit estimates of high-rise building resonance exposure
description: Code, derived data and records for the paper "Systematic biases in global site-frequency proxies limit estimates of high-rise building resonance exposure". The reproduction layer (run_all.py and code/) recomputes every number, table and figure from the derived results and compares each output with reference SHA-256 checksums; README.md gives the requirements and the three third-party files that some figures read. The archive layer holds the analysis scripts as run, for inspection only. Each prespecified criteria file was locked by SHA-256 and time-stamped before its true values were computed. The package ships redacted copies of the locked files, with a table of every change, and English translations. Code: MIT. The two city-cell tables derived from the SoilGrids depth-to-bedrock map: ODbL 1.0. Other files: CC BY 4.0. Third-party raw data are not included.

title: Earthen berm stochastic simulation (Landlab): code and data
description: Model code and simulation output for a global sensitivity study of earthen berms in dryland valleys. Each run is a 100-year Landlab simulation driven by CLIGEN storms for Tucson, Arizona, run once with a berm and once without it, using the same storms. The record contains the model (berm_driver.py) and the CLIGEN station file, end-of-run results and storm-by-storm series for a 1,152-run main ensemble, paired berm and no-berm storm records for 189 runs of an earlier per-storm ensemble, an older per-decile summary of 128 of those runs, the script that extracted the 189 runs from the raw output, and the raw output itself. README.md describes the files, and DATA_DICTIONARY.md describes every column.

title: Supplementary dataset: GCBR funding horizons
description: The figure shows the number of actual full time equivalents employed by 42 of the current set of 52 Global Core Biodata Resources (GCBRs), as designated by GBC, for each of five years up to 2024. For each year from 2025, the bars show the number of FTEs for whom funding was currently assured as at the date the data was submitted. The data was collected between February and April 2025 via an Excel template sent to each of the 52 GCBRs by the GBC Secretariat. 42 GCBRs were able to provide data in the timeframe of the request. GCBRs were asked to either provide average FTE counts for each year or provide a FTE count at a fixed time point in each year, with the proviso that the method used to measure this was consistent year on year.

title: Land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026
description: Description This dataset provides estimates of net land-use change CO 2 emissions (ELUC) and their component fluxes from the three bookkeeping models used in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026): BLUE (Hansis et al., 2015), LUCE (Qin et al., 2024), and OSCAR (Gasser et al., 2020). Peat drainage emissions are from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021), and peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). The dataset further includes the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026, including estimates from national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset also includes global and gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL), which is the difference in ELUC between a simulation with transient carbon densities and a simulation with pre-industrial carbon densities. The reported net ELUC estimates already include the environmental contribution (δL). Net ELUC and its component fluxes are available as global and national annual time series for 1850–2025. Net ELUC is also available as gridded annual time series (0.25° resolution) for 1959–2025. The data describe CO 2 emissions and removals expressed as mass of carbon (C). For ELUC and its component fluxes, positive values denote emissions and negative values denote removals. The sign convention for δL is explained below. Empty cells in .xlsx files denote missing values. The dataset contains 20 files: One .xlsx file with global estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) Fourteen .xlsx files with country-level estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR, one for each of the net and component fluxes listed below (units: TgC/yr) Two NetCDF files with gridded net ELUC estimates for BLUE and LUCE (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) One .xlsx file with the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One .xlsx file with the global estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One NetCDF file with the gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) Global, country-level, and gridded data The dataset includes the following net and component fluxes. The identifiers shown in monospace are used in the corresponding country-level filenames and as worksheet names in the file with global estimates. “SC” denotes shifting cultivation, and “nonforest” refers to shrub and herbaceous vegetation: net-eluc (net ELUC): Net CO 2 emissions from land-use change. clearing-allveg-total (deforestation and clearing of other vegetation (total)): Total CO 2 emissions from deforestation and the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent clearing and clearing within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-allveg-total ((re-)growth of forest and other vegetation (total)): CO 2 removals through the growth and regrowth of forests and shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent (re-)growth and (re-)growth within shifting cultivation cycles. wood-harvest-management (wood harvest & other management): CO 2 emissions from the decay of harvested wood products and residues left on site, and CO 2 removals through regrowth following harvest. cropland-pasture-urban (cropland-pasture-urban transitions): CO 2 fluxes from transitions between cropland, pasture, and urban areas. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): CO 2 emissions from peat drainage and anthropogenic peat fires. Peat drainage emissions are the average of estimates from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021). Peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO 2 emissions from permanent deforestation. clearing-forest-sc (deforestation in SC cycles): CO 2 emissions from deforestation within shifting cultivation cycles. clearing-nonforest-permanent (permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO 2 emissions from the permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation. clearing-nonforest-sc (clearing of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO 2 emissions from the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-forest-permanent (permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation): CO 2 removals through forest growth and regrowth following permanent afforestation and reforestation. regrowth-forest-sc (forest (re-)growth in SC cycles): CO 2 removals through forest regrowth within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-nonforest-permanent (permanent (re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO 2 removals through the growth and regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation following permanent land-use changes. regrowth-nonforest-sc ((re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO 2 removals through the regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. Components 2–6 sum to net ELUC (component 1). Components 7–10 are subdivisions of component 2 and sum to its total. Components 11–14 are subdivisions of component 3 and sum to its total. Environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) The environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) is defined as the difference in ELUC between simulations using transient and pre-industrial carbon densities (transient minus pre-industrial). Positive values indicate higher ELUC under transient carbon densities, and negative values indicate lower ELUC. Annual estimates are provided for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR in two files: GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_global_1850-2025.xlsx : Global estimates for 1850–2025 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr). GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_gridded_1959-2025.nc : Gridded estimates for 1959–2025 (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area). For OSCAR, country-level estimates were spatially disaggregated to a 0.25° grid using the spatial patterns of gross emissions and gross removals from BLUE (see Supplementary Section S.2.2 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Data underlying Figure 8 The file GCB2026_Figure8_Data.xlsx contains the datasets used in Figure 8 (a-c) of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr), within the period 1990–2025 for bookkeeping estimates and the sink in managed forests and for the period 2000–2025 for national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs; 2024 data replicated in 2025) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset groups and variables are as follows: Bookkeeping models (BMs) and peat datasets net-eluc (net ELUC) : Component 1 in the above list. clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation) : Component 7 in the above list. other-transitions (other transitions) : CO 2 fluxes from transitions between shrubland, herbaceous vegetation, cropland, pasture, and urban areas, corresponding to the sum of components 5, 9, 10, 13, and 14 in the list above. forest (fluxes on forest land) : CO 2 fluxes on forest land, including permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation, net CO 2 fluxes from shifting cultivation in forests, and net CO 2 fluxes from wood harvest & other management, corresponding to the sum of components 4, 8, 11, and 12 in the above list. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): Component 6 in the above list. National greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) Inventory estimates are from Melo et al. (2026). net-lulucf-flux (net LULUCF flux) : Net CO 2 fluxes from land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation) : CO 2 emissions from permanent deforestation. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires) . Emissions from drainage of organic soils and fires on organic soils. other-transitions (other non-forest land uses): Net CO 2 fluxes from cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements, and other land, including land remaining in these categories and transitions between them. Emissions from organic soils are reported under peat-emissions . forest (fluxes on forest land): Net CO 2 fluxes from forest land remaining forest land and land converted to forest land, including harvested wood products and excluding organic soils. Dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) managed-forest-sink : The CO 2 sink in managed forests estimated by DGVMs (see Supplementary Sections S.2.4 and S.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Atmospheric inversions net-lulucf-flux : The net LULUCF flux estimated by atmospheric inversions (see Supplementary Section S.2.4 in Friedlingstein et al. (2026)). Citation and data policy When using this dataset, please cite the specific dataset version used and the accompanying Global Carbon Budget 2026 publication: Schwingshackl, C., Gasser, T., Qin, Z., Seeberg, G., Fu, Z., and Pongratz, J. (2026). Land-use change CO 2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (Version 1.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902 Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data Discussions [preprint]. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2026-895 For analyses using individual model estimates or the additional datasets underlying Figure 8, we also recommend citing the relevant references listed below. Gridded data for the individual ELUC component fluxes are available from the authors upon request. For studies using gridded data, the contributing modellers should be offered the opportunity to participate early in the research process. Potential co-authorship should be discussed at that stage, taking into account the role of the data in the study and the modellers’ contributions. References Conchedda, G., and Tubiello, F. N. title: The LULUCF Data Hub: translating global land use emissions estimates into the national GHG inventory framework (Version 4.1.0, 2026 NGHGI release)
description: This repository includes the data displayed in the LULUCF Data Hub , an online platform hosted by the EU Forest Observatory. It compiles various datasets of country-level CO₂ and non-CO₂ emissions and removals from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF). The LULUCF Data Hub is described by Melo et al. (ESSD Discussion) . The NGHGI LULUCF database is compiled and maintained by the European Commission (EC) Joint Research Centre (JRC) and was first described by Grassi et al. 2022 . It includes CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes from LULUCF sourced from the National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (NGHGIs) submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), using methodologies established by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes reported by countries in IPCC categories and sub-categories are allocated to the classes Forest (excl. organic soils, excl. HWP), Deforestation (conversion of forest land to other land uses), Other non-forest land uses , Organic soils , and Harvested wood products (HWP) (see Box 1). In the LULUCF Data Hub, and through a multi-disciplinary collaboration, we show results from global key initiatives estimating anthropogenic land use GHG fluxes translated to conceptually align with NGHGI and IPCC Guidelines definitions. In version 4.1.0 we present CO₂ data from carbon cycle modelling (Global Carbon Budget, GCB 2026 ; Friedlingstein et al., ESSD Discussion ), CO₂ and non-CO₂ data from Global Nature Watch (formerly Global Forest Watch, GNW 2026 ; update of Gibbs et al., 2025 ), and CO₂ data from EDGAR LULUCF ( Rossi et al., ESSD Discussion ). Data is available in Mt CO₂ yr⁻¹ and, where available, Mt CO₂e yr⁻¹ . Net CO₂ fluxes include emissions by sources and removals by sinks; non-CO₂ emissions, where available, are reported separately. Countries are identified by their ISO3 code. In addition, the timeseries files also include aggregated estimates for World (WRD) and the European Union (EU27). Version 4.1.0 (NGHGI 2026 release) Contents Files made available in version 4.1.0 New in version 4.1.0 NGHGI database 4.1.0 Independent datasets translated to NGHGI/IPCC Guidelines definitions 4.1.0 Versioning and citation policy 1) Files made available in version 4.1.0 File Status vs. previous version timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv New data (NGHGI 2026 release), now covering 1990-2025, including CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes and, where available, the split of the FOREST class into FOREST_REMAINING and LAND_TO_FOREST; replacing v4.0.0 NGHGI content. timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv New data (NGHGI 2026 release) covering 1990-2025, with only the values actually reported by countries (not gap-filled) for CO₂ and non-CO₂ fluxes and, where available, the split of the FOREST class into FOREST_REMAINING and LAND_TO_FOREST; replacing v4.0.0 NGHGI content. timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026, 1990-2025, CO₂ only (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026, 1990-2025, CO₂ only (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GCB_spread_4.1.0.csv New file, not present in earlier versions: spread of the Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026 CO₂ estimates across the underlying bookkeeping models (BLUE, OSCAR, LUCE) and DGVMs (n=24), for both the original/reclassified and translated datasets, alongside the ensemble average, min/max and standard deviation reported in timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv . timeseries_GNW_original_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Nature Watch (GNW) 2026 (formerly Global Forest Watch), 2001-2025, now including non-CO₂ fluxes for the Forest and Deforestation classes (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. timeseries_GNW_translated_4.1.0.csv New data from Global Nature Watch (GNW) 2026 (formerly Global Forest Watch), 2001-2025, now including non-CO₂ fluxes for the Forest and Deforestation classes (no FOREST split); replacing v4.0.0 content. text_box_iso3_4.1.0.csv Updated: discussion notes on the data by country, alongside data-source information. chart_sectors_4.1.0.csv Updated file replacing v4.0.0: all-sector (Energy, IPPU, Agriculture, LULUCF, Waste) summary from CRT Table 10s1/10s2, in both CO₂ and CO₂e (n=121 countries). managed_land_country_classification_4.1.0.csv Updated file replacing v4.0.0: per-country classification of the use of the managed land proxy (Decision tree A: use of managed land proxy; Decision tree B: treatment of CO₂ removals from forest land), used to inform the translation of the independent datasets to the NGHGI managed-land definition (see Figure 1 below). Includes area of managed and unmanaged forest reported to the UNFCCC in 2000, 2010 and 2020. 2) New in version 4.1.0 Extended time series (1990-2025) The NGHGI and GCB time series now cover the period 1990 (previously 2000) to 2025: timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv for NGHGI; timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv for GCB. Non-CO₂ fluxes The NGHGI and GNW datasets now also report non-CO₂ fluxes alongside CO₂: NGHGI identifies these via the new Gas column (CO₂, CO₂e, non-CO₂), and GNW adds them for the Forest and Deforestation classes only. timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv for NGHGI; timeseries_GNW_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GNW_translated_4.1.0.csv for GNW. Split of the Forest class Where available, the Forest class is further split into FOREST_REMAINING (forest land remaining forest land) and LAND_TO_FOREST (land converted to forest land), reported alongside FOREST (FOREST = FOREST_REMAINING + LAND_TO_FOREST where both are available; left blank where a country reports FOREST only — see Box 1): timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv . GCB model spread The new file timeseries_GCB_spread_4.1.0.csv reports the Global Carbon Budget (GCB) 2026 CO₂ estimates across the underlying bookkeeping models (BLUE, OSCAR, LUCE) and DGVMs (n=24), alongside the ensemble average, min/max and standard deviation already reported in timeseries_GCB_original_4.1.0.csv and timeseries_GCB_translated_4.1.0.csv . 3) NGHGI database 4.1.0 Version 4.1.0 of the LULUCF Data Hub updates the NGHGI LULUCF database with data submitted to the UNFCCC up to August 2026 for the period 1990-2025. We provide data as submitted by countries in their inventories ( timeseries_NGHGI_not-gap-filled_4.1.0.csv ) and gap-filled without altering the levels and trends of the reported data ( timeseries_NGHGI_gap-filled_4.1.0.csv ). Gap-filling applies linear interpolation between reported years and flat extrapolation beyond the first or last reported year, independently for each country, category and gas; no values are generated where a country has not reported a given category at all.
