title: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget
description: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget — 2026 Release This dataset provides gridded terrestrial biosphere model output from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional Scale Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, contributing to the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026). TRENDY is an international model intercomparison project that brings together simulations from dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) to investigate the global terrestrial carbon cycle and its response to environmental change, including atmospheric CO₂, climate variability and land-use change. This release contains the final gridded model output submitted for GCB2026. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability. Experimental design and simulations The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026. The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions: Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed S1 Transient Fixed Fixed S2 Transient Transient Fixed S3 Transient Transient Transient S4 Fixed Fixed Transient S5 Transient Fixed Transient S6 Fixed Transient Transient Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers. Changes introduced in GCB2026 In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses. For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover. The land carbon sink is calculated as: SLAND = S3 − (S4 − S0) + δL where δL represents the transient environmental effects on land-use change emissions, estimated using bookkeeping models - and can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902 The contributions from atmospheric CO₂ and nitrogen deposition and from climate are estimated as: CO₂ and nitrogen deposition: S3 − S6 + δL Climate: S3 − S5 + S0 These simulations provide a consistent framework for investigating terrestrial carbon fluxes under historical changes in environmental conditions and land use. Further methodological details are provided in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 Supplementary Information. Data availability Access and download the data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ The complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. The underlying NetCDF model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. This Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination The TRENDY-GCB2026 simulations were contributed by international modelling groups. The creators listed in this record include the TRENDY coordinators and a representative of each contributing model. TRENDY coordination: Stephen Sitch, Pierre Friedlingstein and Mike O'Sullivan. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. Release information This dataset corresponds to TRENDY version 15, the final version of the land model simulations used for the Global Carbon Budget 2026. Please use the naming convention "TRENDY-GCB2026" in publication/presentations. The Zenodo deposit contains the following files: trendy_listofvariables_GCP2026.xlsx — definitions and specifications of model output variables. TRENDY-GCB2026-manifest.csv — inventory of externally hosted gridded model output files, including filenames, paths, sizes and modification dates. TRENDY-GCB2026-model-credits.csv — contributing models, model representatives and TRENDY coordinators. TRENDY-GCB2026-data-policy.md — data usage, attribution and co-authorship requirements. The underlying gridded model output is hosted on Wasabi and is accessible through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. These model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. How to cite this dataset When using the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output, users should cite all three of the following resources: Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026 . This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the terrestrial carbon sink. TRENDY model intercomparison: Sitch et al. (2024) — This publication describes the TRENDY model intercomparison framework and its application to understanding the terrestrial carbon cycle. [https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102] TRENDY-GCB2026 dataset: O'Sullivan et al. (2026) — TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget , version v15. Zenodo. [10.5281/zenodo.23561904]. This dataset record provides access to the gridded model output and formally credits the participating modelling groups. These three citations are complementary and should be included when publishing analyses based on the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output. Users should also cite relevant individual model publications where appropriate. Citation of these resources does not replace the TRENDY data policy, including the requirements for prior circulation of manuscripts and invitations to co-authorship where the data make a significant contribution. Data use and licensing The underlying model output is provided through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser and remains subject to the TRENDY data policy, including its acknowledgement, attribution and co-authorship requirements. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the TRENDY coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate. The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies only to the documentation and metadata deposited on Zenodo . It does not apply to the underlying gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the TRENDY data policy governs use and redistribution. The TRENDY data policy and model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ Related publication Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data , XX, XXXX–XXXX. [LINK] Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated terrestrial carbon sink estimates derived from the DGVM ensemble, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal: https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026 The ICOS data supplement and the TRENDY gridded model output are complementary resources. The former provides the published Global Carbon Budget synthesis results, while the latter provides access to the underlying spatially resolved terrestrial model simulations.

title: SeaWiFS Chlorophyll Concentrations: Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska
description: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center's SeaWiFS Project (Sea-viewing Wide Field-of-view Sensor) is utilized to measure bio-optical properties of our global oceans. Located on Orbiting Sciences Corporationメs (OSC) SeaStar spacecraft, the SeaWiFS instrument collects ocean color data. The satellite has a sun synchronous orbit at 705 km above the earthメs surface and collects data in eight wavelength bands and two telemetry streams. The Global Area Coverage (GAC) sensor gathers data in a 1502 km-wide swath with a resolution of 4.5 km, whereas the Local Area Coverage (LAC) encompasses a 2801 km-wide swath with 1.1 km coverage. LAC data is used on this site. A Sea-Air-Land Modeling and Observing Network (SALMON) Project. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

title: Zooplankton Samples Collected in the Bering Sea On Board the F/V Northwest Explorer from September to October, 2002
description: Zooplankton samples collected between September 8 and October 6, 2002 as part of the BASIS survey by the F/V Northwest Explorer . A total of 44 rope trawl stations were sampled along the Aleutian chain in the Bering Sea basin or within the proximity of the Aleutian Islands and stations on or adjacent to the Eastern Bering Sea shelf. Zooplankton were collected using a bongo net (mesh sizes: 333 and 505 microns) towed obliquely between the surface and 200 meters, or 20 meters from the sea floor. Zooplankton samples were split onboard the vessel with a Matoto splitter and sample halves were preserved in formalin and frozen. Formalin preserved specimens have been sent to the Polish sorting center for species identification; frozen specimens will be used for stable isotope analysis. Surface water samples were collected and filtered for stable isotopes, coccolithophores, and chlorophyll. Filters were frozen and 250 ml of the filtered water was retained for nutrient analysis (NO 2 , NO 3 , PO 4 , and SiO 3 ). [Reference: Murphy, J., N. Davis, O. Ivanov, M. Rohr, S. Elmajjati, and W. Barber. 2003. Cruise report of the 2002 F/V Northwest Explorer BASIS survey in the Bering Sea, September- October. (NPAFC Doc. 676 Rev. 1) 23 p. title: TROFSIF: A global full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset from TROPOMI enabled by radiance-spectrum denoising (Part 2: November 2022–July 2026)
description: This repository provides Part 2 of TROFSIF, a global Level-2 full-spectrum solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) dataset derived from TROPOMI observations, covering November 2022 to July 2026. The dataset provides footprint-level full-spectrum SIF observations over terrestrial ecosystems, including red (685 nm) and far-red (740 nm) fluorescence, retrieval uncertainties, and spectral parameters. The dataset contain two SIF basis coefficients that enable reconstruction of the complete fluorescence emission spectrum using the supplementary SIF basis spectra. Additional variables include geolocation, observation time, viewing geometry, and retrieval diagnostics. Daily HDF5 files are distributed in monthly archives. By providing multi-year global observations of both fluorescence magnitude and spectral characteristics, TROFSIF supports studies of vegetation photosynthesis, phenology, productivity, ecosystem stress, and terrestrial carbon-cycle dynamics. This repository constitutes Part 2 of the complete TROFSIF dataset spanning May 2018 to July 2026. Part 1, covering May 2018 to October 2022, is available in the companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23463271).

title: National Extraction-based CO2 Emissions
description: This is a draft release of annual national emissions accounts based on extracted fossil fuels and carbonates: emissions from oxidation of the fuels (or venting of fossil CO 2 ) and decomposition of the carbonates (only in cement so far) are allocated to the country that extracted them regardless of where in the world oxidation / venting / decomposition occurs. These can be seen as a complement to territorial and consumption-based emissions (as well as emissions aligned with National Accounts). Estimates are derived from energy data published by the Energy Institute , Mohr et al. (2014) , UN Statistics Division, JODI, and the Global Carbon Budget (for both flaring/venting and cement). Where available, national emissions are reported from 1850, while the per capita series starts in 1950. These start years may be pushed back to earlier periods in future releases. The final year of data is 2025. As a draft release, there are some issues with the estimates. For example, in some years the global total is less than the sum of the individual countries reported. Further, while the global totals are in general very close to the territorial emissions estimates in GCP's fossil CO 2 dataset , there are some divergences. These things will be worked on as time permits.

title: Data and code for "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows"
description: # Data and code for "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" Version 1.0 (2026-10-23) This archive contains all data products of the study "Reservoirs worldwide retain only about one third of flood inflows" and the code that produced them. Using SWOT lake observations densified with Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery, we observed storage changes at 1,447 reservoirs in 96 countries during 5,399 floods between August 2023 and August 2026, and corrected the bias from sparse satellite sampling with daily in-situ storage from the USA, Brazil and Australia. The median reservoir retained about one third of the flood inflow (corrected retention ratio 0.33; raw satellite lower bound 0.22). ## Contents ``` reservoir_flood_retention_v1.0.zip ├── README.md this file ├── dataset/ data products of the study (about 47 MB) │ ├── README.md field-by-field documentation │ ├── D1_flood_events.csv │ ├── D2_storage_series.zip │ ├── D3_pld_grand_map.csv │ ├── D4_calibration_pairs.csv │ ├── D5_cama_scenarios.zip │ └── D6_cama_obs_module.zip └── code/ full processing code and the data needed to redraw the figures (about 82 MB) ├── README.md workflow and usage ├── LICENSE ├── scripts/ ├── data/ └── figures/ ``` ### dataset/ | File | Content | |---|---| | D1_flood_events.csv | Flood-event retention dataset (core product): 5,399 floods × 88 fields, including raw and corrected retention ratios, pre-flood headroom, GloFAS reservoir-module retention and reservoir attributes | | D2_storage_series.zip | Reservoir storage time series: SWOT-only (3,033 reservoirs) and SWOT + optical fused (2,938 reservoirs) | | D3_pld_grand_map.csv | Lookup between the SWOT Prior Lake Database and GRanD: 12,729 lakes matched to 6,719 reservoirs | | D4_calibration_pairs.csv | Satellite–in-situ calibration pairs: 732 floods at 171 reservoirs | | D5_cama_scenarios.zip | CaMa-Flood v4.3 results for seven reservoir scenarios at dam sites and downstream | | D6_cama_obs_module.zip | Observation-constrained CaMa-Flood reservoir module (Fortran), daily input tables and run scripts | D2, D5 and D6 are themselves zip files because they contain many files or large tables; unzip them where needed. See `dataset/README.md` for every field. ### code/ Scripts for the full workflow, in eight steps: | Folder | Step | |---|---| | scripts/01_swot | SWOT download, lake–reservoir matching, storage series, water-level validation | | scripts/02_optical | Sentinel-2/Landsat water-area extraction and fusion with SWOT | | scripts/03_glofas_events | GloFAS inflow, return periods, flood event detection | | scripts/04_insitu | In-situ data download (USACE CWMS, BoM, ONS) and in-situ checks | | scripts/05_calibration_drivers | Bias correction and analysis of controlling factors | | scripts/06_cama | CaMa-Flood forcing, observation-constrained module, scenario runs and comparison | | scripts/07_figures | Main figures | | scripts/08_release | Dataset release package | `code/data/` contains the inputs needed to redraw the four main figures. To redraw them: ```bash cd code/scripts/07_figures python fig_main_v8.py ``` The output PNGs are byte-identical to the figures in the paper. See `code/README.md` for the full workflow, the software environment (Python 3.9; gfortran for CaMa-Flood) and the raw data that must be downloaded separately (SWOT, GloFAS, ERA5-Land; several hundred GB in total). ## How the two folders relate - `dataset/` holds the final data products; `code/` holds the scripts that produce them and a copy of the intermediate tables needed for the figures. - `code/scripts/08_release/make_release.py` builds the files in `dataset/` from the full working data. - The Python scripts and run scripts inside `dataset/D6_cama_obs_module.zip` are identical to those in `code/scripts/06_cama/`. - All tables are linked by the GRanD reservoir identifier `GRAND_ID`; flood events are identified by `event_id` (`GRAND_ID_peakdate`). ## Main caveats 1. The bias correction is trained on in-situ data from the USA, Brazil and Australia only; applying it elsewhere is an extrapolation. The raw satellite retention ratio (`ret_wm`) is provided as a lower bound. 2. Single-event corrected retention ratios are uncertain; aggregate by reservoir, region or group. 3. All analyses use SWOT observations with quality flag good (quality_f = 0). The SWOT-only series in D2 also keep suspect observations (quality_f = 1), which should normally be removed. 4. In-situ reservoir records from USACE, ONS and BoM, and the flood storage capacity estimates of Shen et al. (2025), are not redistributed. ## Licences | Part | Licence | |---|---| | Data in `dataset/` and `code/data/` | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) | | Scripts written for this study in `code/scripts/` | MIT (`code/LICENSE`) | | Files derived from CaMa-Flood (`code/scripts/06_cama/fortran/`, `code/scripts/06_cama/gosh/`, and the module and run scripts in D6) | Apache License 2.0, as the original CaMa-Flood code (licence text in `code/scripts/06_cama/LICENSE-Apache-2.0.txt` and in D6) | Third-party sources must also be cited under their own terms: SWOT LakeSP (doi:10.5067/SWOT-LAKESP-D), GloFAS v4 and ERA5-Land (Copernicus), GRanD and Global Dam Watch, GRDL (doi:10.1029/2023WR035781), GROWL (doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.31225405), Sentinel-2 and Landsat, and the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators.

title: SeaWiFS Data by NASA Goddard
description: Consists of satellite measurements of global and regional ocean color data obtained by the Sea-viewing Wide Field-of-view Sensor, in orbit on the OrbView-2 (formerly SeaStar) platform. The concentration and predominant identity of substances and particles in the euphotic (lighted) zone of the upper ocean influences the apparent color of the ocean, which can range from deep blue to varying shades of green and ruddy brown. Living phytoplankton (which contain chlorophyll and associated photosynthetic pigments), inorganic sediments, detritus (particulate organic matter), and dissolved organic matter all contribute to the color of the ocean. The data are primarily intended for used by marine researchers. All SeaWiFS data files are in Hierarchical Data Format (HDF). [ Reference: PICES Scientific Report No. 18 2001, Proceedings of the PICES/CoML/IPRC Workshop on "Impact of Climate Variability on Observation and Prediction of Ecosystem and Biodiversity Changes in the North Pacific", http://www.pices.int/publications/scientific_reports/Report18/default.aspx. ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

title: Nimbus-7 Coastal Zone Color Scanner (CZCS) Data
description: A global ocean color data set derived from satellite observations. In most oceanic regions, the color of the ocean is primarily determined by the abundance of phytoplankton and their associated photosynthetic pigments. As phytoplankton pigment concentration increases, ocean color gradually shifts from blue to green. NASA developed the CZCS to utilize this characteristic of ocean color for the observation of pigment distribution in the oceans. The CZCS was launched on the Nimbus-7 satellite in October 1978. During the 91 months of its operation (October 1978 - June 1986), CZCS acquired nearly 68,000 images, each covering up to 2 million square kilometers of ocean surface. Data can be obtained directly at ftp://daac.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/czcs. [ Reference: PICES Scientific Report No. 18 2001, Proceedings of the PICES/CoML/IPRC Workshop on "Impact of Climate Variability on Observation and Prediction of Ecosystem and Biodiversity Changes in the North Pacific", http://www.pices.int/publications/scientific_reports/Report18/default.aspx. ] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

title: Canal-irrigated wheat in Punjab, Pakistan: district and grid-cell analysis panels, estimation code, and dated design declarations, 2015–2024

title: One island, three countries: aquaculture ponds explain the cross-border gap in mangrove loss on Borneo
description: Borneo's mangroves share one coastline, one climate and one sediment regime, yet they are governed by three countries. Using the annual Global Mangrove Watch v4.1 series and open data, this study asks why mangrove in Indonesian Kalimantan is lost faster than in Malaysian Borneo and Brunei, and tests three explanations: protected-area performance, conversion pathways and El Niño sea-level fall. Between 2010 and 2020, Kalimantan lost 1.23% of its mangrove a year, against 0.43 to 0.74% in Malaysian Borneo and 0.50% in Brunei; it held 59% of the island's mangrove and 77% of its gross loss. Matched comparisons show long-standing strict protected areas reduced loss in Malaysian Borneo by about 2 percentage points but had no detectable effect in Kalimantan. Protection nonetheless explains little of the gap: 84% of it arises in unprotected mangrove, and Sabah's 2015 upgrades of low-loss production reserves to full protection added nothing measurable. Classifying what replaced mangrove lost from 2000 to 2024 shows that conversion to aquaculture ponds, concentrated in the early 2000s, accounts for all of Kalimantan's 15.9-point excess loss, while loss away from ponds was similar in total on both sides of the border (clearing in Kalimantan and Sarawak, mostly edge change in Sabah) and oil palm replaced little mangrove. Annual loss outside conversion was lowest in El Niño years and highest in high-sea-level years, consistent with humid mangroves buffered against El Niño sea-level fall. Reducing Borneo's mangrove loss therefore depends on governing pond expansion in unprotected mangrove more than on adding protected areas. Keywords: Mangrove loss; aquaculture; protected areas; Borneo; El Niño; Global Mangrove Watch

title: Monthly Global LAI and FAPAR with Mapped Managed Land Excluded, 1982–2024 (0.25°)
description: This dataset contains monthly global leaf area index (LAI) and fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR) from January 1982 to December 2024 at 0.25° resolution. The source data are harmonized AVHRR–MODIS vegetation records described by Jeong et al. (2024, 2026). Four static masking scenarios exclude mapped managed land, pasture-associated areas, water, and permanent snow or ice. Three CCI-based masks identify 0.05° cells where the ESA-CCI/C3S managed-cover fraction reaches α = 0.05, 0.10, or 0.20 in at least three annual maps. The GLC-based mask identifies 0.05° cells classified as cropland or urban in at least three GLC_FCS30D observations. All scenarios also exclude areas where LUH2 pasture overlaps mapped grass cover. The masks are applied at 0.05° resolution before area-weighted aggregation to 0.25°. Each 0.25° value is the area-weighted mean of its valid retained 0.05° subcells. Areas retained after masking have lower mapped managed-land influence according to the selected datasets and masking criteria. The four scenarios represent alternative retained spatial domains. Two ZIP archives contain 516 monthly GeoTIFF files for each masking scenario and vegetation variable. The files use the EPSG:4326 coordinate reference system. LAI is expressed in m² m⁻², and FAPAR is dimensionless.

title: Code and derived data for "Cascading vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo"
description: This repository accompanies the article "Cascading Vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo: Dry-Season Drought, Tree-Cover Loss, and Vegetation, Lake, and Rice Responses, 2001–2025" by Pramono Putra S. Pido (Department of Geography, Universitas Indonesia). The article tests whether dry-season drought amplified by El Niño propagates from rainfall to soil moisture, vegetation, tree cover, Lake Limboto, and rice production in Gorontalo Province, on the northern arm of Sulawesi, Indonesia. The analysis compares three non-overlapping zones within the province (the North zone, the South zone, and the Limboto Basin) and also covers the province as a whole; tree-cover loss is examined in the HydroBASINS level 8 watershed unit that contains Lake Limboto and in the province. The analysis combines openly available satellite, reanalysis, and climate-index data with official rice statistics: CHIRPS v2.0 rainfall, expressed as the 1- and 3-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-1 and SPI-3), and ERA5-Land soil moisture and skin temperature for 1981–2025; GPM IMERG rainfall and SMAP L4 soil moisture as comparison products; the MODIS Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI) for 2001–2025, computed with and without pixel-quality filtering; Hansen Global Forest Change v1.12 tree-cover loss and ESA WorldCover 2021 at 30 m; FIRMS active-fire detections on a 1 km grid and MODIS MCD64A1 burned area; the water area of Lake Limboto from JRC Global Surface Water (1984–2021) and Sentinel-2 (July–October, 2019–2025); MODIS EVI over cropland in the Limboto Basin (2018–2024); the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the monthly Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly, and the Dipole Mode Index (DMI); and rice harvested area, yield, and production for 2018–2025 from BPS-Statistics Indonesia and BPS-Statistics of Gorontalo Province. The Python scripts compute July–October (dry-season) composites; lagged correlations with an effective sample size, prewhitened cross-correlations, and bidirectional Granger causality tests, including conditional tests, along the monthly chain from rainfall to soil moisture to vegetation; correlations, partial correlations, and Granger tests between the climate indices and SPI-1; zone-specific regressions of the vegetation indices on SPI-3 and a pooled Zone × SPI-3 model with standard errors clustered by year; comparisons of tree-cover loss between dry-season drought years and other years; a two-way (cell and year) fixed-effects model that relates the tree-cover loss rate of 1 km cells to active-fire detections, together with a partition of the excess loss in dry years between fire-detected cells and cells without fire detections; annual summaries of the water area of Lake Limboto; summaries of rainfall, soil moisture, and cropland EVI by cropping-season window, set against the rice statistics; and a simulation of the effect of the ONI running mean on the Granger test. The archive Limboto_cascading_vulnerability_v1.0.zip contains the Google Earth Engine scripts that extract the satellite and reanalysis data; the Earth Engine exports and the small external input files used in the reported run; the Python scripts that compute the numbers, tables, and figures reported in the article and its Supplementary Material; the outputs of that run; Figures 1–10 in English and Indonesian; and a manifest that lists the size and SHA-256 checksum of every file. The README, which is also provided as a separate file, gives the order in which the scripts are run and links each table and figure in the article to its output files. The station data, the publications read by two of the scripts, and the FAO GAUL boundaries and the zone polygons derived from them are not redistributed; the README explains how to obtain or recreate them. The code is released under the MIT License. The README, the results, the figures, and the Earth Engine exports are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0), without prejudice to the terms of the source datasets; the files in data/external/ remain under their providers' terms.

title: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - Models and data sets for the ocean sink estimate in the Global Carbon Budget
description: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - 2026 Release This dataset provides surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs), surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products) and the ocean inverse model OCIM (interior ocean observationally-constrained estimate). Types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series (2) one file per GOBM and simulation (A, B) with gridded fields (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations (4) the gridded file of the natural steady state fluxes from simulation B of six GOBMs that exclude riverine fluxes and have a globally-integrated natural steady state CO2 flux within ± 0.2 GtC yr-1. This data is used to subtract the natural steady state fluxes from the fCO2-products in regional anaylses (Figures 14 and 15) (5) A file for the gridded CO2 fluxes and one file for the global time-series of the ocean inverse model OCIM (simulations C and B) that is used as an observationally-constrained interior ocean data-product in GCB. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2026, are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 spreadsheet (https://globalcarbonbudget.org/datahub/). The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2026 paper, the river flux adjustment needs to be added and an adjustment for the natural steady state fluxes needs to be subtracted from the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (River flux adjustment: North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2026 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Three of the ten fCO2-products (UExP-FFN-U, JMA-MLR and AOML-ET) include a temperature adjustment to correct the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files. fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude (3) One file 'GCB2026_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. (4) One file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_1959_2025.nc) that contains the gridded field and one file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc) that contains the global time-series of CO2 fluxes of OCIM for simulations C and B. Further data availability: Access and download the additional data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ In addition to the zenodo deposit, the complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. In addition to the data described above, this Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination: The GCB2026-OCEAN data sets were contributed by international research groups. The creators listed in this record include the GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators and a representative of each contributing data set. title: Zambia Decoupling Dataset, 1950–2024: Annual Emissions, Economy, Energy and Land-Use Indicators
description: The Zambia Decoupling Dataset 1950–2024 is an annual country-level time series for Zambia. It has 75 rows, one per year from 1950 to 2024, and 62 columns, in a CSV of about 29 KB. It was assembled to test whether Zambia’s economic growth has been decoupled from its carbon emissions. It brings together fossil, cement and land-use CO₂, primary energy, electricity generation by source, population, GDP and forest area. Sources are the Global Carbon Budget 2025, Jones et al. via Our World in Data, the Energy Institute and EIA, Ember, World Bank World Development Indicators via Gapminder, the Maddison Project 2023 and FAO’s Forest Resources Assessment 2020. Beyond the copied series, the file includes per-capita and intensity indicators, and a set of exploratory electricity-sector CO₂ estimates built on assumed emission factors. The manuscript does not use those estimates. Coverage differs by variable and thins out in 2023–24, and blank cells are gaps rather than zeros. The main caveats are that land-use CO₂ is model-based and uncertain, that primary energy excludes traditional biomass, and that the 2024 hydro value is provisional. The GDP series also differ between Maddison and the World Bank, so use one series per analysis. The full variable dictionary and handling guidance are in the data description doc.

description: This dataset provides global monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°, with the latest update extending through September 2026. The estimates are generated using a deep learning–based framework that employs a convolutional neural network as its backbone and incorporates a mask fusion module to address spatially missing input data. The framework integrates satellite observations, meteorological reanalysis data, and temporal and spatial encoding features to estimate anthropogenic CO₂ emissions at a global scale. The data are provided in NetCDF format on a global 0.1° × 0.1° grid (1800 × 3600 cells) using the WGS84 geographic coordinate system. title: Global Mangrove Watch: GMW v4.0 Reference Samples 2020
description: We randomly defined 44 sites for which approximately 1000 points were randomly stratified using the mangrove / non-mangrove proportions of the scene. A minimum of 250 mangrove points were generated, and therefore, the total number of points for a site could be higher than 1000. In total, 49,600 points were generated. The points were individually assessed using a combination of the Sentinel-2 imagery for 2020, the NICFI Planet base maps and higher resolution Google base maps to identify the points as mangroves or non-mangroves. These points are provided within the gmw_v4_baseline_acc_pts_all_sites.geojson vector layer where the attribute ‘ref_col’ identifies each point as “Mangrove” or “Other”.

title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate and Regime-Aware Evolutionary Optimization for Climate-Adaptive Eco-Hydrological Wetland Restoration
description: Overview This record contains the de-identified eco-hydrological restoration benchmark used to evaluate PG-RAMEO (Physics-Guided Regime-Aware Multi-objective Evolutionary Optimization), a surrogate-assisted many-objective framework for climate-adaptive wetland restoration. The benchmark couples two-dimensional Saint–Venant shallow-water hydrodynamics with multi-decadal vegetation, salinity and soil-organic-carbon succession across 240 wetland restoration units spanning three geomorphological archetypes (Floodplain Marsh, n = 96; Coastal Estuarine, n = 84; Depressional Peatland, n = 60) under three hydro-climatic forcing regimes (Historical, CMIP6 SSP2-4.5, CMIP6 SSP5-8.5). Source data and de-identification. Hydrological boundary conditions, bathymetric depths, porewater salinity gradients and archetype proportions are anchored to three public monitoring repositories: the USGS Everglades Depth Estimation Network (EDEN) and NWIS ( sofia.usgs.gov/eden , waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis ), the CAMELS catchment dataset ( ral.ucar.edu/solutions/products/camels ), and the Global Lakes and Wetlands Database GLWD v2 / HydroSHEDS ( hydrosheds.org/products/glwd ). All station identifiers and geographic quasi-identifiers have been replaced by randomized hash codes ( WRU_xxxx ), calendar dates are omitted, and the spatial partition is encoded in the split column (train = 144, val = 36, test = 60). Contents data/processed/ — granular evaluation records (8 files, 8,315 data rows): wetland_basins_metadata.csv — 240 rows. Physical, hydrological and biogeochemical attributes of every restoration unit: area, drainage area, cell count, control structures, inflow, mean depth, hydroperiod, reference evapotranspiration, salinity, initial biomass, soil organic carbon, Manning roughness, bathymetric discontinuity, critical salinity (22.5 ppt) and anoxic (42.0 d) thresholds, and sensor missing rate. method_basin_regime_evaluations.csv — 5,760 rows (240 units × 3 regimes × 8 methods). Four-objective hypervolume ( hv ), igd_plus , candidate and feasible counts, ecological regime violation counts by mechanism ( salinity_violations , anoxia_violations , desiccation_violations ), surrogate state errors ( rmse_h , rmse_biomass , mass_balance_err ), individual objective scores ( obj_hsi , obj_ncsr , obj_faee , obj_lcec ), and computational speedup . seed_level_test_runs.csv — 720 rows (30 seeds × 3 regimes × 8 methods) on the held-out test split, the input to all paired significance tests. ablation_basin_evaluations.csv — 1,440 rows across the eight variants ( Full , Abl-C1 , Abl-C1b , Abl-C2 , Abl-C2a , Abl-C2b , Abl-C3 , Backbone ). surrogate_operator_grid.csv — accuracy and mass-balance consistency of seven neural and statistical operator architectures. sensitivity_sweep_grid.csv — sweeps over flux weight λ flux ∈ [0.0, 2.0], high-fidelity query ratio ρ HF ∈ [0.05, 0.20], repair step η rep ∈ [0.02, 0.40] and solver budget B HF ∈ [60, 480]. pareto_front_solutions.csv — representative non-dominated solutions per method. regime_shift_trajectories.csv — monthly coupled state trajectories ( S ( t ), h ( t ), B ( t )) over a 36-month SSP5-8.5 compound drought–flood sequence, comparing unrepaired offspring, random-mutation repair and CR-FEH directional physics-Jacobian repair. data/derived/ — the summary tables behind every reported result (7 files, 182 rows): main_table.csv (primary comparison on val and test), regime_archetype_table.csv (subgroup breakdown), ablation_table.csv , surrogate_consistency_table.csv , sensitivity_table.csv , dataset_summary_table.csv , and failure_mode_breakdown.csv (violation counts by physical failure mechanism under SSP5-8.5). Every file in data/derived/ is regenerated deterministically from data/processed/ by the companion code record. Reuse Released under CC BY 4.0. If you use these data, please cite this record together with the associated article. The columns obj_hsi , obj_ncsr , obj_faee and obj_lcec denote habitat suitability index, net carbon sequestration rate, flood attenuation efficiency and lifecycle engineering cost respectively; ehr_fr is the ecological regime feasibility ratio.
keywords: surrogate-assisted evolutionary optimization; multi-fidelity graph neural operator; physics-informed neural networks; shallow-water equations; wetland eco-hydrological restoration; climate adaptation; wetland restoration benchmark; multi-objective optimization

title: Harmonised fractional land cover time series for the Mediterranean region derived from ESA CCI LC and GLC_FCS30D
description: Overview This dataset provides harmonised annual fractional land cover representations derived from ESA Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (ESA CCI LC) and GLC_FCS30D for the Mediterranean area. The original categorical land cover legends were reclassified into ten broad, FAO LCCS-compatible classes, following the thematic harmonisation approach described by Bratic et al. (2023), and aggregated to a common 0.1-degree latitude-longitude grid. Each valid grid cell contains class-specific fractional cover values between zero and one, describing the mapped composition rather than a single dominant class. The datasets support cross-product comparisons of multi-temporal land cover composition. Fractions remain dependent on the accuracy and temporal characteristics of their original source products. Included files cci_reclass_lc_fractions_1992_2022.nc - ESA CCI LC-derived fractional land cover dataset (nominal coverage 1992-2022) glc_reclass_lc_fractions_1985_2022.nc - GLC_FCS30D-derived fractional land cover dataset (the source maps are annual from 2000 to 2022, with earlier maps in 1985, 1990 and 1995). GLANCE_LC_Fractions_User_Guide_v1.pdf - technical documentation including the complete thematic crosswalk. Data structure and methods NetCDF variables: `forest`, `shrubland`, `grassland`, `cropland`, `wetland`, `lichens_and_mosses`, `bareland`, `built_up`, `water`, `permanent_ice_and_snow`. Dimensions: `year`, `y`, `x`. Coordinate reference system: EPSG:4326. Nominal grid: 0.1 degrees; fractional values are dimensionless in [0, 1]. No-data source pixels are excluded from the valid-pixel denominator. For the full legend and reclassification rules, refer to the User Guide. Project context Developed within ESA GLANCE (AGricultural Land AbandoNment and ClimatE change) project, which investigates Mediterranean agricultural land abandonment and its interactions with forest dynamics and water, energy and carbon cycles. Project: https://climate.esa.int/en/Cross_ECV_Projects/glance . Source datasets and required attribution ESA CCI Land Cover / Copernicus Climate Data Store: https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.006f2c9a . The applicable ESA CCI LC source licence requires explicit credit to the ESA Climate Change Initiative Land Cover project. Licence text: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/licences/satellite-land-cover GLC_FCS30D: Liu, L., Zhang, X., and Zhao, T. (2023), original Zenodo version v1, DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8239305 . Licence: CC BY 4.0. Associated data description: Zhang et al. (2024), Earth System Science Data, DOI: https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-1353-2024 Thematic harmonisation reference: Bratic, G., Oxoli, D., and Brovelli, M. A. (2023). Map of Land Cover Agreement: Ensambling Existing Datasets for Large-Scale Training Data Provision. Remote Sensing , 15(15), 3774. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15153774 . Rights and re-use The GLC-derived component is subject to GLC_FCS30D CC BY 4.0 upstream attribution. The CCI-derived component is subject to the ESA CCI Land Cover licence, which explicitly allows educational/scientific use with attribution but does not explicitly establish unrestricted commercial redistribution.

title: A 1-km monthly surface air temperature dataset for Arctic land (2000–2025)
description: Monthly mean near-surface (2 m) air temperature at 1-km resolution over Arctic land for March 2000 to December 2025 (310 monthly fields), reconstructed by an ensemble of Random Forest, LightGBM and XGBoost regressors trained separately for each calendar month on station observations (CRUTEM5 station archive, release 5.1.0.0) with MODIS predictors: Terra and Aqua day-time and night-time land surface temperature (MOD11A2, MYD11A2), Terra and Aqua NDVI (MOD13A3, MYD13A3), MCD12Q1.061 LC_Type5 land-cover fractions, latitude and longitude. Elevation is deliberately not a predictor; the reasons, and the measured consequence, are given in the accompanying paper. What changed in version 3.0. The predictor values of the training table are now pooled from the same gridded stacks the prediction reads, rather than from a separate extraction of the granules, so that training and prediction use one source. The land surface temperatures entering training are screened with three checks of the GHCN-Daily quality-assurance system at their published thresholds (world-record exceedance, a climatological outlier check at six biweight standard deviations, and spatial corroboration against the nearest neighbours); 3860 values, 0.50 % of the land surface temperatures, were found to be invalid — seven satellite month-year composites had reached the table with MODIS fill values that had not been masked when the monthly means were formed — and are treated as missing. The gridded predictor stacks were checked for the same signature and carry none of it, so no field of version 2.0 was affected by that defect. The models were refitted and the whole record re-predicted. Hold-out accuracy at the 120 withheld stations improves from 1.50 to 1.48 °C root-mean-square error. Data are on the native MODIS 1-km sinusoidal grid (34 tiles h09–h26, v00–v02, mosaicked to 3600 × 21600 cells, pixel 926.625433 m) with 2-D latitude/longitude and a CF grid mapping, so no resampling has been applied to the values. Water pixels are removed with the MOD44W mask and Greenland is excluded. Each annual file ( ArcticSAT1km_monthly_YYYY.nc , CF-1.8 netCDF4) contains: sat — monthly mean near-surface air temperature (°C), ensemble mean of the three models; sat_model_spread — the per-pixel standard deviation of the three individual model predictions for the same month, a measure of structural (model-choice) uncertainty. Both are stored as int16 with scale_factor 0.01 °C (precision 0.01 °C), zlib-compressed, chunked one MODIS tile per chunk. ArcticSAT1km_grid.nc holds the static 2-D lat , lon , the MOD44W land_mask and tile_index ; ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc holds the monthly climatologies, the warm (April–October) and cold (November–March) seasonal means, the number of valid years per pixel and the mean inter-model spread. Note on coverage: a fixed subset of land cells never has a valid MODIS/Terra night-time LST retrieval. The pattern is static — identical in every month and year of a given tile — and varies strongly between tiles (measured examples, as a fraction of the tile's land cells: h22v02 0 %, h24v02 12.3 %, h19v02 43.4 %). There the missing night-LST predictor enters the models as zero, so the prediction rests on the remaining predictors and is less well constrained. Nothing is blanked and no quality-flag variable is provided; every file carries this note in its comment global attribute, and README_data.md lists it under "Known limitations". The climatologies in ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc use the period 2001–2025 (25 years), the earliest period in which all twelve calendar months are complete, since January and February begin in 2001. MANIFEST_md5.txt allows md5sum -c verification, MANIFEST_sizes.tsv lists file sizes, PROVENANCE.json gives a machine-readable provenance record, and README_data.md documents every variable, the method and the known limitations. Processing code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23490034 ( https://github.com/SeoyeonLee-rosee/arctic-1km-sat ).

title: Data and code for comparing the cooling of urban water bodies and green spaces across the aridity gradient of 229 Chinese cities
description: This record contains the data and the code of the main calculations of a study that compares the daytime and nighttime land surface temperature (LST) of urban water bodies, green spaces and built-up land in 229 Chinese cities on a 1 km grid (June–August, 2018–2023). Contents: data/cells_1km.csv.gz: 746,554 cells of 1 km with LST by day and night, water occurrence, vegetation and built-up shares, elevation, background air and dewpoint temperature, NDVI, evapotranspiration and residents; data/cities.csv: the 229 cities with their aridity index and zone and summer climate; data/results/: city-level and station-level results underlying the figures and tables of the paper; code/: Python code of the main calculations (cooling intensity, the adjusted advantage of Eq. 1, the cover effects of Eq. 2 and the water demand), with a README that lists the variables, sources and steps. Source datasets: Global Urban Boundaries, MODIS Aqua LST (MYD11A2, MYD11A1), ESA WorldCover v200, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land, TerraClimate, MODIS NDVI (MOD13A2), ET (MOD16A2GF) and albedo (MCD43A3), PML-V2.2a, Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2, WorldPop 2020, gridded GDP per capita (Kummu et al., 2025) and the Integrated Surface Database. Only derived values are included; the source data are available from their providers. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information 2026.

title: Bitemporal Sentinel-1/2, forest-loss and forest-carbon cells for 16 disaster and clearing sites in Indonesia
description: One row per 500 m forest cell inside an 80 × 80 km box around each of 16 Indonesian sites: 11 natural disasters (peat fires, a pyroclastic flow, eruptions, a tsunami, landslides, a cyclone, floods) and five human-clearing reference sites, 268,217 cells in total. Each cell has Sentinel-2 optical indices and Sentinel-1 radar backscatter before and after the event, the Hansen Global Forest Change loss label of the event years, terrain, ESA CCI above-ground biomass, and the carbon stock and carbon lost. Also included: independent event footprints (MODIS burned area, a Sentinel-1 flood signal, hazard-zone rules), out-of-fold and leave-one-site-out model predictions, attribution and benchmark results, supplementary tables S1–S6, Hansen loss time series 2001–2024, daily weather, hazard records, a data dictionary, and a notebook that reproduces every number of the related article (204 checks). Dataset_Description_NusaCarbon.pdf (3 pages) explains every folder and column and links every source. All inputs are public: ESA / EU Copernicus (Sentinel-1/2, Copernicus DEM, CCI Biomass), University of Maryland and Google (Hansen GFC v1.12), NASA (MODIS MCD64A1, POWER), ECMWF (ERA5), NOAA NCEI and USGS. See README.md for the folders, definitions and source terms. How to use: unzip Indonesia_disaster_forest_cells_v1.zip, read README.md, and join any files on case_id, row, col. To reproduce the article, run pip install -r code/requirements.txt , open code/reproduce_paper_results.ipynb and Run All. Related article: R. Hans et al., "Mechanism-Stratified Detection and Quantification of Disaster-Induced Forest Carbon Loss in Indonesia Using Bitemporal Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 Multispectral Observations", 2026.
keywords: forest carbon; Sentinel-1; Sentinel-2; forest loss; natural disaster; remote sensing; Indonesia; machine learning

title: SIAS: Stem Internal Architecture Spectrum: grass stem-architecture trait data and analysis code
description: Trait data, analysis code and result tables for the hollow-versus-solid stem-architecture dimension of the grasses (Poaceae; Cyperaceae as a solid-stemmed outgroup). DATA: 12,208 Poales species (11,602 Poaceae + 606 Cyperaceae) with stem hollowness and woodiness states compiled from Kew GrassBase, Flora of China (iPlant) and the official Flora of North America Poaceae treatment (2,054 species with documented stem state, 1,448 of them grasses); species- and genus-level environment (GBIF coordinates, WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids, with CHELSA V2.1 and TerraClimate cross-checks, Last-Glacial-Maximum anomalies and the Global Aridity Index v3); an 11,287-tip Open Tree phylogeny with fossil-calibrated time-tree derivatives; and the result tables behind every manuscript number. CODE: the final analysis and figure chain (phylogenetic logistic regression, dual-axis independence tests, ancestral states, HiSSE/BiSSE diversification, Euler biomechanics, hydraulic bounds, environment PCA, coverage/resolution sensitivity matrices), the regex-extraction protocols for all grass sources, the LLM-extraction protocol of the eudicot screen, and the PCD expression-screen subproject. Entry points: run_all_analyses.sh / reproduce_analyses.sh (R 4.5: phytools, phylolm, MCMCglmm, caper, ape; Python 3.13, see requirements.txt; HiSSE fits included as RDS). NOT REDISTRIBUTED: raw floristic texts, rasters, GBIF downloads, source trees and RNA-seq reads (licensing and size). License: CC BY-NC 4.0 (data and code).

title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data
description: This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP. From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it. The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1); • The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp); • Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted); • Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution. NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts. A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code. Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010.
prose_spatial_evidence_sentence: The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimate

title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Global mangrove stand age in 2023
description: This dataset provides global mangrove stand age in 2023 at a spatial resolution of 30 m, derived from the annual mangrove extent maps of the Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics (CGMD) dataset. Stand age is defined as the number of consecutive years of mangrove presence, counted backwards from 2023 to the first year of the most recent uninterrupted period detected by CGMD. Mangroves continuously present throughout 1984–2023 are assigned to the ≥40-year age class, as their establishment may predate the satellite record. The attribute fields include age — Mangrove stand age in years. A value of 40 represents stands aged ≥40 years. Area_ha — Mangrove patch area in hectares, calculated using the World Behrmann equal-area projection. Region — Geographic region in which the mangrove patch is located. The dataset is currently under embargo and will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the associated manuscript. Please contact us if you require access before its public release.
prose_spatial_evidence_sentence: This dataset provides global mangrove stand age in 2023 at a spatial resolution of 30 m, derived from the annual mangrove extent maps of the Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics (CGMD) dataset.

title: Mangrove canopy height measurements from GEDI spaceborne LiDAR in 2023 and 2024
description: This dataset provides mangrove canopy height measurements acquired by the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) in 2023 and 2024. Canopy height estimates from the GEDI Level 2A RH98 metric were corrected using ground elevations from DeltaDTM to reduce height underestimation and improve agreement with independent airborne LiDAR measurements. Each footprint was also assigned a mangrove stand age from our global mangrove age map for 2023 . The attribute fields include Attribute — GEDI shot number identifying each footprint. year — Year of the GEDI observation. rh98 — Original RH98 canopy height estimate from the GEDI Level 2A product, in metres. rh98_Corre — Corrected canopy height estimate using DeltaDTM ground elevations, in metres. age — Mangrove stand age in 2023, derived from our age map and expressed in years. Stands continuously present throughout 1984–2023 are classified as ≥40 years old. The dataset is currently under embargo and will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the associated manuscript. Please contact us if you require access before its public release.

title: Bolivia Fire benchmark data and reproduction artifacts
description: Bolivia Fire version 0.1.0 provides a weekly VIIRS S-NPP standard-processing satellite-detection benchmark for Bolivia and its retained reproduction evidence. The strict panel contains 37,146 cells, 678 Monday issues from 2013-01-07 through 2025-12-29 and 25,184,988 cell-weeks. The target is a selected satellite detection, not a count of fires, ignitions or burned area, and is not an official warning. Three independently extractable ZIP64 archives use repository-relative paths: benchmark-data : panel, cells, CHIRPS rainfall, MOD13A2 vegetation, MapBiomas Collection 4 land-cover and combined features, schemas and manifests. reproduction-artifacts : configurations, environment lockfile, fitted models and calibrators, retained predictions and alternative-learner cached vectors, evaluation history, figure JSON, family-specific producing revisions and historical source registries. raw-inputs : FIRMS CSV snapshots, MOD13A2 AppEEARS subset, CHIRPS native windows, MapBiomas aggregate exports, boundaries, GeoNames and outage HTML. Top-level README, licence notices, data dictionary, member inventory and SHA-256 checksums describe the files. Dataset reuse is supported. Recalculation from saved predictions is partially supported: strict primary validation/test exports and alternative-learner cached vectors are retained; rainfall, sensitivity and vegetation, land-cover and combined covariate per-row prediction exports and standalone scored-row masks are absent. Their result records and fitted models remain available. Recomputing any final-test metric is a logged test opening under the frozen protocol; release verification does not open the test. Rebuilding from raw inputs is partially supported. Global CHIRPS rasters, MODIS HDF granules and native MapBiomas 30 m maps are not supplied; MapBiomas re-extraction requires an Earth Engine account. Operational live forecasts, serving derivatives, regenerable caches, temporary files and logs are excluded. Later environmental experiments are separate from the original CHIRPS comparison; retained 2026 availability evidence does not establish a completed confirmation evaluation. Known discrepancies include an older unmatched cell-place manifest hash, fourteen unretained intermediate states, the MOD13A2 acquisition AOI buffer of 0.05 degrees versus the registered 0.1 degrees, and CatBoost GPU digit-level nondeterminism. See the record README for details and producing-code revisions. Load serialized model files only from trusted sources. Compiled and derived data are licensed under CC BY 4.0 . Upstream raw inputs retain NASA open-data/public-domain or attribution terms detailed in LICENSES.md, including CHIRPS, MapBiomas and GeoNames CC BY 4.0 and GeoBolivia public-domain boundaries. Code is separately MIT licensed at Cupesi/bolivia-fire . Cite the dataset version and the software separately.

title: Pre- and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and elevation differences for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli/Rasuwa catastrophic flood
description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal and Tibet. We provide here pre-event and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from Pléiades, SPOT6 and SPOT5 stereo-images. Date were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES. The collection includes three files : Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_pre-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_post-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_dh.tif =========================== Methods The post-event DEM is purely based on Pleiades stereo images. The pre-event DEM is based mostly Pléiades and SPOT6 stereopairs. A small fraction of the pre-event DEM was derived from 10 m SPOT5-HRS images. All DEMs were generated at a ground sampling distance of 4 m using the semiglobal matching algorithm of the Ames Stereo Pipeline (Beyer et al., 2018; Shean et al., 2016) and the processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). A ground sampling distance of 10 m was used for SPOT5-HRS. All individual DEMs were first co-registered and vertically adjusted to the Copernicus 30 (GLO-30) DEM, masking out glaciers using the Randolph Glacier Inventory v7 (RGI 7.0 consortium, 2023). Next, the individual pre- and post-event DEMs were co-registered in pairs to construct the most accurate DoD possible. Finally, those individual DoDs were mosaicked in a single map of elevation difference. The uncertainty on the mean elevation change was calculated using the patch method (Dussaillant et al., 2018). This approach aims to empirically determine the uncertainty associated with the mean elevation change by sampling patches (or tiles) of stable terrain of various sizes to constrain the decay of error with increasing averaging area (Miles et al., 2018; Wagnon et al., 2021). The stable terrain was defined here as excluding glaciers and a buffer around the river channels where erosion or deposition has occurred. For a 1 km² averaging area, the 1-sigma (68th percentile) error and the 2-sigma (95th percentile) error were calculated to be ±0.8 and ±1.8 m, respectively. Beyer, R. A., Alexandrov, O., and McMichael, S.: The Ames Stereo Pipeline: NASA's Open Source Software for Deriving and Processing Terrain Data, Earth and Space Science, 5, 537–548, https://doi.org/10.1029/2018EA000409, 2018. Deschamps-Berger, C., Gascoin, S., Berthier, E., Deems, J., Gutmann, E., Dehecq, A., Shean, D., and Dumont, M.: Snow depth mapping from stereo satellite imagery in mountainous terrain: evaluation using airborne laser-scanning data, The Cryosphere, 14, 2925–2940, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-14-2925-2020, 2020. Dussaillant, I., Berthier, E., and Brun, F.: Geodetic Mass Balance of the Northern Patagonian Icefield from 2000 to 2012 Using Two Independent Methods, Front. Earth Sci., 6, 8, https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2018.00008, 2018. Miles, E. S., Watson, C. S., Brun, F., Berthier, E., Esteves, M., Quincey, D. J., Miles, K. E., Hubbard, B., and Wagnon, P.: Glacial and geomorphic effects of a supraglacial lake drainage and outburst event, Everest region, Nepal Himalaya, The Cryosphere, 12, 3891–3905, https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-12-3891-2018, 2018. title: Simulated OCO-2 data, split tables, trained model weights, and predictive artifacts for amortized probabilistic CO2 retrieval
description: Simulated OCO-2 soundings and everything needed to reproduce the amortized probabilistic retrieval described in the accompanying paper. Version 3 adds the operational a priori of every reference sounding in February, March and July 2020 (oco2_apriori.tar.gz): the a priori state vector and its covariance, and the a priori XCO 2 and its pressure-weighting function. These are the prior baselines added to the paper in its second revision. Every other archive is unchanged from version 2. Version 2 adds, to the February 2020 delivery already in version 1: the reference-disjoint, within-reference, all-February and training-size split tables, each with the standardization constants estimated from its own training partition (oco2_splits.tar.gz); the trained checkpoints of all six models on each of the three splits reported in the paper (oco2_model_weights_v2.tar.gz); the two held-out months, March and July 2020, as the archives the scoring jobs consumed — spectra, ACOS profile covariances, covariates and the month split table (oco2_month_202003_full.tar.gz, oco2_month_202007_full.tar.gz); and the per-sounding predictive artifacts from which every table and figure in the paper is regenerated without a GPU (oco2_scoring_artifacts.tar.gz). Version 1's archives are included unchanged. oco2_model_weights.tar.gz is the original submission's checkpoints, kept for provenance and superseded by the _v2 archive. The paper's numbers come from the reference-disjoint split table group_split_v1_cov.csv and the _v2 weights. CONTENTS.md describes each archive and SHA256SUMS.txt covers all of them. The code that reads them is at https://github.com/acallesalda/oco2-amortized-uq, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22667577 ; scripts/get_data.sh downloads, verifies and unpacks everything to the paths the code expects. The simulation experiment, its a priori and the operational ACOS L2FP retrievals were produced at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

title: Knowledge graph and dataset of global storms (1990–2023)
description: Storms of the eleven storm subtypes recorded in the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) from 1990 to 2023, in 3,492 storm-country records, with the hazard, exposure, vulnerability and cascade context that can shape their impacts. For each record with administrative units from Geo-Disasters, hazard and exposure measures suited to its subtype were read over the storm's units and days in Google Earth Engine: ERA5 and ERA5-Land, the Gridded Population of the World v4, the Global Human Settlement Layer, SRTM, ESA WorldCover, the low elevation coastal zone grid v3, MERRA-2, CHIRPS and Global Mangrove Watch. Storm surge comes from the Global Tide and Surge Model v3, and best tracks from IBTrACS, with wind fields modelled in CLIMADA. Displacement records of the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) and appeals of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) are matched to storms. Vulnerability comes from UNDP's Human Development Index and the World Bank's World Development Indicators and Worldwide Governance Indicators. Cascades link storms to disasters that struck the same area within 91 days. Every value has a status column and, when empty, a gap column that gives the reason, and every link states its method and confidence. Files: - Tables of comma-separated values, one per class of the graph, linked by the keys in schema.yaml - storms_public.ttl.gz: the Resource Description Framework knowledge graph (Turtle), linked to Wikidata, with its vocabulary, SHACL shapes and VoID description - data_dictionary.csv: every column, its unit and its meaning - query1.rq–query6.rq: the competency questions in SPARQL Storms of the eleven storm subtypes recorded in the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT) from 1990 to 2023, in 3,492 storm-country records, with the hazard, exposure, vulnerability and cascade context that can shape their impacts. EM-DAT's values are not redistributed, as its licence forbids it. Records are keyed by EM-DAT's disaster number, and users can obtain the values from CRED at https://public.emdat.be. The processing code rebuilds the full dataset, with the SQLite database and the complete graph, from a user's own export.

title: Riparian agroforestry insetting in the climate refugia of the Paraná–Paraguay Basin: data and code
description: This dataset provides the result tables and the analysis code underlying the article "From phantom to functional: riparian agroforestry insetting for fruit-eating migratory fish" (submitted to Academia Environmental Sciences and Sustainability). The study starts from the climate refugia identified for two fruit-eating migratory fishes of the Parana-Paraguay Basin, Piaractus mesopotamicus and Myloplus tiete, in do Couto et al. (2026), Academia Biology 4(2), doi 10.20935/AcadBiol8362. Within the 1935 refugia cells of 10 km that require riparian restoration, it maps the riparian vegetation deficit in 100 m buffers, estimates the potential carbon dioxide sequestration, compares the 20-year net present value of passive regeneration, assisted regeneration and agroforestry with yerba mate and native fruit trees, and ranks micro-basins into investment tiers with a composite insetting index. The dataset contains three parts. 1. Refugia cells (GeoPackage, EPSG:6933). The 1935 cells of 10 km x 10 km that require riparian restoration, with the attributes inherited from the previous study. 2. Tables (CSV and JSON). Riparian vegetation deficit per micro-basin and landscape composition per cell; current and reference above-ground biomass, soil organic carbon and potential carbon dioxide sequestration of the 450,512 riparian pixels of 1 ha, with centroid coordinates; for the 171,192 restorable pixels with carbon gain, the climatic suitability of yerba mate, the land opportunity cost, the net present value of the three scenarios, the internal rate of return and the payback period; the 10,000 Monte Carlo draws and the Sobol indices of the economic assumptions; the five sub-indices and the composite insetting index per pixel; and the index, carbon, net present value and investment tier of the 2462 micro-basins. A pixel identifier links all pixel tables, and micro-basins are identified by the HydroBASINS level 10 code. 3. Code. The Python and Google Earth Engine scripts of the five phases of the analysis, of the successive re-runs and of the figures, including the final economic analysis (spatial land cost, suitability-scaled revenue, Monte Carlo simulation and Sobol decomposition) and the script that audits the consistency of the results. Monetary values are given in Brazilian reais and in United States dollars, converted at R$5.4443 per USD (mean PTAX selling rate of the Central Bank of Brazil from 16 October 2024 to 15 October 2026). The input datasets (HydroRIVERS, HydroBASINS, MapBiomas, ESA CCI Biomass, SoilGrids, JRC Global Surface Water, Global Dam Watch, GBIF and WorldClim) are not redistributed and are available from their providers. The dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY 4.0). Please cite this dataset and the associated article.

title: 16 October 2022 Pléiades (CNES) pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Rasuwa catastrophic flood
description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Rasuwa region in Nepal and Tibet : https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/ We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades stereo acquired on the 16 October 2022, 4 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The collection includes two DEM: 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_20m_aligned.tif 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total DEMs in 2x2m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean’s dem_align implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). 2022-10-16_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the 2 m and 20 m described above DEMs retaining the highest resolution where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. title: Global-scale streamflow simulation framework used in the paper of "Abrupt surface water decline during 2023–2024 record warming"
description: Summary: This repository contains the data and source code for a global-scale streamflow simulation framework utilizing an ensemble of machine learning models. The methodology addresses the challenge of hydrological variability by implementing a climate-zone-specific training approach. Results from the Step 3 script can be extrapolated globally to simulate monthly streamflow across all HydroSHEDS basins in the subsequent step. Key technical features: Specialized ensembles: The framework employs five machine learning architectures: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, SVM, Neural Networks, and Gaussian Process Regression. Climate segmentation: Basins are categorized using an Aridity Index (AI) threshold of 0.65. Asymmetric weighting: To mitigate common overestimation issues in arid hydrology, dry-region models are trained with a 2x penalty for overestimation errors. Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA): Individual model outputs are integrated using climate-zone-specific BMA weights to produce a robust final simulation. Dataset contents: Input data: Compiled monthly training features, observed monthly streamflow for 150 basins (lat/long for each gauge provided), optimized hyperparameters, and geospatial shapefiles. Output data: Fully trained model objects, calibrated annual time series, and performance evaluation visualizations. Source code: A comprehensive MATLAB script for data imputation, model training, and metric calculation (see step3_ML_DL_fulltraining_inputs_outputs_rep3_PWeighted_optim.m). Temporal Coverage: 1991 – 2025.
