Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes albopictus
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes albopictus*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 which is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes aegypti*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047a-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-aegypti). ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for three other climate change scenarios (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 6.0), as well as results produced by different climate models, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Land Cover Map
description: ### Overview The global land use and land cover maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution for 2000 and 2020. The GLAD laboratory used the spatiotemporally consistent [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard) to quantify changes in forest extent and height, cropland, built-up lands, surface water, and perennial snow and ice extent over the twenty year period. Each thematic product was independently derived using state-of-the-art, locally and regionally calibrated machine learning tools. The dataset was validated using a statistical sampling which confirms its high accuracy. The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) laboratory derived most global thematic products, except open water, using consistently processed [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard). The annual GLAD ARD data time series were integrated into a set of phenological metrics that enabled global model calibration and application. The water mapping was performed using the Landsat data processed in the Google Earth Engine using an approach similar to the GLAD ARD. GLAD used a separate supervised classification model to map each thematic class. The decision tree models calibrated with manually collected training data were implemented for water, cropland, and perennial snow and ice mapping. Forest height was estimated using the regression tree model calibrated with Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation Lidar (GEDI) forest structure measurements. The built-up lands were mapped using a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm trained using Open Street Map (OSM) data. The models were calibrated locally (for forest height and cropland mapping) or regionally (all other products). GLAD independently validated each global thematic product using statistical sample analysis. The sample reference data were collected through visual image interpretation using the best available high-resolution satellite data and Landsat time series. The GLAD ARD product consists of 16-day global Landsat normalized surface reflectance and brightness temperature composites combined from the best quality observations. Each 16-day composite includes the normalized surface reflectance for visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared Landsat bands and brightness temperature, along with the data quality layer. GLAD integrated the annual GLAD ARD 16-day clear-sky time series into a set of rank-based statistics, hereafter named phenology metrics, that enabled the application of the multitemporal classification and regression models. GLAD augmented the Landsat reflectance metrics with topographic metrics, including elevation and slope. GLAD defined forest as wildland, managed, and planted tree cover, including agroforestry and orchards. The forest extent was defined as an area with tree cover ≥ 5 m, to ensure consistency with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) forest definition. Nevertheless, their forest definition differs from the one used by the FAO by the inclusion of trees outside forests (agroforestry, orchards, parks) and the exclusion of temporally unstocked forest areas. GLAD employed the global Landsat-based forest height model calibrated for the year 2019 using GEDI observations. For the boreal forests north of 52°N, where GEDI data are absent, GLAD used a regional model approach. Three separate models were calibrated for North America, Europe, and Northern Asia. The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to 2000, 2001, 2003, 2017, 2019, and 2020 annual metrics.The forest height values for the years 2000 and 2020 were calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003, and 2017, 2019, 2020 products, respectively, unless forest loss for the years 2001-2003 or 2017-2020 was indicated by the forest disturbance data (in such case, only the year 2000 or 2020 product value was used, respectively). GLAD produced the year 2000 and 2020 forest extent maps by attributing pixels with ≥ 5 m forest height as the “forest” land cover class. The forest extent change (net forest extent loss and gain) was derived directly from the year 2000 and 2020 map comparison. Cropland was defined as land used to produce annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. The definition excludes tree crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation. Consistent with the FAO arable land category, the fallow length was limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland mapping was performed for two four-year epochs, 2000-2003 and 2016-2019. For each epoch, they attributed a GLAD ARD pixel as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any year within the interval. The cropland mapping model was calibrated with manually delineated training areas which were extrapolated in space and time through a three-stage algorithm. Supervised classification (bagged decision tree ensembles) was implemented at each of these three steps. The final products were filtered by removing artifacts and cropland patches smaller than 0.5 ha. Built-up land consists of man-made land surfaces associated with infrastructure, commercial and residential land uses. At the Landsat spatial resolution, GLAD defined the built-up land class as pixels that include man-made surfaces, even if such surfaces do not dominate within the pixel. Due to the contextual nature of built-up lands, particularly settlements, they employed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm to map this thematic class. Final 2000 and 2020 per-pixel class presence probabilities were generated, and validation data were used to assist in the final thresholding of the layers in depicting 2000 and 2020 extents and 2000-2020 gain in built-up lands. Loss of built-up lands, which represents a small proportion of the year 2000 class area, was not mapped by this provisional product. Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥ 50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects above the surface.The presented multidecadal surface water change product is based on the annual water presence dataset produced by Pickens et al. (2020). Water presence is a percent of Landsat observations classified as surface water of all annual clear-sky observations calculated per pixel. Instead of the GLAD ARD, the algorithm employed the original Collection 1 Tier 1 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 1999-2020. GLAD classified each Landsat scene into the land, water, and unusable data classes using an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees developed for ARD data processing. The perennial snow and ice layer includes land covered by glaciers and snow which remains during the entire year. The map is limited to the GLAD ARD tiles where perennial snow and ice areas were detected using the ARD observation quality layer. GLAD mapped permanent snow and ice using regionally calibrated supervised classification models (decision tree ensembles). Overall, they used fourteen models, one model per mountain system or a geographic region. Each classification model was calibrated with manually collected training data from multitemporal Landsat metrics. Wetlands are treated as a landform containing multiple land cover classes. Topographical metrics, including slope, curvature, and a series of relative elevation layers from variably sized catchments were used to determine wetland versus terra firma. Percent bare ground was included from a previous assessment. GLAD validated each thematic product separately using an independently collected reference data sample. GLAD used different strata designs for each thematic product to target not only the LCLU class of interest but also the potential class omission errors. For product validation, the map and reference data were presented as discrete LCLU classes. The map accuracy metrics include overall accuracy (the proportion of correctly mapped sample pixels), user’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class commission), and producer’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class omission). Map accuracy statistics were accompanied by the standard error of the estimate (s.e.). We also estimated sample-based areas of LCLU classes and changes with the corresponding s.e. The global composite maps were created by layering an annual vegetation fraction layer with the bare land, wetland landform, followed by the superseding classes of ice, water, cropland, and built-up. The 2019 global composite map can be viewed and downloaded [here](https://glad.umd.edu/dataset/global-land-cover-land-use-v1). For the full documentation of the [landform classes](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ac46ec) and other [thematic classes](https://doi.org/10.3389/frsen.2022.856903), please see the original methodology. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), and [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Uttarakhand Change in Rainfall
description: The data represents annual and seasonal change in the rainfall for baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 emission scenarios in millimetre (mm). This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Global Soil Properties
description: ### Overview This dataset describes select global soil parameters regridded and upscaled from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2. The HWSD provides information for addressing land competition for food production, bio-energy demand, and biodiversity threats. It is also used as an input to model global carbon cycles. The data are presented as a series of five critical layers at 0.05-degree (~5 km) spatial resolution. ### Methodology **Data Sources:** The Harmonized World Soil Database integrates over 15,000 different soil mapping units, combining global, regional, and national updates (SOTER, ESD, Soil Map of China, WISE) with the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World (FAO, 1971-1981). **Estimation Methods:** HWSD v1.2 (FAO 2012) provides the most comprehensive database of soil characteristics available for global analysis. Soil characteristics are derived from real soil profiles considering pedogenic development, land use, land use history, and disturbances. Properties in HWSD are available for both surface soil horizons (0-30 cm) and deeper soil profiles (30-100 cm). ### Description of the Layers **Topsoil Clay Fraction (% weight):** Percentage clay in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Clay consists of fine-grained particles (<0.002mm) that exhibit plasticity when wet and harden when dried or fired. **Topsoil Silt Fraction (% weight):** Percentage silt in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Silt results from mechanical weathering of rocks through glacial grinding, wind abrasion, or river erosion. It is primarily composed of quartz and feldspar. **Topsoil Sand Fraction (% weight):** Percentage sand in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Sand particles range from 0.0625 mm to 2 mm and feel gritty when touched. Classified into very fine, fine, medium, coarse, and very coarse based on size. **Topsoil pH (-log(H+)):** The acidity or alkalinity of topsoil (0-30 cm) measured in a soil-water solution. Categories include: - Extremely Acidic (pH < 4.5): Found in Acid Sulfate Soils (e.g., mangrove soils, cat clays). - Very Acidic (pH 4.5–5.5): Often influenced by aluminum toxicity. - Acidic to Neutral (pH 5.5–7.2): Optimal for nutrient availability and most crops. - Carbonate-Rich (pH 7.2–8.5): May reduce nutrient availability like phosphorus and iron. - Highly Alkaline (pH > 8.5): Typically sodic with high sodium, affecting soil structure. **Topsoil Organic Carbon Content (% weight):** Indicator of soil fertility and health. Classified as: - Very Low (<0.2%): Requires significant soil amendments. - Low (0.2%–0.6%): Poor in organic matter. - Moderate (0.6%–1.2%): Better fertility and structure. - High (1.2%–2.0%): Favorable conditions for crop growth. - Very High (>2.0%): Highly fertile and well-structured. ### Visualizing the Data The dataset is available at ~5 km resolution. Lighter shades indicate lower values, while brighter shades (orange-red) indicate higher values. ### Excerpts of this description were taken from the source.

title: Projected Cooling Degree Days (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Global Material Flows
description: ### Overview The Global Material Flows Database holds a variety of datasets on material extraction and consumption. The dataset displayed on Resource Watch shows global material consumption and extraction of nonmetallic minerals, biomass, fossil fuels, and metal ores at a national scale. This data is available at the source for every year between 1970 and 2017, but only the 2017 data is mapped on Resource Watch. The dataset also contains additional data on the overall consumption and extraction for each country at a per capita rate for the year 2015. Consumption and extraction are expressed in units of metric tons. This dataset was created using national statistics from a combination of local government organizations and international organizations like the United Nations, Eurostat, and the United States Geological Survey. This dataset was developed to assist governments in creating strategies to increase efficiency of material production and consumption activities. The dataset can help in better understanding how economic growth patterns influence resource use. It can also be used to evaluate the impacts of policies that have been adopted in the past. Additionally, the dataset can be used to develop effective strategies to minimize future resource use through targeted consumption and production policies. This database is used by academics around the world, integrated into several multi-regional input-output databases such as [EXIOBASE](https://www.exiobase.eu/) and featured in reports by international organisations, such as the United Nations Environmental Program and the European Economic Area. This database was created by the United Nations Environment Programme International Resource Panel (UNEP IRP) and developed as part of a collaborative effort by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Sustainable Resource Use research group of the Vienna University of Economics and Business, the Institute of Social Ecology Vienna, the Nagoya University, and University of Sydney’s Integrated Sustainability Analysis. ### Methodology This dataset was created by combining data from multiple sources. Data for all categories of extraction were taken from national production statistics. These datasets were collected from individual government ministries, industrial associations, and Eurostat's production statistics (PRODCOM) whenever available. Additional available data from international organizations, like the British Geological Survey and United States Geological Survey, were also used. Some categories, like metal ore extraction, were estimated using techniques in the [Eurostat: Economy-wide Material Flow Accounts Compilation Guide 2013](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191533/2013-EW-MFA-Guide-10Sep2013.pdf/). Data reported using different units was converted to a standard unit by using category-specific conversion factors. Data on domestic material consumption was calculated by finding the sum of each country’s domestic extraction and import values and subtracting total exports. Data on imports and exports was taken from national offices when available and United Nations reports when not available. Both per capita datasets were created by dividing each country’s total extraction and consumption by its population. The final datasets were produced in tabular format at a national level. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for categories such as crops, natural gas and petroleum are available from the data provider. For each of these categories, data on trade, raw material consumption, raw material consumption per capita, raw material inputs, raw material equivalents of imports, raw material equivalents of exports is also provided. Lastly, data for each year from 1970 to 2017 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](b2f00f99-46ed-43e6-a7a1-a5809d9369d4) as a replacement.**_ The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2019. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) categories. This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions. Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data from 2013. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 28 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2019. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: [Archived] Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](4d2d47c1-fed1-4484-83e3-c91c3f6f7315) as a replacement.**_ The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index of climate change adaptation potential annually from 1995 to 2015. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. Infrastructure Investment Outlook
description: ### Overview This dataset from the Global Infrastructure Hub (GI Hub) shows national infrastructure investment gaps in 2015 U.S. dollars for the following sectors: energy, telecommunications, airports, ports, rail, road, and water. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total sectors. An investment gap represents the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued.The investment gap of a country where the investment trends meet their future investment needs is zero. This dataset was developed by the Global Infrastructure Hub. The data covers a total of 56 countries for the years 2016 to 2040. ### Methodology The Global Infrastructure Outlook was calculated using a “top-down” approach, beginning with existing cross-country datasets on infrastructure spending and filling in data gaps, where necessary. Sources for the initial cross-country datasets include the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Infrastructure in Latin America (INFRALATAM), and Eurostat. The infrastructure investment gap for each year was calculated as the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued for that year. Gaps in national data were filled using data from national statistics agencies and major infrastructure companies. In areas where no data sources could be identified, econometric estimation was used to compute values. In countries where a time series existed but was incomplete, further manipulation was often required to fill in the gaps in that series. For data gaps in the middle of a time series, interpolation was used to fill the gaps. When data was missing from the beginning or the end of the time series, forecasting and/or backcasting were used to develop a longer time series. In the case where data was attributed to a broader sector, secondary data sources were used to align the data with the preferred sector definition. In some countries, data related to investment in utilities was used to attribute the investment into more detailed sectors like water and energy. For example, if energy accounts for 60% of the country's utilities investment, then 60% of the utilities investment would be allocated to the energy sector. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://cdn.gihub.org/outlook/live/methodology/Global+Infrastructure+Outlook+-+July+2017.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: This data set estimates large-scale wetland distributions and important wetland complexes, including areas of marsh, fen, peatland, and water (Lehner and Döll 2004). title: Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels
description: ### Overview The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset shows the species richness and number of threatened species for amphibians and mammals. Species richness is defined by the number of mammal or amphibian species present in a given area. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) [Red List](https://www.iucnredlist.org/about/background-history) defines a [threatened species](https://www.iucn.org/resources/conservation-tools/iucn-red-list-threatened-species) as one that is threatened with global extinction (critically endangered, endangered, or vulnerable). The Red List is the world’s most comprehensive list of species status and extinction risk, with assessments for over 120,000 species. The data shown here evaluated 5,198 amphibian species and 5,488 mammalian species in 2013. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 kilometer (km) x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Biodiversity – the variety of life on earth – is essential to a healthy and stable environment. Biodiversity conservation is critical for food supply, fighting climate change, and providing natural resources for humans. However, human activities such as pollution, farming and deforestation have negatively impacted biodiversity, causing the loss of species and their habitats. Amphibians are facing the highest rates of decline: almost 50% of amphibian species are threatened, primarily in South America and Southeast Asia. Similarly, almost 50% of mammal species are in decline and 20% are threatened. Marine mammals are among the most threatened species. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset is an important tool for wildlife conservation efforts. Understanding the magnitude and geographic focus of threatened species is important for making policy decisions and allocating conservation resources. Additionally, this dataset can be used for biodiversity modeling studies and understanding human interactions with the environment. Founded in 1948, the [International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)](https://www.iucn.org/about) comprises more than 1,400 governmental and civil member organizations. Its mission is to influence, encourage and assist conservation of natural diversity, and ensure that the use of any natural resources is equitable and sustainable. The IUCN provides the Red List as a tool to inform conservation decisions and protect the natural resources necessary for human life. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Level dataset was aggregated by [Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN)](http://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/) using data from the IUCN Red List. CIESIN specializes in online data management and spatial data integration for interdisciplinary research related to human interactions with the environment. ### Methodology The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset was created from species distribution shapefiles from the IUCN Red List. The shapefile data is from 2013 and has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 km at the equator). The number in each grid cell represents the number of species present or the number of species threatened within that cell. CIESIN created the richness and threat level rasters by converting the shapefiles to GeoTIFF rasters based on attributes from the IUCN data. Amphibian and mammalian richness maps were created by aggregating individual species maps with the **Extant** class attribute. This attribute refers to species that are currently surviving in the wild. Threat level maps were created in the same way using the **All Threats** IUCN threat category. The All Threats category includes species classified as Critically Endangered (extremely high risk of extinction in the wild), Endangered (very high risk of extinction in the wild ) or Vulnerable (high risk of extinction in the wild). Species within these categories are undergoing reversible declines in population, geographic extent, habitat, and mature individuals. Red List species assessments follow a specific set of guidelines and undergo review before publication. More information about the Red List assessment process can be found [here](https://www.iucnredlist.org/assessment/process). Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Heating Degree Days
description: A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows HDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Environmental Democracy Index
description: The Environmental Democracy Index (EDI) was developed by The Access Initiative (TAI) and World Resources Institute (WRI) in collaboration with partners around the world. The index evaluates 70 countries, across 75 legal indicators, based on objective and internationally recognized standards established by the Bali Guidelines of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). Legal indicators test both the extent of provisions that promote environmental democracy and the strength of a given provision in providing an enforceable legal right for the public. Each of these indicators is scored on a range from 0 (lowest) to 3 (highest). A score of 3 means that the respective provision exemplifies accepted good practice. A score of 2 indicates that a majority—but not all—of environmental decision-making includes a certain provision, or indicates moderately strong provision. A score of 1 translates to a weaker provision that grants significant discretion to government agencies to fulfil these rights, or that a right only applies to a minority of environmental decision-making processes. A score of 0 indicates that the law is either silent or prohibits some aspect of procedural rights, depending on the indicator. The overall EDI score is the average of the scores of the 75 legal indicators. The EDI also includes a supplemental set of 24 limited practice indicators that provide insight on a country’s performance in implementation. The national laws and practices were assessed and scored by more than 140 lawyers around the world. Country assessments were conducted in 2014 and will be updated every 2 years. title: Gender Gap Index
description: ### Overview The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time. Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania. The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth. ### Methodology The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored. First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: - Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. - Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/). - Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho). - Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm). [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2019, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2019 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. The GHI classifies countries by the following severity layers: low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores. title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for black carbon (BC). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. Black carbon is the sooty black material emitted from gas and diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, and other sources that burn fossil fuel. It is made up of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter. PM2.5 can have significant health risks for people with compromised respiratory systems, the young, and the old. Black carbon is a global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate. Inhalation of black carbon is associated with health problems including respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and even birth defects. Black carbon also contributes to climate change causing changes in patterns of rain and clouds. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25). ### Methodology The black carbon station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25). Cropland and Pasture Area
description: ### Overview The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset shows the global distribution of agricultural activities for the year 2000. It is a combination of both satellite based datasets and agricultural inventory data from censuses. The dataset displays the percentage of land used for farming (cropland) and livestock (pasture area) for each grid cell. Each grid cell has a value of 0% to 100% coverage. A value of 0% means there are no agricultural activities present and 100% means the gridcell is completely used for cropland or pasture area. The dataset is displayed at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (around 10 kilometers). The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset was created by EarthStat with assistance from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE), and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It was created to help understand the positive social and economic benefits, as well as the negative environmental consequences, of agricultural land use. ### Methodology The Cropland and Pasture Area in 2000 dataset was created by combining two different high-resolution satellite based land cover datasets and agricultural inventory data. The agricultural inventory data is allocated to the 10 kilometer resolution using the higher resolution land cover datasets and statistical modeling. The two satellite based land cover datasets used were the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Land Cover Type Product and the Satellite Pour l’Observation de la Terre (SPOT) VEGETATION based Global Land Cover 2000 (GLC2000) dataset. The MODIS dataset was created with data collected from October 2000 to October 2001 and was analyzed using remote imaging with a globally consistent classification scheme. The SPOT dataset was created with data from November 1999 to December 2000 and used a variable land use classification scheme that included information from regional institutions. Both datasets have a spatial resolution of about 1 kilometer. A single land cover dataset was created by overlaying the MODIS and GLC2000 datasets, where each classification was the combination of the MODIS and GLC2000 classifications. This combination land cover product was found to provide more accurate results when calibrated against the inventory data, as opposed to using either data set individually. Cropland and pasture inventory data was compiled for the globe at the national and subnational level for circa year 2000. This resulted in compiled data for 15,990 different administrative units of the world, ranging from political units like countries, states and counties. Inventory data was found from either census data or the Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) [FAOSTAT database](http://faostat.fao.org). The cropland and pasture data was compiled to be consistent with the FAO definition of “Arable lands and permanent crops” and “Permanent pastures” respectively. The agricultural inventory data were seldom available exactly for the year 2000, therefore the authors collected inventory data between the years 1998 to 2002 where possible, but in several instances relied on older data. Information within the final Cropland and Pasture Area dataset for areas that were clearly non-agricultural (tundra, boreal forest, and protected land) were masked to reduce the possibility of misclassification. For full information, please see the source [methodology](http://www.earthstat.org/cropland-pasture-area-2000/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: The GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) was created by NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) and is now run by NOAA's Earth System Research Laboratory Physical Sciences Division (ESRL-PSD). GISTEMP provides an estimate of global surface and air temperature changes. The basic GISS temperature analysis scheme was defined by James Hansen in the late 1970s, when a method of estimating global temperature change was needed for comparison with 1-dimensional global climate models. The scheme was based on the finding that the correlation of temperature change was reasonably strong for stations separated by up to 1,200 km, especially at middle and high latitudes. This fact proved sufficient to obtain useful estimates for global mean temperature changes. The analysis method was fully documented in Hansen and Lebedeff (1987), including quantitative estimates of the error in annual and 5-year mean temperature change. This was done by sampling at station locations a spatially complete data set of a long run of a global climate model, which was shown to have realistic spatial and temporal variability. This however only addresses the error due to incomplete spatial coverage of measurements. As there are other potential sources of error, such as urban warming near meteorological stations, many other methods have been used to verify the approximate magnitude of inferred global warming. These methods include inference of surface temperature change from vertical temperature profiles in the ground (bore holes) at many sites around the world, rate of glacier retreat at many locations, and studies by several groups of the effect of urban and other local human influences on the global temperature record. All of these yield consistent estimates of the approximate magnitude of global warming, which reached about 0.8°C in 2010, twice the magnitude reported in 1981. Further affirmation of the reality of the warming is its spatial distribution, which has largest values at locations remote from any local human influence, with a global pattern consistent with that expected for response to global climate forcings (larger in the Northern Hemisphere than the Southern Hemisphere, larger at high latitudes than low latitudes, larger over land than over ocean). More recent documentation compares alternative analyses and addresses questions about perception and reality of global warming; various choices for the ocean data are tested; it is also shown that global temperature change is sensitive to estimated temperature change in polar regions, where observations are limited. A multiyear smoothing is applied to fully remove the annual cycle and improve information content in temperature graphs. Despite large year-to-year fluctuations associated with the El Niño-La Niña cycle of tropical ocean temperature, the conclusion could be drawn that global temperature continued to rise rapidly in the 21st century, new record heights being reached in every decade. One of the improvements—introduced in 1998—was the implementation of a method to address the problem of urban warming: The urban and periurban (i.e., other than rural) stations are adjusted so that their long-term trend matches that of the mean of neighboring rural stations. Urban stations without nearby rural stations are dropped. This preserves local short-term variability without affecting long-term trends. Originally, the classification of stations was based on population size near that station; the current analysis uses satellite-observed night-lights to determine which stations are located in urban and periurban areas. description: ### Overview The biodiversity intactness map shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in an area. This data is important because if biodiversity loss goes unchecked, it will undermine efforts toward long-term sustainable development. The data, created by [Newbold et al. (2016)](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288), represents intactness in 2005 at a 1 kilometer resolution. ### Methodology The Biodiversity Intactness dataset shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in samples from local terrestrial ecological assemblages. The map represents the average losses of originally present species. The datasets used 2,382,624 data points from the Projecting Responses of Ecological Diversity in Changing Terrestrial Systems (PREDICTS) database, a global database of how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human impacts. The map modeled how richness and abundance respond to land use pressures. The models included 4 pressure variables—land use, land use intensity, human population density, and proximity to the nearest road. The values of the response variables were expressed relative to an intact assemblage undisturbed by humans. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index
description: ### Overview The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually. The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being. ### Methodology The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types: Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance) Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. title: Gender Inequality Index
description: The Gender Inequality Index (GII), released by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is an inequality index for 159 countries from 1995 to 2015. It measures gender inequalities and is calculated using 3 important aspects of human development: (1) reproductive health, measured by maternal mortality ratio and adolescent birth rates; (2) empowerment, measured by proportion of parliamentary seats occupied by females and proportion of adult females and males aged 25 years and older with at least some secondary education; and (3) economic status, expressed as labor market participation and measured by labor force participation rate of female and male populations aged 15 and older. The index ranges from 0, where women and men fare equally, to 1, where one gender fares as poorly as possible in all measured dimensions. The higher the GII value, the more disparities between females and males and the more loss to human development. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
