Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas
description: ### Overview The Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, models human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. When human sewage flows into coastal waters it contributes to increased nitrogen levels and pathogens in coastal systems. This dataset quantifies and maps the flow of nitrogen and pathogen input to the ocean from nearly 135,000 watersheds using a high-resolution geospatial model. The sources of nitrogen inputs are separated by source into treated (sewered systems), septic, and untreated (open defecation) inputs. The dataset provides global rasters of the modeled plume, or extent, of the nitrogen in coastal waters. Nitrogen plume data is shown at ~1 km resolution. Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management. The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this dataset to inform marine conservation and public health work. The model allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources with traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. ### Methodology Nitrogen concentration (grams/yr) was modeled using a high-resolution geospatial model. Population and settlement data were grouped into rural and urban classes. These data were then combined with national-level statistics on protein consumption and the proportion of the population’s access to various types of wastewater treatment facilities. Wastewater treatment types were grouped into three categories - open defecation (untreated), septic tanks (septic), or some level of sewered treatment. The three sewage treatment categories of nitrogen were assigned a nitrogen removal efficiency based on literature. The model assumed that populations with inputs from septic tanks or open defecation that are more than 1km away from surface waters and coastlines do not contribute to effluent totals. The dispersion of the wastewater pollution into the ocean was then modeled from each basin’s pourpoint, which describes the location where freshwater enters the ocean. For each watershed with a pourpoint draining into the ocean, nitrogen inputs were calculated by summing the values for all grid cells falling within the watershed boundary and this value was assigned to the corresponding coastal pourpoint. At each pourpoint, the level of nitrogen was spread into the coastal waters using a plume model based on a logarithmic decay function. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also provides data on nitrogen inputs at the watershed level in [Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/784732cc-8e7e-4dac-be51-d4506ff2ee04) and for the associated coastal “pourpoint” or the location where the watershed empties into the ocean in [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/ocn_027a_rw0_nitrogen_plumes/). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: ### Overview The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS). Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch. ### Methodology Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646). After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by all vessels other than trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW data for [Trawling Activity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6ccfb266-20cd-4838-82b0-5309987a62f0). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030a_rw1_fishing_activity) ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. description: The Annual Precipitation data set was adapted from the University of California, Berkeley's WorldClim V1 Bioclim, which produces bioclimatic variables derived from the monthly temperature and rainfall in order to generate more biologically meaningful values. The data product covers the period January 1, 1960, to December 31, 1990, and has global coverage at 1 km resolution. The bioclimatic variables represent annual trends (e.g., mean annual temperature, annual precipitation), seasonality (e.g., annual range in temperature and precipitation), and extreme or limiting environmental factors (e.g., temperature of the coldest and warmest month, and precipitation of the wettest and driest quarters). Climate data sets were created based on data from various sources, including the Global Historical Climate Network data set, the World Meteorological Organization's Climatological Normals (CLINO), the FAOCLIM 2.0 global climate database, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture, and various regional climate databases. The data set contains the following bands: Annual Mean Temperature; Mean Diurnal Range; Isothermality; Temperature Seasonality; Max Temperature of Warmest Month; Min Temperature of Coldest Month; Temperature Annual Range; Mean Temperature of Wettest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Driest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Warmest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Coldest Quarter; Annual Precipitation; Precipitation of Wettest Month (mm); Precipitation of Driest Month (mm); Precipitation Seasonality; Precipitation of Wettest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Driest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Warmest Quarter (mm); and Precipitation of Coldest Quarter (mm). This scheme follows that of ANUCLIM, except that for temperature seasonality the standard deviation was used because a coefficient of variation does not make sense with temperatures between -1 and 1. title: Positive Peace Index
description: ### Overview The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace. Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains: 1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights. 2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health. 3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are. 4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is. 5. *High Levels of Human Capital:* The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country. 6. *Low Levels of Corruption:* High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society. 7. *Sound Business Environment:* This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment. 8. *Well-Functioning Government:* A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country. The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as: improved economic productivity and social advancement. ### Methodology The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_092_positive_peace_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: India Projected Change in Average Temperature
description: This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in average temperature over the Indian subcontinent. These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp). Projected change in average temperature is computed using daily mean near-surface air temperature in degrees Celsius for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average. The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.

title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Soil Erosion
description: ### Overview The Soil Erosion Prevalence dataset, produced by the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), provides predictions for the percentage of area with soil erosion across the global tropics (between the parallels of 40° south and 40° north). The authors predicted soil erosion for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2020 from satellite imagery at 500 m resolution using machine learning algorithms trained with field observations. Soil is eroding more quickly than its being formed, contributing to the degradation of millions of hectares of land globally. The nutrient rich layer of soil on the surface, called topsoil, is vulnerable to wind and water erosion and its loss is accelerated by modifications in land use. Erosion of this critical layer of soil comes at a [major economic and environmental cost](https://www.wri.org/insights/causes-and-effects-soil-erosion-and-how-prevent-it). It causes [billions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264837718319343) of dollars of losses due to decreased soil fertility, reduced crop yields, and increased water usage. The eroded soil can be carried into rivers and streams. This creates a heavy layer of sediment which is carried downstream. This process clogs waterways, prevents smooth water flow, and may eventually lead to flooding. Other environmental costs include loss of productivity and biodiversity, decreased resilience of marine and terrestrial ecosystems, and increased vulnerability to climate change and food insecurity. Estimates of both spatial and temporal dynamics of soil erosion are needed to better track the occurrence and severity of erosion in landscapes over time. The main objectives of this dataset are to provide rapid assessments of soil erosion for spatially distributed monitoring as well as assess changes in soil erosion prevalence over time. The spatial assessments of erosion provide estimates of land degradation hotspots and can be combined with other indicators of ecosystem health, including social factors, to better assess and identify drivers of land degradation and target land management interventions to reverse degradation. ### Methodology The authors used a combination of systematically collected field observations of erosion and remote sensing to predict the spatial and temporal distribution of soil erosion prevalence at moderate spatial resolution (500 m) for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2020. The model was trained and tested using field data collected via [the Land Degradation Surveillance Framework](http://landscapeportal.org/blog/2015/03/25/the-land-degradation-surveillance-framework-ldsf) (LDSF). As part of the LDSF, sample sites are divided into plots and subplots. Erosion prevalence was scored at the plot level by summing up the number of subplots with visible signs of erosion, with 0 being no observed erosion and 4 being erosion observed in all four subplots. The authors took a cut-off at three subplots or more (>50%) to represent “severe” soil erosion. Erosion prevalence was modeled using a decision-tree approach known as [Random Forests](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v077i01/v77i01.pdf) to generate a classification model for soil erosion prevalence using imagery from the [Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiomer](https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/) (MODIS) platform. Annual composites were matched to the years of LDSF field data collection and fitted to annual composite reflectance data for 2002, 2007, 2012, and 2017. Soil erosion prevalence is displayed on the maps as the percentage of area (of a pixel) predicted to be eroded. Model accuracy for the detection of erosion was about 86% and accuracy for non-detection was about 91%. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/15/1800). ### Additional Information For access to additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Maximum Arctic Sea Ice
description: ### Overview The Maximum Arctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual maximum extent of sea ice in the Arctic for select years between 1980-2020. Arctic sea ice typically reaches its maximum extent in March. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during March for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual maximum Arctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Maximum Arctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081). Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors: - GSFC data: - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present - NRTSI data: - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Flood Events
description: ### Overview The Flood Events dataset shows major flood events within the last month. This near real-time dataset is created using data from news articles and government sources. While the map only shows the location and extent for floods within the last month, additional information on flood start and end dates, number of deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity are all available in the Custom Visualization tool below. According to the [United Nations](https://www.unenvironment.org/news-and-stories/story/how-climate-change-making-record-breaking-floods-new-normal), floods will become more likely due to global climate change. They can have large consequences for civil society including the loss of life, damage to property, and increasing health risks. This dataset lets viewers monitor where flooding is happening around the world on a near real-time basis. It can also offer a first glance at the communities that have been impacted by flooding. Lastly, it can help government agencies in creating natural disaster management plans and zoning for future urbanization. This dataset was created and is curated by the Dartmouth Flood Observatory located at the University of Colorado’s Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research (INSTAAR). It is a continually updated archive that can show trends in severity, damage, and location of flood events. ### Methodology This dataset was created and is continually updated with information from a wide array of news and government sources, like the North American Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration’s National Climatic Data Center (NOAA NCDC). To identify each flood, researchers used the international [Global Identified Number](https://glidenumber.net/glide/public/search/search.jsp) (GLIDE), which is a unique ID code used to identify disasters that is issued by the [Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT)](https://www.emdat.be/) at the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED). For each flood, event data on location, size, begin & end times, duration, deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity were recorded. Size, times, duration, main cause, and location are all taken directly from the source. Number of deaths were taken from news and government sources when accurate enough, but when only a range of numbers were provided by these sources researchers estimated that “hundreds” meant more than 300 people had died, “more than 100” meant 110 or more had died, and “scores” meant more than 30 people had died. Number of people displaced was based on the quantity of people left homeless after the incident and sometimes the number evacuated during the flood. Severity was determined by reviewing the amount of damage caused by the event and how often similar events have occured in the region. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://floodobservatory.colorado.edu/Archives/ArchiveNotes.html). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Data on flood events for every year between 1985 and present are available from the data provider. Additionally, the data provider also has datasets on river and reservoir discharge, flood and drought-affected watersheds, and precipitation. An interactive map can also be found on the source website. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/wat_040_flood_events) ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Marine Species Richness
description: To calculate the impact of climate change on marine biodiversity, researchers first determined biodiversity distribution ranging from 0 (absence of species) to 1 (maximum species richness) (Ramirez et al. 2017). They calculated the species richness distribution based on the spatially explicit information on the equally weighted distribution of fish (1,729), marine mammal (124), and seabird (330) species. Data on the world distribution species are from BirdLife International (http://www.birdlife.org) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (http://www.iucnredlist.org/). Occurrence shapefiles were transformed to 0.5 degree, dichotomous grid features, with 1 denoting presence and 0 indicating absences. Obtained grid features for different fish, marine mammal, and seabird species were added to obtain 3 maps indicating the number of species per group occurring in each pixel. Each map was standardized by the total number of species per group in order to obtain a relative measure of the spatial distribution of fish, marine mammal, and seabird species richness. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value to obtain a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (absence of species) to 1 (maximum species richness), providing information about the spatial heterogeneity in species richness and highlighting hotspots of marine biodiversity without biases toward those groups (e.g., fish) with a larger number of species. Extreme Heat Days
description: Extreme heat days represent the annual average count of days with heat greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

Projected Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: The Climate Resilience Screening Index (CRSI), developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), characterizes U.S. county and community resilience based on a suite of indicators that are grouped into broad categories of county and community resiliency traits in the context of natural disasters. The index is a composite measure comprised of five domains (Risk, Governance, Society, Built Environment, and Natural Environment), represented by 20 indicators, and calculated from 117 metrics. CRSI characterizes holistic climate resilience throughout the U.S. at the county level (2000-2015); ascertains the relationships among those domains and indicators; and provides information regarding how that resilience score is constructed and the actions a community/county can take to improve their climate resilience. CRSI is intended to be used by EPA Regions and others who work closely with counties and communities to gauge resilience of built and natural systems to acute climate events (e.g., hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, flooding). description: ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. description: The Fragile States Index (FSI), produced by the Fund for Peace (FFP), measures the vulnerability of states to collapse. title: Crop Land Area and Production
description: ### Overview The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice, maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2020 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming. ### Methodology The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2020 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer. The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type: - Irrigated – high input (I) - Rainfed – high input (H) - Rainfed – low input (L) - Rainfed – subsistence (S) The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and country-level statistics by the overall harvested area. The optimization module in SPAM2020 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically. The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others): - Administrative units - Crop Type - Farming system - Adjusted harvested area - Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system - Crop prices - Market accessibility in each grid - Population density Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2020 essential output indicators: - Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size. - Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop. - Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2020 Version 3.0 has data for 36 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. Our data catalog has previously shown data for [2005](https://bit.ly/3CjoFYc). This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_005_rw2_crop_area_production). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Lakes
description: The HydroLAKES database provides a seamless high-resolution map of the world’s lakes and their main characteristics in support of a broad range of global-scale assessments and analyses, with a focus on improving users’ ability to model the important roles that lakes play in the global environment. The HydroLAKES database was designed as a digital map repository to include all lakes with a surface area of at least 10 ha. The current version comprises the shoreline polygons of 1,427,688 individual lakes. HydroLAKES aims to be as comprehensive and consistent as possible at a global scale and contains both freshwater and saline lakes, including the Caspian Sea, as well as human-made reservoirs and regulated lakes. The HydroLAKES database was created by compiling, correcting, and unifying several near-global and regional data sets. Map generalization methods were applied and some polygon outlines were smoothed during the mapping process to ensure spatial consistency of the data. The resulting map scale is estimated to be between 1:100,000 and 1:250,000 for most lakes globally, with some coarser ones at 1:1 million. To enhance the attribute information provided by HydroLAKES, a spatial coregistration to the global river network database HydroSHEDS was established. Literature estimates of lake depths and/or volumes were compiled for all lakes ≥ 500 km2. To predict average lake depths and volumes for smaller lakes, a geostatistical model based on surrounding land surface topography was developed. The addition of high-resolution discharge data allowed the estimation of hydraulic residence times for each lake. All natural lakes of the HydroLAKES database show a combined surface area of 2.67 x 106 km2 (1.8% of global land area), a total shoreline length of 7.2 x 106 km (about 4 times longer than the world’s ocean coastline), and a total volume of 181.9 x 103 km3 (0.8% of total global nonfrozen terrestrial water stocks). Mean and median hydraulic residence times for all lakes were computed to be 1,834 days and 451 days, respectively. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](e32bdaba-5a72-487c-b640-668adaea2976) as a replacement.**_ WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for Water Supply and Sanitation (WHO/UNICEF JMP) reports global annual data on access to an improved water source based on national censuses and nationally representative household surveys from 1990 to 2015. The coverage rates for water and sanitation are based on information from service users on the facilities their households actually use rather than on information from service providers, which may include nonfunctioning systems. The WHO/UNICEF JMP defines an improved drinking-water source as one that, by nature of its construction or through active intervention, is protected from outside contamination, in particular from contamination with fecal matter. The improved drinking water source includes piped water on premises (piped household water connection located inside the user’s dwelling, plot, or yard), and other improved drinking water sources (public taps or standpipes, tube wells or boreholes, protected dug wells, protected springs, and rainwater collection). title: Cold Water Corals
description: This data set, released by the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), shows of the global distribution of cold-water corals that inhabit the colder deep waters of continental shelves and offshore canyons, ranging from 50 to over 1,000 m depths. They lack zooxanthellae and may build reef-like structures or occur solitarily. Occurrence records are given for the subclass Octocorallia (octocorals; also known as Alcyonaria) and 4 Orders (in Class Anthozoa): Scleractinia (reef-forming corals), Antipatharia (black corals), Zoanthidae (encrusting or button polyps), and Pennatulacea (sea pens). Occurrence records are also available for the order sub-Order Filifera (lace corals) in Class Hydrozoa. Depth range, including upper and lower depths, status of the sample, and reference to where the record was first published, is also included. This data set contains data for 132 countries and comprises 32,631 occurrences of cold corals, including locations within the high seas. Occurrence records were obtained from various sources, including reports, peer-reviewed articles, and expert consultations. Many individuals and organizations contributed by providing UNEP-WCMC with their data in electronic form. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in extreme precipitation is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average days of extreme precipitation during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

Coral Reef Locations
description: ### Overview The Coral Reef Locations dataset shows the global distribution of known coral reefs from 1954-2018 in tropical and subtropical regions. The UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), WorldFish Centre, World Resources Institute (WRI), and The Nature Conservancy (TNC) compiled the map to provide a baseline of data to use in monitoring and managing global coral reefs. According to the [UNEP-WCMC](https://biodiversitya-z.org/content/warm-water-coral-reef), warm-water coral reefs are the most biodiverse marine habitats per unit area, due to their rich ecosystems. Coral reefs provide a habitat for a wide array of species and can be the preferred habitat for some critically endangered species. In addition, coral reefs themselves become one of the most endangered habitats on the planet. Their presence is declining as they face bleaching, diseases caused by rising sea surface temperatures and human activity, such as urban runoff and mining. This dataset can be used to reference whether local developments will be at risk of putting pressure on coral reefs. It can also be used as a base layer for further research into threats to global reefs, as was done by the [Reefs at Risk](https://www.wri.org/resources/data-sets/reefs-risk-revisited) project led by WRI. ### Methodology The dataset was compiled using data on coral reef locations from a number of sources. Approximately 85% of this dataset originates from the Millennium Coral Reef Mapping Project. This project used 30 meter resolution multispectral Landsat 7 imagery acquired between 1999 and 2002. The UNEP-WCMC compiled the remaining 15% of data from other sources. These sources include data from the [World Atlas of Coral Reefs](https://www.unep-wcmc.org/resources-and-data/world-atlas-of-coral-reefs-2001) and coral reef maps reproduced with permission from the Controller of Her Majesty’s Stationery Office and the [UK Hydrographic Office](http://ukho.gov.uk/). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/pdfs/1/WCMC008_CoralReefs2010_v4.pdf?1544544636). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. Resource Watch has previously shown data for 2005. This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3624554e-b240-4edb-9110-1f010642c3f3). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/bio_004a_coral_reef_locations). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Heating Degree Days
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c500a521-249e-4c2d-9e1c-50b489a3d55c) as a replacement.**_ ClimateScope is a partnership between Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF), UKaid, and the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) to provide a quantitative assessment of the relative attractiveness of investing in clean energy infrastructure in 58 developing countries around the world. This assessment is based on 4 weighted parameters: Enabling Framework, 40%; Clean Energy Investment and Climate Financing, 30%; Low-Carbon Business and Clean Energy Value Chains, 15%; and Greenhouse Gas Management Activities, 15%. Scores are available at the country level, where they are scaled from 0 to 5, and are published yearly. The data used to score countries on these 4 parameters come from a variety of sources. For some indicators, panels of experts were convened to assess the energy policies of the studied countries in each of the 4 parameters mentioned above. These assessments were used to assign scores for each country on a variety of metrics relevant to clean energy policy. Other elements of a country's final score are determined by reference to published indices, such as the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators 2015 index, which is used to address the question of political risk in countries. Still other elements were determined according to primary research performed by BNEF team members, such as information regarding the amount and source of investment made in clean energy projects to date. The data set spans 2014-2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
