description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](79f16b9a-a062-4820-822d-7858609a8fd5) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2018. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center. ### Methodology Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and 2018. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal. Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. Weekly snowmelt averages were derived using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) macroscale hydrologic model, which simulates spatially distributed total runoff and snowmelt over all global land areas for two time periods (past period covers 1961-1990; future period, 2025-2054). Areas where peak snowmelt varied little throughout the averaged year were also excluded by using a mask of cells greater than one standard deviation of the past peak snowmelt range. title: Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector
description: ### Overview The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset estimates the share of household income that is spent on various types of products and services. Spending was analyzed for four consumption segments: lowest, low, middle, and higher. The four levels of consumption segments were based on income per capita: - Lowest: below $2.97 per capita a day - Low: between $2.97 and $8.44 per capita a day - Middle: between $8.44 and $23.03 per capita a day - Higher: above $23.03 per capita a day This dataset shows the percent of the household income that is spent on each type of product or service within each of these consumption segments. This dataset was developed by the World Bank Group as part of its Global Consumption Database. The data covers both urban and rural households in developing countries and is reported at the national level for the year 2010. ### Methodology The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset was developed using multiple different surveys, depending on data availability, including household budget survey, living standard measurement surveys, and various kinds of country-specific socioeconomic surveys. All surveys measure consumption at the household level; however, different surveys collected data over different time periods. Some conducted surveys over a period of 12 months to account for seasonality, while others collected data over a shorter period (a few weeks or a few months). Most surveys rely on the "recall method," in which households are asked to report what they can recall spending over a given period. The choice of recall period may have a significant impact on the level of consumption reported by the households. Data was collected for households in various developing countries. These households were categorized by their consumption segments for the Global Consumption Database. The consumption segments are based on the global income distribution data, which rank the global population by income per capita. The lowest consumption segment corresponds to the bottom half of the global distribution, or the 50th percentile and below; the low consumption segment to the 51st-75th percentiles; the middle consumption segment to the 76th-90th percentiles; and the higher consumption segments to the 91st percentile and above. The purchasing power parity (PPP) US dollar threshold was converted into annual expenditure in local currency (as of 2010). The Global Consumption Database draws on a diverse array of data surveys, so standardization was applied, to the extent possible, through a six-step process. The first step consisted of annualizing each household's consumption or expenditure data for each commodity. The second step was to detect and fix outliers. The third step was to map commodities found in each survey dataset to a standard classification of products and services. In the fourth step, extrapolations were done to convert all consumption and population data to a common reference year. In the fifth and sixth step, the resulting data was compared with data from other sources and used to generate a standard set of tables for each country showing consumption and demographic patterns across consumption segments. title: National Populations
description: The 'Population, total' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship. The values shown are midyear estimates. Population estimates are usually based on national population censuses. Estimates for the years before and after the census are interpolations or extrapolations based on demographic models. Errors and undercounting occur even in high-income countries. The spatial coverage of this data set is global and on the national level, and the temporal coverage runs from 1960 through present day. In developing countries errors may be substantial because of limits in the transport, communications, and other resources required to conduct and analyze a full census. The quality and reliability of official demographic data are also affected by public trust in the government, government commitment to full and accurate enumeration, confidentiality and protection against misuse of census data, and census agencies' independence from political influence. Moreover, comparability of population indicators is limited by differences in the concepts, definitions, collection procedures, and estimation methods used by national statistical agencies and other organizations that collect the data. The currentness of a census and the availability of complementary data from surveys or registration systems are objective ways to judge demographic data quality. Some European countries' registration systems offer complete information on population in the absence of a census. The United Nations Statistics Division monitors the completeness of vital registration systems. Some developing countries have made progress over the last 60 years, but others still have deficiencies in civil registration systems. International migration is the only other factor besides birth and death rates that directly determines a country's population growth. Estimating migration is difficult. At any time many people are located outside their home country as tourists, workers, or refugees or for other reasons. Standards for the duration and purpose of international moves that qualify as migration vary, and estimates require information on flows into and out of countries that is difficult to collect. Population projections, starting from a base year are projected forward using assumptions of mortality, fertility, and migration by age and sex through 2050, based on the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects database medium variant. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Subnational Infant Mortality
description: ### Overview This dataset includes estimated infant mortality rates (IMR) for 234 countries and territories at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds (about one kilometer at the equator) for the year 2015. 143 countries are recorded with subnational units and 91 countries include only national units. IMR is defined as the number of children who die before their first birthday for every 1,000 live births. IMR can be used as a proxy measurement for poverty and wellbeing within a population. This dataset can also be useful for a wide user community in interdisciplinary studies of health, development, sustainability, and the environment. This dataset was compiled by the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) of Columbia University and is managed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC). ### Methodology Infant mortality rate (IMR) data were either acquired or calculated by CIESIN. Acquired means that IMRs were collected from trusted sources. Calculated by CIESIN means that IMRs were calculated by taking the number of infant deaths, dividing them by the number of live births, and multiplying the results by 1,000. Researchers collected the most recent IMR data from national offices, Demographic Health Surveys (DHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) and other sources. Data collected from national offices included information from either a national Human Development Report, National Statistical Office (NSO), or ministry of health. Since the IMR input data spanned from 2006 to 2014, researchers adjusted the rate for the year 2015 based on the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation. Boundary data came from the IMR data source when possible and when not available the Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4), was used. Against the boundary data, IMR data were assigned to grid cells at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds to allow for easy integration with other spatial data like demographic and environmental datasets. Water features were collected from GPWv4 and categorized as no population or uninhabited areas. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/povmap-global-subnational-infant-mortality-rates-v2/docs). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,400 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Air Quality: Fine Paritculate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements
description: OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy and empower the public to fight air pollution.” The data include air pollutant measurements for [PM10](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [PM2.5](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/0c3ed5b9-94b4-4fc5-9208-bf749f0a5052) from over 5,400 locations in 48 countries as of June 2017. Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. OpenAQ has 5 criteria for including data sources in its platform: 1) Data must represent one of these pollutant types: PM10, PM2.5, SO₂, CO, NO₂, O₃, or BC; 2) Data must be from an official-level stationary, outdoor air quality source, defined as data produced by a government entity or international organization; 3) Data must be "raw" and reported in physical concentrations on their originating site; 4) Data must be at the "station-level," not aggregated into a higher (e.g., city) level; 5) Data must be from measurements averaged between 10 minutes and 24 hours. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants, industries and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. Exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Extreme Precipitation Days
description: Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). NO₂ is a highly-reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid. NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2) (EPA), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposures to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted O₃ concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). description: Increased mortality is associated with increased heat. Climate change is projected to increase the number of heat related deaths. As such, tracking the number of heat related deaths may help public health professionals design targeted adaptation and response options for their specific regional requirements. The Heat-Related Mortality: Number of summertime (May-Sep) heat-related deaths by year is derived by the Center for Disease Control and Prevetnion's (CDC) Environmental Health Tracking Branch using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data with appropriate ICD-10 codes to calculate the total number of deaths by year during summer (May - September) period by year for the United States. Deaths from excessive heat exposure are defined based on codes from the tenth revision of International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10). Such deaths included those in which exposure to excessive natural heat (code X30) was reported as either the underlying or a contributing cause of death. title: Energy Intensity
description: ### Overview This dataset shows energy intensity in 259 countries from 1990 to 2015. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy (energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form) is used to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within an area. Energy intensity is expressed as megajoules (MJ) of primary energy available per GDP produced, based on [purchasing power parity (PPP)](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/ppp.htm) in 2011 U.S. dollars (USD). PPP is a factor used to convert local currencies to one comparable unit of measure based on the local cost of goods and services in each country. Low energy intensity is desirable, as it means that less energy is used to produce one more unit of economic output. Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative. The database is intended to help policymakers in government, business, and civil society work toward doubling the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology Energy intensity was measured as the ratio of total primary energy supply to the value added to the economy. Primary energy supply data came from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database. The value added to the economy was expressed in 2011 USD, adjusted for PPP. The data for GDP PPP came from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://trackingsdg7.esmap.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/431f7c9e-7ef5-4f00-a5dc-8845fcb3a9a9) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data related to electricity access and renewable energy electricity is available from the data provider. Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquitoes
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmissions by two of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible, under current conditions, as well as in the years 2050, and 2080. The two mosquitoes are *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus*. They transmit diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the current temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 2.5 represents the best-case scenario for mitigation and adaptation, and RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the other three general circulation models (GCMs) besides the Had-GEM2-ES model is available from the data provider. Agricultural Trade Statistics
description: ### Overview The Agricultural Trade data and statistics compiled by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) are key economic indicators, used to track trade flows between nations. Metrics are aggregated annually at the country level. The dataset comprises four categories: import quantity, import value, export quantity, and export value, and are available for all food and agricultural products for each country in the world. Quantity data is measured in weight (tonnes), while value is measured in 1,000 United States Dollars (USD). Agricultural commodity flows are especially important for actors along the agricultural supply chain. The metrics included in this dataset are standardized across countries, enabling comparisons to be made. This provides important information about what commodities are in surplus/deficit at the national level and elucidate linkages in the global flow of agricultural goods. The FAO has an institutional mandate to “collect, analyze, interpret, and disseminate information relating to nutrition, food and agriculture.” A primary purpose of this dataset is to ensure that there is a source of current, relevant, and reliable statistics for crop and livestock products that is applicable on the global scale. ### Methodology The FAO collects trade data from various entities including the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), Eurostat, and other national authorities. Trade data is collected, processed, and disseminated according to the standards outlined by the International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) [Methodology](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/default.asp). The database includes annual information on the import quantity, export quantity, import value, and export value of all crop and livestock products for all countries in the world. Our data catalog only shows certain products that are derived from three crops: coffee, cotton, and rice. Additionally, only data from 1990 to 2020 is shown here , as it provides a firm historical understanding of these metrics. Trade quantity refers to the net weight (in tonnes) of the commodity and excludes containers. Export quantities are defined by IMTS methodology as the physical quantity of crop products originating or manufactured in and shipped out of the reporting country and include [re-exports](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). Import quantity is essentially the reverse: referring to the import of products for domestic consumption or processing within that country and includes re-imports. Trade values (measured in one thousand USD) are reported as the value of the products or goods as well as the value of the services performed to deliver the goods from border to border. Trade data is compiled by the domestic customs office. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1961 and 2020 and more crops and livestock products are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data See the documentation on how our team retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_039_rw0_agricultural_trade_statistics). description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) publishes annual national account balance in the form of balance of payments (BoP), that is, the sum of net exports of goods and services, net primary income, and net secondary income. BoP is a double-entry accounting system that shows all flows of goods and services into and out of an economy; all transfers that are the counterpart of real resources or financial claims provided to or by the rest of the world without a quid pro quo, such as donations and grants; and all changes in residents' claims on and liabilities to nonresidents that arise from economic transactions. All transactions are recorded twice—once as a credit and once as a debit. In principle, the net balance should be zero, but in practice the accounts often do not balance, requiring inclusion of a balancing item, net errors and omissions. The concepts and definitions underlying the data are based on the 6th edition of the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6), published by the IMF. Balance of payments data for 2005 onward will be presented in accord with the BPM6. The historical BPM5 data series will end with data for 2008, which can be accessed through the World Development Indicators archives. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: Food environment factors—such as store/restaurant proximity, food prices, food and nutrition assistance programs, and community characteristics—interact to influence food choices and diet quality. These interactions are complex and more research is needed to identify causal relationships and effective policy interventions. The Food Environment Atlas, developed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Economic Research Service, contains over 275 variables at the U.S. state or county level covering these factors. The objectives of the Food Environment Atlas are to assemble statistics on food environment indicators to stimulate research on the determinants of food choices and diet quality, and to provide a spatial overview of a community's ability to access healthy food and its success in doing so. title: Coral Reef Connectivity
description: ### Overview This dataset estimates the level of connectivity between each area containing coral reefs and other such areas. Connectivity refers to the extent to which populations are linked by the exchange of eggs, larval recruits, juveniles, or adults—an exchange which is primarily conducted via ocean currents. A coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by Wood et al. was applied by the 50 Reefs Project to simulate coral exchange between 2003 and 2011, ultimately yielding connectivity estimates globally at 0.05° resolution. These estimates were based on potential dispersal only; settlement and post-settlement survival were not modelled. Connectivity within and between protected areas is important for maintaining diversity, fish stocks, and especially important for maintaining ecological resilience. While poorly understood, it is a key factor to consider in marine reserve design as it may enhance resilience to disturbance and be important for the persistence of populations. Both of these are important processes in the context of conservation planning under climate change, the dominant threat to coral reefs in the coming decades. Even if the goals of the Paris Climate Agreement are achieved, 70-90% of coral reef areas are likely to cease to be suitable for coral growth by mid-century. Coral communities that survive will play a key role in the regeneration of reefs by mid-to-late century. The purpose of the 50 Reefs Project was to develop a long-term strategic plan for the conservation of coral reefs by identifying 50 large (500 km²) regions that are the least vulnerable to climate change and which are positioned to facilitate natural coral reef regeneration. These locations constitute important opportunities for novel conservation investments to secure less vulnerable yet well-connected coral reefs that may help to repopulate degraded areas after the climate has stabilized. The strategy and actions proposed by the project should strengthen and expand existing conservation efforts for coral reefs as the world faces the long-term consequences of intensifying climate change. ### Methodology The authors used a coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by [Wood et al.](https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.12101), basing their findings on simulations of larvae dispersal over a 93 month period. Within this modeling, 115 million particles (representing larvae from a generic broadcast spawning coral) were released from each of 12,397 habitat cells on a monthly basis between 2003-2011. Again following Wood et al., the authors used two measures of connectivity: (i) outgoing settlement, which is the proportion of particles that reached any habitat cell, including the source cell, and (ii) export, which is the proportion of particles reaching any cell other than the source cell, hence omitting self-seeding. These were combined into an overall "connectivity" score. The dataset contains entries for each of the approximately 54,586 0.05° degree (approximately 25 km² but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616)) raster cells identified as containing coral habitat by a dataset from [Coral Reef Watch](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/). The values were standardized to mean 0 unit variance for subsequent analysis by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The resulting scores reflect how far the values were below or above the population mean. The data table also contains: (1) an ID field that assigns a unique numeric identification number to each cell; (2) two fields representing the latitude and longitude of the center of the cell; (3) scores corresponding to other essential components of the 50 Reefs assessment; and (4) one final variable representing the aggregate score of the 50 Reefs analysis. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/conl.12587). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The 50 Reefs initiative generated scores for several other factors crucial to their assessment: thermal history and recent thermal conditions, predicted future thermal conditions, and cyclone and storm risk. In total, the component scores were derived from 174 separate variables relevant to these topics; these components were also combined into one final assessment score using a custom weighting. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Aqueduct Untreated Connected Wastewater
description: ### Overview Untreated connected wastewater measures the percentage of domestic wastewater that is connected through a sewerage system and not treated to at least a primary treatment level. Higher values indicate higher percentages of point source wastewater discharged without treatment. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<30%) to extremely high (>100%). Wastewater discharge without adequate treatment could expose water bodies, the general public, and ecosystems to pollutants such as pathogens and nutrients. The indicator compounds two crucial elements of wastewater management: connection and treatment. Low connection rates reflect households’ lack of access to public sewerage systems; the absence of at least primary treatment reflects a country’s lack of capacity infrastructure, institutional knowledge) to treat wastewater. Together these factors can indicate the level of a country’s current capacity to manage its domestic wastewater through two main pathways: extremely low connection rates (below 1 percent), and high connection rates with little treatment. Values are available per country. ### Methodology Sewerage connection and wastewater treatment data come from a white paper published by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and Veolia (Xie et al. 2016). In brief, Xie et al. aggregate three of the leading research papers on country-level connection and treatment rates into one data set through a hierarchical methodology. The data includes the percentage of households connected to sewerage systems (percent connected), and the percentage of wastewater connected left untreated (i.e., not treated using primary, secondary, or tertiary treatments) (percent untreated). The calculation is based on the Yale Environmental Performance Index’s Wastewater Treatment (WWT) indicator [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). WWT examines the performance of wastewater treatment [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). The untreated, connected wastewater indicator reverses the WWT to instead examine the hazard. The first step in the calculation was to group all countries with a household sewage connection rate of less than 1% into the “Low to no wastewater connected” category. For all remaining countries, the percent of wastewater treated to at least primary treatment (100% - percent of untreated wastewater) was calculated. This was multiplied by the household connection rate to find the percent of treated connected wastewater. Next, the percent of treated connected wastewater was subtracted from 100% to find the percent of untreated connected wastewater. Finally, raw untreated connected wastewater values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw untreated connected wastewater values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 30% - Low to medium (1-2): 30 - 60% - Medium to high (2-3): 60 - 90% - High (3-4): 90 - 100% - Extremely high (4-5): 100% - Low to no wastewater (5): -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

Potential Evapotranspiration
description: ### Overview This dataset details global potential evapotranspiration of a reference crop at 30 arc-seconds resolution (approximately 1km at the equator) for the 1970-2000 period. Evapotranspiration is the simultaneous process of evaporation and transpiration. Evaporation is the process in which liquid water is converted to water vapor. Transpiration is when plants take up water with their roots and release water vapor to the atmosphere through stomata in their leaves. The unit for evapotranspiration is total millimeters (mm) per year. A higher value in mm suggests more water is lost from that cropped surface. Potential evapotranspiration measures the ability of the atmosphere to remove water through evapotranspiration. In this dataset crop evapotranspiration (ET₀) is used as a measure of the evapotranspiration rate from a referenced and standardized vegetated surface (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nation ([FAO](http://www.fao.org/3/X0490E/x0490e04.htm)). This concept of ET₀ is useful to study evaporative demand of the atmosphere in relation to climatic factors and independently of crop type, crop development, and management practices. This dataset was developed by Antonio Trabucco and Robert Zomer with the support of the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI). The dataset can be used to support studies on sustainable development, poverty alleviation, and climate change adaptation. It is particularly relevant to crop and yield modeling and studying the impacts of climate change on future crop production. ### Methodology The widely-used standard equation to estimate potential evapotranspiration is the FAO Penman-Monteith equation (FAO-PM). Researchers used the FAO-PM equation in combination with data on multiple climate variables to produce an estimated ET₀ for a reference crop (well-watered grass at 12 cm of height). A reference crop was used to ensure the final results provided ET₀ information solely based on climate information of a region. Climate data was collected from [WorldClim 2.0 dataset](http://worldclim.org/version2). The World Clim 2.0 dataset includes monthly data on temperature, solar radiation, wind speed and water vapor pressure. description: This data set represents the extent, approximate location and type of wetlands and deepwater habitats in the United States and its Territories. These data delineate the areal extent of wetlands and surface waters as defined by Cowardin et al. (1979). The National Wetlands Inventory - Version 2, Surface Waters and Wetlands Inventory was derived by retaining the wetland and deepwater polygons that compose the NWI digital wetlands spatial data layer and reintroducing any linear wetland or surface water features that were orphaned from the original NWI hard copy maps by converting them to narrow polygonal features. Additionally, the data are supplemented with hydrography data, buffered to become polygonal features, as a secondary source for any single-line stream features not mapped by the NWI and to complete segmented connections. Wetland mapping conducted in WA, OR, CA, NV and ID after 2012 and most other projects mapped after 2015 were mapped to include all surface water features and are not derived data. The linear hydrography data set used to derive Version 2 was the U.S. Geological Survey's National Hydrography Dataset (NHD). Specific information on the NHD version used to derive Version 2 and where Version 2 was mapped can be found in the 'comments' field of the Wetlands_Project_Metadata feature class. Certain wetland habitats are excluded from the National mapping program because of the limitations of aerial imagery as the primary data source used to detect wetlands. These habitats include seagrasses or submerged aquatic vegetation that are found in the intertidal and subtidal zones of estuaries and near shore coastal waters. Some deepwater reef communities (coral or tuberficid worm reefs) have also been excluded from the inventory. These habitats, because of their depth, go undetected by aerial imagery. By policy, the Service also excludes certain types of "farmed wetlands" as may be defined by the Food Security Act or that do not coincide with the Cowardin et al. definition. Contact the Service's Regional Wetland Coordinator for additional information on what types of farmed wetlands are included on wetland maps. This data set should be used in conjunction with the Wetlands_Project_Metadata layer, which contains project specific wetlands mapping procedures and information on dates, scales and emulsion of imagery used to map the wetlands within specific project boundaries. title: Global Change Assessment Model Projections
description: GCAM is a dynamic-recursive model with technology-rich representations of the economy, energy sector, land use, and water linked to a climate model that can be used to explore climate change mitigation policies including carbon taxes, carbon trading, regulations, and accelerated deployment of energy technology. Regional population and labor productivity growth assumptions drive the energy and land-use systems employing numerous technology options to produce, transform, and provide energy services as well as to produce agriculture and forest products, and to determine land use and land cover. Using a run period extending from 1990 to 2100 at 5-year intervals, GCAM has been used to explore the potential role of emerging energy supply technologies and the greenhouse gas consequences of specific policy measures or energy technology adoption including CO2 capture and storage, bioenergy, hydrogen systems, nuclear energy, renewable energy technology, and energy use technology in buildings, industry, and the transportation sectors. GCAM is an representative concentration pathway (RCP)-class model. This means it can be used to simulate scenarios, policies, and emission targets from various sources including the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Output includes projections of future energy supply and demand and the resulting greenhouse gas emissions, radiative forcing, and climate effects of 16 greenhouse gases, aerosols, and short-lived species at 0.5 × 0.5 degree resolution, contingent on assumptions about future population, economy, technology, and climate mitigation policy. title: Freshwater Ecoregions
description: The Freshwater Ecoregions of the World (FEOW), an updated version of the original data set produced by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), provides a global biogeographic regionalization of the Earth's freshwater biodiversity. The freshwater major habitat types (MHTs) reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics and are roughly equivalent to biomes for terrestrial systems. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them within the broad environmental and geographic ecoregion conditions. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in freshwater systems. Covering virtually all freshwater habitats on Earth, this ecoregion map, together with associated species data, is a useful tool for underpinning global and regional conservation planning efforts, particularly to identify outstanding and imperiled freshwater systems; for serving as a logical framework for large-scale conservation strategies; and for providing a global-scale knowledge base for increasing freshwater biogeographic literacy. This version of the FEOW, modified by The Nature Conservancy, includes additional tabular data describing MHTs (similar to terrestrial biomes). The freshwater ecoregion map encompasses 426 units, whose boundaries generally, though not always, correspond with those of watersheds (also known as drainage basins or catchments). Within individual ecoregions there will be turnover of species, such as when moving up or down a river system, but taken as a whole an ecoregion will typically have a distinct evolutionary history and/or ecological processes. Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted PM2.5 concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2f6f2860-9c27-4062-a72a-066f62a56891) as a replacement.**_ The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, particularly in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1950 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere, measured in this database by millimeters of water evaporated per month. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. The Food and Agriculture Organization Penman-Monteith (FAO-PM) equation incorporates these factors into a calculation of PET that is widely considered to be the best estimate of actual PET available: PET = 0.0023 * RA * (Tmean + 17.8) * TD^(0.5), where RA represents extraterrestrial radiation in millimeters per month, Tmean is the mean temperature in degrees Celsius, and TD is the daily temperature range in degrees Celsius. These variables are not always available at every point on Earth, which prevents calculation with the FAO-PM. This Global PET database is calculated using a simpler equation attributed to Hargreave, which requires monthly average data sets of mean temperatures, daily temperature range, and extraterrestrial radiation. These variables are all available in the WorldClim Global Climate Data database. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled 5-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks, or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing, or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure. Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators. GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website. ### Methodology The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module. All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). title: Access to an Improved Water Source (Rural)
description: ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017 for rural populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water. WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. ### Methodology This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average was calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria (accessibility and availability). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS). ### Additional Information Additional data for the percentage of the population with access to an improved water source at [urban]((https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-Urban) and [national](https://.resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat005a-Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-National-Level_1) levels is available on Resource Watch. title: Current and Projected Food Insecurity
description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Urban Population Living in Slums
description: ### Overview The Urban Population Living in Slums is a global dataset that shows the percentage of a country's urban population living in slum households. A slum household is defined as a group of individuals living under the same roof lacking one or more of the following facilities: improved water, improved sanitation, sufficient living area, durable housing, and security of tenure. The dataset includes information on 97 countries utilizing the most recent survey and census data available, which ranges between 1990 and present, depending on the country. The dataset is presented at a national resolution. This dataset was created as part of the United Nations Millennium Development Goals (MDG) and was compiled by The United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-HABITAT). The overall goal of MDG is to fight poverty in its many dimensions. This dataset was created to be used as an indicator for MDG Target 7D. Target 7D’s goal is by 2020, to have achieved a significant improvement in the lives of at least 100 million slum dwellers. ### Methodology The Urban Population Living in Slums dataset was created by using a proxy measurement based on access to some basic facilities. A household was determined to be living in a slum if atleast one of the following services were unavailable to them: - Access to improved drinking water sources that are protected from outside contamination and in particular from contamination with fecal matter. - Access to improved sanitation services that hygienically separates human waste from human contact. - Durable house that can protect its residents from extremes of climatic conditions, such as rain, heat, cold and humidity. - Sufficient living area so that more than three people don't have to share the same room that is a minimum of four square meters in area. - Secure tenure which ensures all individuals and groups have effective protection by the State against forced unlawful evictions. This data was collected by combining information from a variety of household surveys. Household surveys used varied by region and country, but included Urban Inequities Surveys (UIS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), Demographic Health Surveys (DHS), World Health Surveys (WHS), Living Standards and Measurement Surveys (LSMS), Core Welfare Indicator Questionnaires (CWIQ), and the Pan Arab Project for Family Health Surveys (PAPFAM). The number of people living in urban households that were determined to be lacking one or more basic service was divided by the total urban population, and then multiplied by 100 to create the final value. National Statistics Offices typically carried out household surveys every 3-5 years and population censuses every 10 years. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://mdgs.un.org/unsd/mi/wiki/7-10-Proportion-of-urban-population-living-in-slums.ashx). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. It was designed as a tool for planning conservation across a range of scales and assesses conservation efforts and gaps worldwide. title: Renewable Energy Investment by Sector
description: All figures in the report, unless otherwise credited, are based on the output of the Desktop database of Bloomberg New Energy Finance, an online portal to the world’s most comprehensive database of investors, projects, and transactions in clean energy. The Bloomberg New Energy Finance Desktop collates all organizations, projects, and investments according to transaction type, sector, geography, and timing. It covers many tens of thousands of organizations (including start-ups, corporate entities, venture capital, and private equity providers, banks, and other investors), projects, and transactions. The following renewable energy projects are included: all biomass and waste-to-energy, geothermal, and wind generation projects of more than 1 MW; all hydropower projects of between 1 MW and 50 MW; all wave and tidal energy projects; all biofuel projects with a capacity of 1 million litres or more per year; and all solar projects, with those less than 1 MW estimated separately and referred to as small-scale projects, or small distributed capacity, in this report. The 2017 Global Trends report concentrates on renewable power and fuels---wind, solar, biomass and waste, biofuels, geothermal, marine, and small hydroelectric projects of less than 50 MW. It does not cover larger hydroelectric dams (ones of more than 50 MW), except briefly in the Executive Summary and Chapter 5. Energy-smart technologies such as smart grid, electric vehicles, and energy storage are also outside the main scope of the report, but they are discussed briefly in a section in Chapter 2. Where deal values are not disclosed, Bloomberg New Energy Finance assigns an estimated value based on comparable transactions. Deal values are rigorously back-checked and updated when further information is released about particular companies and projects. The statistics used are historical figures, based on confirmed and disclosed investment. Annual investment is estimated for small-scale commercial and residential projects such as rooftop solar. These figures are based on annual installation data, provided by industry associations and REN21. Bloomberg New Energy Finance continuously monitors investment in renewable energy. This is a dynamic process: as the sector’s visibility grows, information flow improves. New deals come to light and existing data are refined, meaning that historical figures are constantly updated.
