title: Mangrove Forests
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the global extent of mangroves for 1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2015 and 2016. This is the first global map of mangrove extent produced using an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, using a combination of optical and radar satellite data. Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology. The dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. ### Methodology The mangrove maps were derived in two steps: 1) generation of a baseline map of global mangrove extent for the year 2010 and 2) detection of changes between the 2010 baseline and each of the other six years. **2010 global mangrove extent baseline map:** The 2010 baseline map was derived by the Random Forest Classification algorithm that used a combination of L-band radar (ALOS PALSAR) and optical (Landsat-5, -7) satellite data. Approximately 15,000 Landsat scenes and 1,500 ALOS PALSAR (1 x 1 degree) mosaic tiles were used to create optical and radar image composites covering the coastlines along the tropical and sub-tropical coastlines in the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Oceania. The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). Classification accuracy of the 2010 baseline dataset was assessed with approximately 53,800 randomly sampled points across 20 randomly selected regions. Overall accuracy was 95.25 %, while User’s and Producer’s accuracies for the mangrove class were estimated at 97.5% and 94.0%, respectively. **1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2015 and 2016 maps of mangrove extent and changes:** The maps for the other six years were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996), ALOS PALSAR (2007, 2008 & 2009) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2015 & 2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new yearly extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0 %. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Plastic Inputs from Rivers into Oceans
description: ### Overview This dataset shows a global estimate of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans for 2010, expressed in kilograms per year. The authors used data on waste management, population density, and hydrological information to create this model. The dataset includes information on 40,760 watersheds and 182 different countries. The data is presented in a vector format. Plastic pollution in our oceans and on our coastlines have become a major threat to ocean health worldwide. A better understanding and quantification of marine plastic sources can help in implementing mitigation strategies to alleviate the issue. The dataset can help in identifying places that require higher attention in terms of plastic waste monitoring and mitigation plans. This data can also be used as a baseline measurement for ocean plastic mass balance exercises. This data was developed by researchers funded by The Ocean Cleanup Foundation. ### Methodology The amount of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans was estimated by using data on mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) per country, population density, topographic elevation, and location of artificial barriers (weirs and dams). For each catchment area mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) rates per day were calculated by combining data on waste generation by inhabitant per day and population density for the area. This data was combined with water flow per river catchment area to provide a final value for the mass of plastic released at the river’s mouth. This data was extrapolated using seasonal variations in water flow to create a year dataset. Data on population density was derived from the dataset Global 15 x 15 Minute Grids of the Downscaled Population by the Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) for 182 countries. Data used to calculate MPW rates were collected from seven peer reviewed studies. Topographic information was taken from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) hydrological model for surface/subsurface runoff and location of artificial barriers was taken from AquaStat and Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD). In total the dataset includes information for 40,760 watersheds worldwide. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15611#Sec6). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for plastic input in tonnes per year, plastic input in tonnes per month, and average monthly water runoff in catchment area in mm per day are also available from the data provider. title: Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), and [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. title: Global Surface Heat Flow
description: The Global Map of Solid Earth Surface Heat Flow was created by J. Huw Davies of the School of Earth and Ocean Sciences at Cardiff University (CU SEOS) using a raw heat-flow data set provided by Gabi Laske and Guy Masters of Reference Earth Model at the University of California San Diego (REM UCSD). The data behind the Global map of Earth Surface Heat Flow uses ocean heat flux estimates in mW m-2 in regions with oceanic crust younger than 67.7 million years. The data and geology correlation components use the median as opposed to the mean in deriving the estimates in the merged polygons. The map was presented on an equal 2°x 2° area grid. The result was calculated assuming the median of the data measurements and the median of the geology correlation in the merged polygons; and then also the median of the heat flow value in the union polygons in a grid cell. The resulting data was used to create a map on GIS. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

For an ecoregion or collection of ecoregions, TNC develops and disseminates finer-scale data on the distribution and status of biodiversity, habitat condition, current and future threats, and the sociopolitical conditions that influence conservation success within those ecoregions. These finer-scale data allow TNC to set long-term conservation goals for ecosystems, natural communities, and imperiled or declining species representative of an ecoregion, and to establish ecoregional priorities for resource allocation—specific landscapes, threats to biodiversity, and strategic opportunities that affect one or more ecoregions and demand immediate attention. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](85a08a4d-9336-4d18-9aaa-b7cb97bc6abf) as a replacement.**_ This cumulative impact index ranging from ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change) for the impact of climate change on oceans was calculated using sea surface temperature (SST), ocean productivity measured by chlorophyll (CHL), and ocean circulation by Ramirez et al. (2017). The data to calculate were from the longest time series of remote-sensing records (annual composites) on SST (1980-2014), CHL (1979-2014), and marine currents (1980-2014) available to provide finest-scale measurements of the impacts of climate change on the marine environment globally. Pixel basis, least-squares linear regression of annual information from SST, CHL, and the eastern and northern components of water speed were used for deriving the significance of temporal trends and its magnitudes (slopes; that is, annual changes in target features) over the past 3 decades. CHL data were sourced online as annual composites, whereas data on SST and marine currents were obtained on a monthly basis and averaged yearly to generate a linear relationship to extract slopes. This calculation was repeated for every pixel of the globe. These magnitudes were combined to obtain the spatially explicit Cumulative Impact Index. Different layers were first resampled following a bilinear interpolation procedure to match the spatial resolution of the coarsest SST product (that is, 1° grid). Absolute values for the slopes of obtained trends (a proxy to the magnitude of environmental changes) were then standardized to the maximum value to make all variables comparable. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value. In this way, researchers obtained a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change), thereby providing information about spatial heterogeneity in the magnitude of environmental changes and highlighting those marine areas that have undergone the largest changes in their environmental conditions. title: Average High Temperature
description: Annual average high temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions Projections
description: The Climate Analysis Indicators Tool (CAIT) Emissions Projections is part of the larger CAIT Climate Data Explorer. CAIT is a suite of online data and visualization tools that support the many dimensions of climate policy making. It provides free, open, user-friendly access to world-class climate data. The projections tool allows users to view projected emissions from national and international sources and compare policy assumptions and drivers between countries and among sources. The tool aims to increase the transparency of each scenario by publishing key assumptions and other related information. The CAIT Emissions Projections tool collates emission projections for major emitters through the year 2100, or earlier if limited data are available. Each data subset, such as GHG Emissions Data or Socioeconomic Data, has indicators, such as Gross Domestic Product or Population, that influence the projection. Predictions are created through scenarios. These describe possible future pathways under existing policies and actions, or, in other words, in the absence of further mitigation efforts. CAIT draws on key climate-relevant data from respected research centers, government agencies, and international bodies. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average minimum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Annual Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Malaria Extent
description: The Malaria Extent dataset is provided by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and shows the estimated proportion of 2-10 year olds in the general population that are infected with P. falciparum at any one time at a global scale. Malaria is a disease caused by parasites that are transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. Two related parasite species cause the majority of disease and death from malaria: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. In areas affected by malaria, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, a condition further compounded by poverty. MAP conducted surveys to collect data on malaria cases. Each survey included in the MAP parasite database has been disaggregated to individual sites (geographical points), individual dates (if the same site was sampled repeatedly), and individual parasite species. Conversely, individual-level survey data have been aggregated up to the community level at a particular site and time. MAP data spans 2000-2017. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Seychelles Storm Surge and Sea Level Rise Exposure
description: This dataset was developed in 2019 by a team of researchers at the University of Michigan. The map shows the geographic distribution of an index developed to represent the exposure of Mahé’s coastline to the impacts of a storm surge event. Due to the minimal record of storm surge data in Seychelles, the difficulty of gauging how global climate change could increase the probability of a storm surge occurring, and the fact that data parameters typically used in storm surge prediction models weren’t made available to the research team, this data set identifies the regions that would be most exposed to the impacts of a storm surge, rather than the likelihood of a storm surge occurring. Considering these existing constraints, this model is processes-based and not calibrated by existing storm surge data; therefore, it is purely theoretical. The data was created in ArcGIS using a multi-criteria analysis model with elevation, slope, topographic wetness index, cost distance from river, soil type, and vegetation cover as criteria of interest. These variables were scaled, weighted, arranged into a pairwise comparison matrix, assigned relative importance, put into an Analytic Hierarchy Process program to calculate weighted sums, and ultimately produce a storm surge exposure index. A more comprehensive explanation of how this index was created can be found in the report linked below.

title: Cumulative Tree Cover Height Gain
description: This data set shows tree cover regrowth for South America for the period 1987-2016. Tree cover height is estimated annually using Landsat satellite imagery calibrated with LIDAR data. Pixels are marked as having regrowth when they pass above 5 meters for three consecutive years. The data for 2015-2016 is considered preliminary, as there have only been two or one, respectively, height observations - data for these years will be updated in future years and may change. This is a provisional version of the data: the full version will be released in the coming months and expanded to other parts of the tropics. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Ozone (O₃) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of O₃ for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to the maximum 8-hour concentration. Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that is harmful to breathe and damages crops and other vegetation. Unlike stratospheric ozone in the upper atmosphere, which protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays and forms naturally, ground-level ozone forms when emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides react in the presence of heat and sunlight. Gasoline-burning vehicles are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Other sources include consumer products such as paints, insecticides, cleaners, as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution/health-effects-ozone-pollution), ozone irritates respiratory systems, can aggravate asthma, and can damage cells that line your lungs. Ozone may also aggravate chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and bronchitis and may cause permanent lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults. The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world. These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis. ### Methodology Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/). Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md). Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry. The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions. The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for fine particulate matter [(PM2.5)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f5599d62-7f3d-41c7-b3fd-9f8e08ee7b2a) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Forecasted data at an hourly time step is available from the source. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_004_city_aq). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

City Expansion Index
description: ### Overview The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city. ### Methodology This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Historical Imagery
description: ### Overview The Historical Imagery dataset is a compilation of high quality Landsat imagery for each year from 2013-2016. These images show a detailed picture of the landscape at the Earth’s surface, e.g., forests, ice, freshwater, grasslands, desert and urban areas. Landsat data was collected continuously by satellite sensors. These sensors collected approximately 22 complete pictures of the Earth per year, with a spatial resolution of 30 meters (m). The satellite imagery was processed with Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm. This algorithm converts the images to [top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance](https://un-spider.org/node/10958) values and removes cloud-covered pixels. Understanding the Earth’s changing landscape is critical to many environmental issues: agriculture, water usage, forest coverage and natural disasters. In agriculture, Landsat data can be used to predict crop production, help farmers make planting decisions and settle water usage disputes. Landsat imagery shows changes in forest coverage, which is crucial to forest management and protection. Forest coverage influences the environment in many ways, including carbon storage and flood control. Landsat imagery is also a valuable tool for analyzing natural disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and volcanic eruptions. In areas affected by natural disasters, before and after imagery can be used to map damage, plan recovery efforts, and assess future risk. The Historical Imagery dataset was generated by [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/). Earth Engine is a tool for visualizing and analyzing geospatial datasets. The platform hosts satellite imagery in a public data archive for academic, non-profit, business and government users. In addition to hosting data, Earth Engine provides a variety of algorithms and processed datasets, including climate, surface temperature, weather and land cover. Earth Engine is part of Google’s overall mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible. The satellite data used to generate the Historical Imagery dataset was provided by [Landsat](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat). Landsat is a joint effort between the [United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/) and the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/). Founded in 1972, Landsat manages satellites that continuously acquire images of the Earth. Landsat’s mission is to provide uninterrupted data and imagery of the Earth to help with decision-making about natural resources and the environment. ### Methodology The Historical Imagery dataset was generated from images of the Earth collected by instruments aboard the [Landsat satellites](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/landsat-satellite-missions?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con). These satellites crossed every point on Earth once every 16 days and each provided 22 complete pictures of the Earth each year. Each pixel in these images has a resolution of 30 m. The satellite imagery was processed using [Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/apidocs/ee-algorithms-landsat-simplecomposite). This algorithm selected a subset of pixels at each location and converted them to top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance. This conversion is a linear transformation used to correct satellite data for variations in solar angle and the scattering of light that occurs as light travels through the atmosphere and reflects off the Earth. The simple cloud score was used to find the images with the least cloud cover. This algorithm scored TOA data pixels by their relative cloudiness from 0 (least cloudy) to 100 (most cloudy). After the pixels were scored, the median of the least cloudy pixels were used, thus selecting the least cloudy images. These images were used to generate the Historical Imagery composites. description: ### Overview This dataset shows boats detected using satellite data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument. VIIRS only detects the activity of lit boats. The data shows patterns of vessel activity and can provide indications of fishing activity within marine protected areas (MPAs) and across exclusive economic zone (EEZ) boundaries. Generally, EEZs are defined as the area within 200 nautical miles of a country’s coastline. The dataset is published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) and the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). The dataset has global spatial coverage, gives point location (latitude and longitude) of boat detections. The data collection began in 2017 and is updated daily. ### Methodology Lit fishing boat features detected by the VIIRS day/night band (DNB) data show up as spikes of light. A set of algorithms has been developed for automatic detection of spikes and characterization of the sharpness of spike features. A spike detection algorithm generates a list of candidate boat detections. A second algorithm measures the height of the spikes for the discard of ionospheric energetic particle detections and to rate boat detections as either strong or weak. A sharpness index is used to label boat detections that appear blurry due to the scattering of light by clouds. The candidate spikes are then compared with a separate VIIRS gas flares data set to identify detections that were also found to be gas flares. Based on the sharpness index, scan properties, and the gas flare indication, each candidate spike is assigned a quality flag that separates the detections into boats, blurry detections, and gas flares. Based on the location of the boat detections, they are also assigned information such as whether it is in an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) or a marine protected area (MPA). description: ### Overview The Tree Cover Gain dataset measures areas of tree cover gain from 2001 through 2012. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Gain is mapped for all areas that did not have tree cover in 2000 and had ≥ 50% cover in 2012. Longer-lived regrowing stands of tree cover that did not begin as non-forest within the study period were not mapped as forest gain. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the gain in tree cover of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover gain. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. description: Increases in the rates of hospital admission for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking Crude Rate of Hospitalization for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. Heat stress can manifest in a number of clinical outcomes, and people with chronic health problems (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity) are more susceptible to the effects of heat than healthy individuals. For these reasons, heat stress may not be listed as the primary diagnosis. This indicator therefore includes all cases where heat stress is explicitly listed as the primary diagnosis or any other diagnosis. The hospital data shown here are provided by state and/or local public health departments to the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Program. Data are based on the date of admission rather than the date of discharge. For these measures, admission date is limited to between May 1 and September 30 for each year. These data represent number of admissions rather than number of individuals admitted to the hospital. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. description: ### Overview This dataset shows renewable energy consumption in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). In the case of smaller non-OECD countries, extrapolations of country data provided by the UN Statistics Division were used. title: [Archived] Global Hunger Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2018, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2018 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. In the GHI by Severity layers, countries are classified as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child Mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores. description: The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. title: Groundwater Vulnerability to Floods and Droughts
description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). The Map of Global Groundwater Vulnerability (GWV) to Floods and Droughts at the scale of 1:25,000,000 is a WHYMAP product that rates groundwater systems on a scale of 1 to 7 according to their vulnerability to drought and flood events. Vulnerability is defined as a system's sensitivity to natural and/or human impacts, and the ability of the system to cope with these impacts. This information can be used to prioritize which groundwater resources can be relied on in case of a natural disaster. The maps of groundwater systems were sourced from national, regional, and global sources. Many aquifer boundaries were sourced from the WHYMAP Groundwater Resources Map (GRM). The GRM includes major groundwater basins, areas with complex hydrogeological structures, and local and shallow aquifers. These were complemented by aquifers in fluvial deposits of large rivers from the Geological Map of the World, aquifers in carbonate rocks—usually karstified—from the World Map of Carbonate Rock Outcrops, and the WHYMAP database for aquifers with nonrenewable groundwater. The extent of the impact of different natural disasters on aquifers and their groundwater resources differs depending on factors such as the origin of the disaster, its intensity and frequency, the hydrogeological conditions and geographical position of the aquifer (coastal area or a floodplain), and other factors affecting vulnerability (shallow or deep, whether groundwater is nonrenewable). The GWV uses a simplified version of the DRASTIC index for assessing groundwater vulnerability, measuring aquifer vulnerability according to the type of aquifer and the aquifer’s groundwater recharge rate. Aquifer types are assessed according to the map sources mentioned above. Groundwater recharge rates are calculated using the WaterGAP hydrogeological model and categorized as < 20 mm/year, 20-100 mm/year, or > 100 mm/year. A total vulnerability range (TVR) is assigned to each aquifer based on its type and recharge rate. Aquifer type is weighted more than rate of recharge in this calculation, since aquifers in carbonate rocks (often karstified) or in fluvial deposits of large rivers and shallow and local aquifers are all highly vulnerable to natural disasters—particularly floods, storms, and tsunamis—and are also highly vulnerable to droughts in arid and semiarid regions. Natural disasters include 1) hydro-climatic events (floods, droughts, storms); 2) geological events (earthquakes, volcanic activity); and 3) events caused by a combination of hydroclimatic and geological factors (tsunamis, landslides). The GWV focuses on hydroclimatic events, and the vulnerability of each aquifer is assessed for floods and droughts. The map assigns 7 categories of vulnerability based on the combination of flood and drought vulnerability (low, low; low, moderate; etc). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview The Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas dataset as shown on Resource Watch presents marine protected areas (MPAs) that are fully or highly protected. The [Marine Protection Atlas (MPAtlas)](https://mpatlas.org/) uses the [World Database on Protected Areas](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas) as a starting point, then assesses the current protection status of listed MPAs based on additional sources and research. This global dataset was first created in 2020 and in the future will be regularly updated, as new MPAs are created, protections change, and currently designated areas are implemented. MPAs are essential for safeguarding biodiversity and the health of marine ecosystems. They provide sanctuary for species to mature and reproduce, and they help restore healthy populations within and beyond their borders. MPAs also build resilience against threats such as climate change and pollution by maintaining vital natural processes, storing carbon, buffering coastlines, and ensuring sustainable food supplies for coastal communities. However, different MPAs may offer different levels of protection, from minor restrictions to the full exclusion of most commercial activity. Robust scientific evidence indicates that no-take zones (where no extractive activities are allowed) and highly protected areas yield the greatest conservation benefits. The MPAtlas brings together the best available information on marine protection around the world, so that the marine conservation community can work together to protect at least [30% of the world's oceans by 2030](https://www.campaignfornature.org/science-page). This more detailed approach to MPA data provides a more nuanced look at progress toward conservation goals and the outcomes that can be expected from existing protections. ### Methodology MPAtlas takes the WDPA as its starting point and examines the listed MPAs in depth, adding to or replacing WDPA records with information from original research using more detailed or up-to-date sources, such as national or regional databases, official documentation, or management plans. These additions can include more accurate spatial data, such as the addition of boundaries for individual zones within an MPA. It can also include more detailed information about site regulations and management, both of which are directly related to conservation outcomes. MPAtlas coverage numbers differ from those of other sources for two primary reasons: 1. MPAtlas attempts to identify and distinguish protected areas that are legally designated but are still awaiting implementation from those that are fully in effect on the water. The project also identifies committed or proposed protected areas that have not yet achieved legal or authoritative recognition. 2. MPA coverage data is reported by protection level, as no-take and fully and highly protected areas are those which afford the greatest conservation benefits. The project accomplishes this by conducting detailed assessments using widely-accepted, scientifically-based criteria for measuring an MPA’s protection level and associated conservation outcomes. Detailed information about the assessment process [can be found here](https://marine-conservation.org/mpatlas-assessments/). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://mpatlas.org/methods). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) and [the MPA subset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007b-Marine-Protected-Areas), on which the MPAtlas is based. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the Marine Protected Atlas. The MPAtlas includes all MPAs in the WDPA, but because these are already mapped elsewhere, Resource Watch displays only those MPAtlas entries with confirmed partial or complete protections from fishing and extractive commercial activity. description: The global Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness (LHASA) model is developed by NASA to provide situational awareness of landslide hazards for a wide range of users. Precipitation is a common trigger of landslides. The Integrated Multisatellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement mission (IMERG) data shows recent precipitation, updated every 30 minutes. A LHASA landslide “nowcast” is created by comparing GPM data from the last 7 days to the long-term precipitation record provided by the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Multisatellite Precipitation Analysis (TMPA). Because IMERG data are only available starting in 2014, the record of historical rainfall was established by the TMPA, comparing 2001 to the present. The TMPA rainfall probability distributions were then compared to those of IMERG, and the rainfall thresholds were adjusted so that the IMERG data more closely mapped to those of the TMPA archive. The past 7 days of rainfall are considered, with each day weighted according to its date before present, with the last 24 hours having the most impact. In places where precipitation is unusually high, the susceptibility of the terrain is evaluated based on the global landslide susceptibility map, which includes quantitative information on whether (1) roads have been built, (2) trees have been cut down or burned, (3) a major tectonic fault is nearby, (4) the local bedrock is weak, or (5) the hillsides are steep.
