title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description: ### Overview Biodiversity hotspots, a classification system created by the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), include some of our planet’s most biologically diverse yet threatened terrestrial areas. An area is qualified as a hotspot if it contains at least 1,500 species of vascular plants found nowhere else on Earth (known as “endemic” species) and it has lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation. Between 1988 and 2016, 36 biodiversity hotspots have been identified globally. ### Methodology Hotspots were defined by Norman Myers in 1988 when he published a seminal paper identifying 10 tropical forest “hotspots.” These regions were characterized both by exceptional levels of plant endemism, meaning plants found nowhere else on Earth, and serious levels of habitat loss. Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers’s hotspots as its institutional blueprint in 1989. In 1999, CI undertook a global review, which introduced quantitative thresholds for the designation of biodiversity hotspots and resulted in the identification of 25. In 2005, an additional analysis brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots to 34, based on the work of nearly 400 specialists. In 2011, the Forests of East Australia were identified as the 35th hotspot by a team of researchers from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization working with CI. In February 2016, the North American Coastal Plain was recognized as meeting the criteria and became the world’s 36th hotspot. description: Potential Natural Vegetation is a data set created by EarthStat to identify what vegetation would be most likely to exist now in the absence of human activities. In regions not dominated by human land use, the vegetation types are those currently observed from a satellite. This differs from presettlement natural vegetation to the extent that vegetation types have changed because of changing environmental conditions such as climate and CO₂ concentrations. 1 km resolution DISCover data were classified under the Olson Global Ecosystems (OGE) framework to derive the potential vegetation data set. First the 94 OGE classes were reclassified into 15 potential vegetation types and 3 additional classes: land use, wetlands, and water. Wetlands are poorly characterized in the DISCover data and were thus ignored; only upland natural vegetation was considered. Each 5 minute resolution grid cell was searched among the 1 km pixels for the dominant potential upland vegetation class and was assigned to be the potential vegetation. Some grid cells had 2 dominant potential vegetation classes, or none. In these cases, the search was iterated to the adjacent 1 km pixels until a dominant potential vegetation class was found. Non-CO₂ Agricultural Emissions
description: The non-CO₂ agricultural emissions data set, published the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database, contains all the non-CO₂ emissions produced in the different agricultural emissions subdomains (enteric fermentation, manure management, rice cultivation, synthetic fertilizers, manure applied to soils, manure left on pastures, crop residues, cultivation of organic soils, burning of crop residues, burning of savanna, energy use) and provides a picture of their contribution to the total amount of GHG emissions from agriculture. GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. The FAOSTAT emissions database is computed following Tier 1 IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Water Stress Country Ranking
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available freshwater. The dataset was calculated by comparing water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. Higher water stress values indicate that there is more competition among people for available freshwater. The dataset was grouped by water usage for different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand which sectors had the greatest impact on water stress. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments in creating water use policies. ### Methodology The Water Stress Country Ranking is based on baseline water stress measurements. Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Gridded output data from the [PCRaster Global Water Balance](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/2429/2018/) (PCRGLOBWB 2) hydrological model was used for both water withdrawal and available water. The water withdrawal output data from PCRGLOBWB 2 included monthly data from January 1960 to December 2014 for four sectors: domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock. Output data for available water was also available over the same time frame. Data from the model was then aggregated spatially to the sub-basin level using the World Wildlife Fund’s (WWF) [HydroBASINS level 6](https://hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) hydrological sub-basins. Next, the data was regressed at the sub-basin level using an ordinary least square (OLS) regression with a trailing moving window size of 10 years to reduce noise in the data. This process resulted in gross water withdrawal and available water for each month for each sub-basin in the dataset. Next, the overall baseline water stress per month, per year, per sub-basin was determined. This was done by dividing the gross total water withdrawal by the difference between the available water and consumptive water withdrawal. This resulted in 12 time series of baseline water stress for each sub-basin: one time series for each month, with each time series spanning the years 1960-2014. Then, a single baseline water stress value for each month in each sub-basin was calculated by fitting a second OLS regression to each of the 12 time series and using the value for 2014 as the baseline water stress for that month. While the 2014 regression value is used, this value actually represents the baseline value, rather than an estimate of the water stress in 2014. To compute national baseline water stress scores, the sub-basins had to be aggregated to a national scale. Aggregation was made possible by following the steps outlined on page 4 of the [2013 version](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct_coutnry_rankings_010914.pdf) of the methodology. This resulted in raw country score percentages in which water stress was classified as follows: - Low (0-1): <10% - Low to medium (1-2): 10-20% - Medium to high (2-3): 20-40% - High (3-4): 40-80% - Extremely high (4-5): >80% Each category represents the risk of water stress in the country. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct-30-updated-decision-relevant-global-water-risk-indicators_1.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on drought risk and riverine flood risk is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_036_rw1_water_stress_country_ranking). title: [Archived] PRODES deforestation
description: The PRODES deforestation dataset was developed by Global Forest Watch (GFW) at the World Resources Institute (WRI) using data from the PRODES project, which is operated by the National Institute of Space Research (INPE) in collaboration with the Minister of the Environment (MMA) and the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA). The dataset shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon between 2000 and 2015. Since 2002, all PRODES data is publicly available online. Input images for each of the 220 Landsat footprints that cover the Brazilian Amazon are selected based on their lack of cloud cover and their capture date. The PRODES system uses the seasonal year, starting on August 1st, to calculate annual deforestation, so images are selected as near to this date as possible (generally from July, August, and September). From 2003 to 2005, analysts used image transformation to determine the components of vegetation, soil, and shadow using the program SPRING. These components were segmented and classified into the classes of forest, non-forest, deforestation in the target year, previous deforestation, clouds, and water, which are then manually corrected by experts. Starting in 2005, a new methodology was implemented which makes use of the open source TerraAmazon platform. The platform allows the PRODES analysis to be more uniform and can incorporate imagery from a variety of satellites. As before, images are selected to be as cloud free as possible. The images are then masked to exclude non-forest, previous deforestation, and water using the previous year’s analysis. Analysts then delineate deforested polygons in the intact forest of the previous year. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Global Peace Index
description: ### Overview The Global Peace Index (GPI) is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence to assess a nation’s level of peace. This lack of violence is defined as Negative Peace. A higher GPI represents a higher level of violence in a country. The Global Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure global peacefulness. Its goal is to create understanding on the effects of violence and help countries develop the means to create peaceful societies. It measures a country’s level of Negative Peace using three domains of peacefulness: 1. *The extent of Ongoing Domestic and International Conflict:* This investigates the extent to which countries are involved in internal and external conflicts, as well as their role and duration of involvement in conflicts. This is based on six indicators, such as the number and duration of internal conflicts, number of deaths from external organized conflicts, and relationships with neighboring countries. 2. *The level of Societal Safety and Security:* It evaluates the level of harmony or discord within a nation using ten indicators. These indicators include topics like the level of perceived criminality in society, impact of terrorism, and political instability. 3. *The degree of Militarisation:* Militarisation refers to a country’s military build-up and access to weapons. This is determined by using seven indicators, such as military expenditure as a percentage of GDP, number of armed services personnel per 100,000 people, and nuclear and heavy weapons capabilities. The GPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2008 to 2019 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand the economic value and trends of peace, and how to develop peaceful societies. ### Methodology The Global Peace Index uses 23 indicators in three domains to quantify the absence of violence or fear of violence. An international panel of independent experts helped to select the indicators in 2007 and reviews them on an annual basis. These 23 indicators were weighted and combined into two categories to create an overall score for GPI out of 100. The total GPI score was then simplified into a value of 1-5, with 5 being the highest amount of violence or fear being present within a country. The two overarching categories were a measure of how peaceful a country is internally and a measure of how peaceful a country is externally. The value of these two categories out of the total GPI value was 40% for external peace and 60% for internal peace. The weighting scheme was selected based on the relative importance of each indicator to achieve global peace. All scores for each indicator were normalized on a scale of 1-5. Qualitative indicators were banded into five groupings relevant to the indicator. Quantitative indicators were scored continuously based on relevant data and rounded to the third decimal point. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s team of country analysts scored seven of the eight qualitative indicators and also provided estimates about the gaps in the quantitative data. Scoring for qualitative indicators followed a strict set of guidelines to ensure reliability between values. Quantitative values were taken from a variety of international and government organizations. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/07/GPI-2019web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c12446ce-174f-4ffb-b2f7-77ecb0116aba) as a replacement.**_ The STAR Vegetation Health Index is a product from NOAA's National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NOAA-NESDIS) Global and Regional Vegetation Heath (VH) system estimating vegetation health, moisture condition, and thermal condition. VH products can be used as proxy data for monitoring vegetation health, drought, soil saturation, moisture and thermal conditions, fire risk, greenness of vegetation cover, vegetation fraction, leaf area index, start/end of the growing season, crop and pasture productivity, teleconnection with ENSO, desertification, mosquito-borne diseases, invasive species, ecological resources, land degradation, etc. The VH indices range from 0 to 100 characterizing changes in vegetation conditions from extremely poor (0) to excellent (100). Fair conditions are coded by green color (50), which changes to brown and red when conditions deteriorate and to blue when they improve. The VH reflects indirectly a combination of chlorophyll and moisture content in the vegetationhealth and also changes in thermal conditions at the surface.Monitoring vegetation health (condition), including drought detection and watch, is based on radiance measurements in the visible (VIS), near infrared (NIR), and 10.3-11.3 micrometers thermal (T) bands (channels) of the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR). These measurements are processed to reduce long-term noise. The VIS and NIR values were converted to the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI=(NIR-VIS)/(NIR+VIS)) and the T to brightness temperature (BT) using a look-up table. The NDVI and BT were filtered in order to eliminate high frequency noise. They were also adjusted for a non-uniformity of the land surface due to climate and ecosystem differences using multi-year NDVI and BT data. The NDVI and BT were converted to the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI).The Vegetation Health Index (VHI) is a proxy characterizing vegetation health or a combined estimation of moisture and thermal conditions. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Marine Protected Areas
description: ### Overview The Marine Protected Area (MPA) dataset contains officially designated parks, reserves, and other formal conservation areas around the world that have a substantial maritime component. Protected area data are provided via [Protected Planet](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas), the online interface for the World Database for Protected Areas (WDPA). The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data is provided as shapefiles and updates monthly. Each record is either represented as a polygon boundary, or if unavailable, a point location, along with descriptive information, such as the name, legal designation, and mode of administration. As of May 2019, the WDPA included data on 242,784 protected areas, of which 91% were polygons and 9% were points. Over 70% of the surface of Earth is ocean, comprised of highly diverse ecosystems, and providing a wide range of marine ecosystem services that support human society, health and the economy. Much of the recent growth in MPA coverage has been driven by the establishment of very large MPAs over 100,000 (square kilometers) km². These vast MPAs each contribute a significant part of the total global ocean coverage, with the 20 largest making up the majority of the world’s MPA coverage. While these represent huge commitments to conservation, there is a need for international collaboration to ensure that MPAs achieve their desired conservation value. The information contained in the MPA dataset contributes to the UNEP-WCMC's mission to place biodiversity at the heart of environment and development decision-making to enable enlightened choices for people and the planet. The mandate of the database dates back to 1959 when the UN Economic and Social Council called for a list of national parks and equivalent reserves in recognition that they "are valuable for economic and scientific reasons and also as areas for the future preservation of fauna and flora and geologic structures in their natural state." The first UN List of Protected Areas was published in 1962, and subsequently evolved into the WDPA. The database is also used to generate indicators to track progress towards the Convention on Biological Diversity Aichi Biodiversity Target 11 and UN Sustainable Development Goals 14 and 15. ### Methodology Data for protected area records in the WDPA have been obtained from nearly 500 sources. Along with information on the data verifier, these sources are listed in the source table that is included with each monthly release. Data for protected areas designated under international agreements and conventions are often sourced from the relevant convention secretariats. Data for national-level protected areas have been sourced from national authorities wherever possible. Information may also be supplemented by data from other agencies, organizations or individuals. All data in the WDPA have been verified either by the national authorities or by non-government expert partners, with the exception of some data included before the verification process was established. Data in the WDPA must meet the Protected Planet data standards. These were developed in 2010, regularly updated and subsequently revised in 2015 to ensure consistency in the way the WDPA is compiled, checked, managed, and presented. Standards are important to ensure all information is supplied in a common format that is interoperable and useful for a wide variety of reporting and analytical purposes. There are four key requirements: 1. All sites must meet the IUCN definition of a protected area 2. Spatial data from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and an associated list of attributes must be provided 3. Source of information must be provided 4. The WDPA Data Contributor Agreement must be signed The Protected Planet data standards also encompass standards specific to other databases, such as the Global Database on Protected Area Management Effectiveness. The MPA dataset comprises protected areas in the WDPA that intersect with the marine part of an internal base layer—generally, the ocean or seas, but not lakes. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/resources/wdpa-manual). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA dataset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) as accessed through the [Protected Planet API](https://api.protectedplanet.net/documentation#get-v3protectedareas). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Arctic Sea Ice Extent
description: ### Overview The Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Arctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Arctic region. This dataset can be used to understand the current Arctic sea ice extent. Typically, Arctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in March and minimum in September. However, Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property - albedo - keeps polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset. The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. title: Drivers of Deforestation
description: This data set on deforestation drivers was adapted from Hosonuma et al. (2012) and illustrates the contribution of various industries ("drivers") to deforestation in Africa, the Americas and Asia (including Oceania). The driver data are summarized and analyzed for each of the 3 continents. Agriculture is the main driver of deforestation, but with geographic differences in the importance of commercial versus subsistence agriculture. The data include continental-level estimations for the relative area proportion and absolute net forest area change in km2 yr−1 (FAO 2010) for the period 2000–2010, deforestation drivers, and the relative disturbed forest area fraction of degradation drivers. The estimates are based on data from 46 tropical and subtropical countries and were obtained by the authors from REDD+ reports as well as Center for International Forestry Research country profiles (which include driver and activity information for deforestation and forest degradation), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change National Communications, and other reports. In total, driver data were available for 46 of the 100 (sub)tropical non-Annex I countries. These 46 countries account for 78% of the total forest area (in 2010) and 81% of forest loss (in 2000–2010) of the 100 countries under consideration, according to 2010 data from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization Forest Resources Assessment (FAO 2010), and cover a range of forest transition (FT) phases on each continent. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Inflation
description: ### Overview The Inflation dataset shows national annual rates of inflation for each year from 1960-2019. Inflation reflects the annual percentage change in cost to the average consumer of acquiring specific goods and services. The dataset calculates inflation using the consumer price index (CPI), which is a weighted average of prices of a basket of consumer goods and services that can be measured and compared yearly. The dataset includes all countries that have CPI data available and has a national spatial resolution. It uses the units of percent change (% change) to compare how consumer prices have changed compared to previous years. The dataset is created by The World Bank with data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Inflation affects the purchasing power of a currency, so when inflation increases, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services. Understanding and monitoring national inflation rates is important for governments and financial institutions in creating economic policies that reflect the state of their economy. ### Methodology The dataset was created by comparing CPI between years for each country. The CPI and inflation rate for each country was calculated using the Laspeyres formula. When a large range of goods and services are used in the formula it can be used to measure changes in a country’s cost of living. The Laspeyres formula was calculated by working out the cost of a group of commodities at the target year, dividing this by the cost of the same group of commodities at the previous year prices, and then multiplying by 100. The Laspeyres formula uses a base value of 100, so a value of 102 actually means there was an inflation rate of 2%. CPI data was taken from the International Monetary Fund, International Financial Statistics and data files. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c5a62289-bdc8-4821-83f0-6f05e3d36bdc) as a replacement.**_ The International Soil Reference and Information Centre - World Soil Information (ISRIC-WIS) uses machine learning techniques to develop global maps of soil properties at various soil depths, as well as characterizing bedrock depth. Soil organic carbon stocks are reported in tons per hectare for six standard depth intervals: depths of 0-5 cm, 5-15 cm, 15-30 cm, 30-60 cm, 60-100 cm, and 100-200 cm. Soil organic carbon stocks are important because they are correlated with the productive capacity of land to generate food and other plant life. Soil property estimates are generated using machine learning techniques that combine soil samples, expert opinion, and remote-sensing data. 150,000 soil profiles from a variety of reporting organizations are used in conjunction with a stack of 158 remote sensing-based soil covariates (primarily derived from MODIS land products, SRTM DEM derivatives, climatic images and global landform and lithology maps) to fit an ensemble of machine learning methods—random forest and gradient boosting and/or multinomial logistic regression—as implemented in the R packages ranger, xgboost, nnet and caret. The results of 10–fold cross-validation show that the ensemble models explain between 56% (coarse fragments) and 83% (pH) of variation with an overall average of 61%. Improvements in the relative accuracy considering the amount of variation explained, in comparison to the previous version of SoilGrids at 1 km spatial resolution, range from 60 to 230%. Improvements can be attributed to: (1) the use of machine learning instead of linear regression, (2) to considerable investments in preparing finer resolution covariate layers and (3) to insertion of additional soil profiles. Further development of SoilGrids could include refinement of methods to incorporate input uncertainties and derivation of posterior probability distributions (per pixel), and further automation of spatial modeling so that soil maps can be generated for potentially hundreds of soil variables. title: Projected Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Index of Coastal Protection by Coral Reefs
description: ### Overview This dataset is an index that estimates the relative value provided by coral reefs that protect coastlines through reduction of wave height and wave energy. The value as of 2014 is modeled as a function of exposed populations and infrastructure that received some level of protection from coastal and barrier reefs, and is described in relative terms, classified by decile (i.e., grouped into the most valuable ten percent of reefs for protection, the second-most valuable tenth of reefs, etc.). It was calculated at 1 kilometer (km) resolution globally, encompassing all countries and territories containing coral reefs. During storms, low-lying coastal areas are particularly exposed to ocean water and waves, which can threaten human inhabitants and damage infrastructure. Coastal and barrier reefs can reduce erosion as well as inundation, thereby substantially reducing the risk to lives and livelihoods—a valuable ecosystem service. These estimates represent one part of a concerted effort to quantify the value of coral reefs, as well as the spatial distribution of those values, thereby providing an important incentive for sustainable reef management. The dataset was created by researchers from The Nature Conservancy (TNC), World Resources Institute (WRI), and the University of Cambridge (Cambridge). ### Methodology This global examination of the relative value of the shoreline protection service provided by coral reefs proceeded in four main steps. First, the authors identified the areas vulnerable to inundation and erosion during storms. This was primarily based on the dataset "Low Elevation Coastal Zone Urban and Rural Population and Land Area Estimates, Version 2" (LECZ) from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN), which denotes coastal areas at elevations of less than 10 m above sea level (at approximately 1 km resolution). These zones were augmented to maximize shoreline inclusion (further detail is provided in the Cautions section). Second, the resulting map of vulnerable areas was used to assess exposure: the people and infrastructure in those areas potentially at risk. These were considered separately, as there were significant differences in their distributions. Population information was drawn from the LandScan 2007 gridded dataset from Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The stable Nighttime Lights Time Series from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) served as a proxy for the presence of infrastructure. Both of these datasets were also obtained at 1 km resolution. In quantifying the combined exposure, population was weighted as twice as important as infrastructure. Next, the authors calculated which coastal areas were protected by coral reefs. The protected shoreline map used for this purpose was originally created under the social vulnerability analysis of WRI's Reefs at Risk Revisited project, but was updated slightly for this effort. In general, the estimated level of protection offered by a coral reef was inversely proportional to the distance of the reef from the shore (meaning that the closer the reef was to the shore, the more protection it provided). Finally, the authors combined these different analytic elements in order to estimate the relative value of protection of the shoreline by reefs, within each relevant 1 km grid cell. For more information, please see the [source](https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/Atlas-of-Ocean-Wealth.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes aegypti
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes aegypti*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 “business as usual” scenario, which represents how the climate is predicted to change if we continue our current emissions trends. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes albopictus*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047b-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-albopictus). ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. title: Certified Commodity Crops
description: The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification. The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped. Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map. Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. Tree Cover Loss
description: ### Overview The Tree Cover Loss dataset measures areas of tree cover loss from 2000 through 2020. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. It has a spatial resolution of global coverage (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at a 1 arc second resolution, which is approximately 30 meters × 30 meters at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They not only provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species, but also supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is [playing an incredibly important role since it absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the loss in global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2020 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover loss. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. This dataset has been updated annually since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2020. The development of the algorithm has been modified in numerous ways, such as the addition of new data, reprocessed data from 2011 onward, and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve the dataset for 2011-2020, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Tree Cover](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e00ed8ca-ee7a-4539-b6b5-0bf2c30ee0d8) and the [Tree Cover Gain](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d305958d-3468-4a35-9660-5e18aa3e3190) from the same dataset. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and the reference multispectral imagery from 2020 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_008_rw2_tree_cover_loss). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCAdata on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Annual Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description: ### Overview The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index that measures a country’s vulnerability to climate change along with its readiness to respond and adapt. The index assesses 192 countries annually from 1995-2019. The index is on a scale from 0-100, with higher numbers indicating that the country is better poised to respond to climate disruptions. Every country around the world will experience and respond differently to climate disruptions. Due to the unique socioeconomic and geographic locations of each country, some will be more vulnerable from the impacts of climate change and will have differing capacities to adapt. ND-GAIN’s index combines a vulnerability score with a readiness score to assess each country. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. This index provides a standardized way to estimate a country's adaptation risk and opportunity. ND-GAIN is a program within the Notre Dame Environmental Change Initiative with the goal of heightening awareness and understanding of adaptation, providing products and services to spur action, and enhance investments in vulnerable communities. ### Methodology The ND-GAIN index measures both a country's vulnerability to climate change and its readiness to take adaptation actions. Vulnerability is assessed by considering six sectors: food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure. Each sector is composed of six indicators (36 total) that relate to three components: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. - Exposure measures the extent to which society and its supporting sectors are stressed by future climate conditions. - Sensitivity relates to the degree to which people and the sectors they depend on are affected by climate related disturbances. - Adaptive capacity measures the ability of society to respond and decrease the negative consequences of climate related events. Similarly, readiness is assessed by three core components - economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness - and nine indicators to produce an overall readiness metric that gauges a country's ability to leverage investments and adaptation actions. - Economic readiness represents the investment environment which is needed to marshal funds from the private sector. - Governance readiness relates to the conditions (stability of society, institutional arrangements) that contribute to investment risk. - Social readiness measures the social conditions that enable society to make efficient and equitable use of and benefit from an investment. 74 data sources are used to construct the 45 indicators that make up the readiness and vulnerability scores. 20 indicators come directly from raw data sources, the other 25 are computed by the underlying data. The following steps outline how the index is created: 1. Collect the raw data and process 2. Interpolate missing data or denote certain indicators as “missing” for specific countries 3. Identify the baseline minimum and maximum values from the raw data 4. Define a reference point for each indicator (e.g. reference point for child malnutrition is 0%) 5. Scale the raw data to score, from 0 to 1, to allow for comparison 6. Compute the vulnerability and readiness scores 7. Compute ND-GAIN and scale scores to give a value from 0 to 100 (higher values representing greater readiness and lower vulnerability) ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The ND-GAIN dataset also includes data for each vulnerability sector (food, ecosystem services, health, human habitat, infrastructure, water), readiness sector (economic, governance, social), all 45 indicators, and trends. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_029_rw2_vulnerability_to_climate_change). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Burned Areas
description: ### Overview The Burned Areas dataset shows areas that have experienced fire events in near real-time. The dataset provides the approximate date in which the burning occurred for each of the 500 meter (m) grid cells. Data is available starting in November 2000 and is updated on a monthly basis. [According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/land-resources/nli/landsat/landsat-burned-area?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con), data on burned areas is needed to characterize drivers of fire occurrence, project future fire behavior, and help with assessments of fire impacts on both natural and social systems. The dataset was created by the USGS using satellite imagery. The final product has a resolution of 500 m. ### Methodology The Burned Areas dataset was produced and is continually updated by combining data from both 500 m Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Surface Reflectance imagery and 1 kilometer (km) MODIS active fire observations. This hybrid algorithm uses a burn-sensitive vegetation index derived from MODIS short-wave infrared bands 5 and 7. In addition, the active fire maps are used to guide the selection of burned and unburned training samples. If a grid cell has been marked as burned, the dataset identifies the date when the burn occurred within that cell. The dataset also includes special values for missing data, unburned cells, and water grid cells. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/114/MCD64_User_Guide_V6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on the uncertainty of burn date data, quality assurance indicators, and the first and last days of the burn for each burned area can be found in the original source data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. The original dataset contained burned, unburned, and water grid cells. title: Cooling Degree Days
description: A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: The 2011 percent developed imperviousness layer for the conterminous United States for all pixels. The National Land Cover Database (NLCD) Percent Developed Imperviousness Collection is produced through a cooperative project conducted by the Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) Consortium (www.mrlc.gov). The MRLC Consortium is a partnership of Federal agencies, consisting of the U.S. Geological Survey, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Agricultural Statistics Service, the U.S. Forest Service, the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, NASA, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. A primary goal of the MRLC Consortium is to generate current, consistent, and seamless national datasets of land cover, percent developed imperviousness, and percent tree canopy. NLCD 2001 percent developed imperviousness was created by partitioning the conterminous United States into 66 mapping zones, based on ecoregion and geographical characteristics, edge matching features, and the size requirement of Landsat mosaics. NLCD 2001 represents a seamless assembly of percent developed imperviousness for all 66 MRLC mapping zones. NLCD 2001 percent developed imperviousness was developed for all 50 states and Puerto Rico / U.S. Virgin Islands. NLCD 2006 percent developed imperviousness was created on a path/row basis and mosaicked to create a seamless national product. NLCD 2006 percent developed imperviousness was developed for the conterminous United States. NLCD 2011 percent developed imperviousness was created on a path/row basis and mosaicked to create a seamless national product. The data in NLCD 2011 are completely integrated with NLCD 2001 and NLCD 2006. As part of the NLCD 2011 project, the NLCD 2001 and 2006 percent developed imperviousness data products were revised and reissued to provide full compatibility with the new NLCD 2011 products. The 2014 amended version corrects for the over-elimination of small areas of the four developed classes. NLCD 2011 percent developed imperviousness was developed for the conterminous United States and Alaska. Questions about the NLCD Percent Developed Imperviousness Collection can be directed to the NLCD land cover mapping team at USGS EROS, Sioux Falls, SD (605) 594-6151 or mrlc@usgs.gov.
