title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Modeled 5-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks, or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing, or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure. Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators. GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website. ### Methodology The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module. All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Heating Degree Days
description: A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows HDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Tree Height Change
description: ### Overview The global tree canopy height and change dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed through the integration of the [Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI)](https://gedi.umd.edu/) lidar forest structure measurements and [Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD)](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/us-landsat-analysis-ready-data?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con) time series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure, including tree canopy height between 52°N and 52°S globally. The Global Land Analysis and Discover (GLAD) team at the University of Maryland (UMD) integrated the GEDI point-based tree height measurements with the global wall-to-wall Landsat analysis-ready time-series data (Landsat ARD). The GEDI relative height at 95% (GEDI RH95) metric was used to calibrate the model. The Landsat multi-temporal metrics that represent the surface phenology serve as the independent variables for global tree height modeling. The “moving window” locally calibrated and applied regression tree ensemble model was implemented to ensure high quality of tree height prediction and global map consistency. The model was extrapolated in the boreal regions to create the global tree height prototype map. The model was applied for the years 2000 and 2020 and the maps were temporally filtered to provide a two-decade global forest structure and change metrics. The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery are the primary data source and land cover extent and change the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The year 2000 and 2020 global tree height was modeled through the integration of the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) lidar forest structure measurements and Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD) time-series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure between 52°N and 52°S globally [(Dubayah et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666017220300018). The GEDI relative height of returned energy (RH) metrics were filtered to exclude low quality observations and gridded to the Landsat 30-m spatial resolution. The RH metrics were compared with 90th percentile of the tree height at 30-m pixel resolution derived from the airborne lidar instruments and found that the GEDI RH95 (relative height at 95%) metric is highly correlated with the airborne lidar canopy height product. This metric was selected as the calibration data for the global tree height map. To exclude non-woody vegetation from the training, a zero height was assigned to all GEDI observations with RH95 values below 3 meters. A global 16-day normalized surface reflectance Landsat ARD was employed as input data for tree height modeling [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425720305381?via%3Dihub). The per-pixel 16-day time-series data were composed only of clear-sky observations during the snow-free season. A set of annual multitemporal metrics was generated to provide consistent land surface phenology inputs for model application. To facilitate spatiotemporal consistency of the reflectance time-series, gap-filling of the missing 16-day data with data from preceding years was implemented. Annual metrics include selected ranks, inter-rank averages, and amplitudes of surface reflectance and vegetation indices values, and surface reflectance averages for land surface phenology stages defined by vegetation indices (i.e., surface reflectance for the maximum and minimum greenness periods). The Landsat metrics were augmented with elevation data. The 2019 GEDI RH95 was used as a dependent variable and the Landsat multitemporal metrics from the same year as independent variables to calibrate the regression tree ensembles. A separate model was calibrated for each Landsat ARD tile (1×1°) using training data collected within the neighboring tiles. The prototype for the boreal tree height map, where GEDI data were absent (north of 52°N), was calibrated using training data extracted from the modeled tree height between 40°N and 52°N. To address the overestimation of tree height over wetlands and tundra, additional non-forest training was manually collected in areas indicated as treeless by the year 2010 tree canopy cover product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/). The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to the multitemporal metrics for other years (2000-2003 and 2017-2020). The tree height value for the years 2000 and 2020 was calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003 and 2017, 2019, 2020, respectively, unless forest loss was indicated by the forest change product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/). To reduce errors and noise in the model outputs due to remaining atmospheric contamination and differences in the radiometric resolution of Landsat sensors in 2000 and 2020, extensive filtering of the output products was implemented. Pixels that did not experience forest loss according to the Hansen et al. (2013) product and that had an overlap of ranges of tree height values for 2000-2003 and 2017-2020 intervals were considered stable forests. Manual masks were also used to clean up incorrectly mapped forest loss and gain, especially in the short seasonal forests. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Fires
description: ### Overview This dataset includes near-real-time active fires as points that represent the center of a 375 m resolution pixel and is being updated twice daily. The data is collected from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) sensor on Suomi-National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi-NPP) satellite. This dataset is provided through the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) Fire Email Alerts. This dataset provides improved response for smaller fires, mapping of large fire perimeters, and better detection at night, when fire activities usually occur. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of detection. This dataset is well suited for use in near-real time alert systems, fire tracking, and management. ### Methodology Fire detections are determined using a multispectral contextual algorithm to identify subpixel fire activity and other thermal anomalies in the Level 1 (swath) input data. The algorithm uses all five 375 m VIIRS channels to detect fires and separate land, water, and cloud pixels in the image. Fire locations are then given as the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The algorithm first screens for cloud and water pixels. Next potential fires are found using criteria based on brightness detected by the channels. These fires are then filtered by the algorithm to find the distinct radiometric signatures associated with active fires. Finally custom filters are applied to reduce false alarm rates. False alarms usually come from areas of high solar reflection such as metallic rooftops in industrial parks or bright surfaces such as concrete pavement. Confidence values are available for each fire detection. They are based on a collection of intermediate algorithm quantities used in the detection process and are intended to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot/fire pixels. Confidence values are set to low, nominal, and high. Low confidence daytime fire pixels are typically associated with areas of sun glint and lower relative temperature anomaly (<15K) in the mid-infrared channel I4. Nominal confidence pixels are those free of potential sun glint contamination during the day and marked by strong (>15K) temperature anomaly in either day or nighttime data. High confidence fire pixels are associated with day or nighttime saturated pixels. For the full documentation of the initial algorithm methodology, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425713004483). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch displays the most recent fires in the past week. Data older than the last seven days or within the temporal coverage of January 20, 2012, to the present is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Seychelles Population Density
description: This data set displays the population density per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics’ preliminary data from the 2020 Population and Housing Census. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households. Population density was calculated by dividing the total number of individuals in an enumeration area by the area in square kilometers of the respective enumeration area.

Projected Dry Spells U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset in the United States (U.S.) shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Average annual dry spells are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The average annual number of dry spells for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting precipitation data for a given year and summing the number of 5-day periods with less than 1 mm of precipitation. If a dry period lasted longer than 5 days, each additional day without precipitation was counted as a fractional (1/5) dry period. For example, a dry period of 8 days would count as 8/5 of a dry period (1 + 3/5). The average annual number of dry spells were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in dry spells. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Dry Spells
description: Dry spells represent the annual average count of 5-day periods without precipitation, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. title: Nighttime Lights (Annual, Stable Lights)
description: The Defense Meteorological Satellite Program Operational Linescan System (DMSP-OLS) created the Annual Nighttime Lights: Stable Composites from 1992 until 2013 at a 30 arc second grid resolution (approximately 1 km square grids). These composites account for where light has been observed throughout an entire year. Pixels are identified as being "stable lights" when light is detected there in more than 90-94% of valid observations. The long period of observation allows the product to include observations in places that are cloudy or otherwise obscured many days of the year. This data have been shown to be correlated with regional economic development. The DMSP satellites fly in a sun-synchronous low Earth orbit (833 km mean altitude) such that they pass over any given point on Earth between 20:30 and 21:30 local time. With 14 orbits per day, each DMSP satellite provides global nighttime coverage every 24 hours. There are normally 2 satellites orbiting simultaneously, and each satellite has a lifespan of 6 to 8 years. The light intensity is measured by sensors mounted on these satellites. The observations a satellite makes of a given pixel throughout the year will be from various heights and viewing angles. A mathematical procedure is used to average all of these observations to create the annual nighttime lights product. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Indian lands are areas with boundaries established by treaty, statute, and (or) executive or court order, recognized by the Federal Government as territory in which American Indian tribes have primary governmental authority. title: Soil Moisture
description: This Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) L3 Radiometer Global Daily 36 km EASE-Grid Soil Moisture data set, produced by the NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center Distributed Active Archive Center, provides a composite of daily estimates of global soil moisture, from March 31, 2015 to present, retrieved by the SMAP passive microwave radiometer. Soil moisture data is useful for a variety of applications including weather forecasting, modeling of climate variability and change, agricultural productivity, drought precition, and flood mapping, among others. The microwave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, which includes wavelengths from a few centimeters to a meter, has long held the most promise for estimating surface soil moisture remotely. Passive microwave sensors measure the natural thermal emission emanating from the soil surface. The variation in the intensity of this radiation depends on the dielectric properties and temperature of the target medium, which for the near-surface soil layer is a function of the amount of moisture present. SMAP soil moisture data are resampled to a global, cylindrical 36 km Equal-Area Scalable Earth Grid, Version 2.0 (EASE-Grid 2.0). PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in extreme precipitation is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average days of extreme precipitation during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), and [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: ### Overview This dataset shows the total primary energy consumption in 230 countries from 1980 to 2019. Primary energy is energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form. This dataset is published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). EIA defines primary energy consumption to include coal, petroleum, dry natural gas, nuclear electricity, hydroelectricity geothermal, solar, wind, wood, biomass, and [other sources](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=Primary%20energy%20consumption). Energy consumption is a key indicator of the environmental impact and input costs of economic activity. The intensity of energy consumption and the sources of energy are among the key indicators of sustainable energy, as defined by Sustainable Development Goal 7. ### Methodology EIA collected and analyzed consumption data from multiple external sources. The estimates in this dataset are based on a time series analysis, and the performance of the model was evaluated with hold‐out validation. description: The NASA Making Earth System Data Records for Use in Research Environments (MEaSUREs) Global Food Security Support Analysis Data (GFSAD) Crop Mask Global 1 kilometer (km) data set was created using multiple input data including: remote sensing such as Landsat, Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), Satellite Probatoire d'Observation de la Terre (SPOT) vegetation and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MODIS); secondary elevation data; climate 50-year precipitation and 20-year temperature data; reference sub-meter to 5-meter resolution ground data and country statistics data. title: Oceanic pH
description: GLODAPv2 (Global Ocean Data Analysis Project version 2) is an international data synthesis project for interior ocean inorganic carbon data and related variables for the global ocean. The data set shown is the mapped climatology (GLODAPv2.2016b) of ocean biogeochemical variables based on the new GLODAP version 2 data product (Olsen et al., 2016; Key et al., 2015), which covers all ocean basins over the years 1972 to 2013. The quality-controlled and internally consistent GLODAPv2 was used to create global 1 degree x 1 degree mapped climatologies of salinity, temperature, oxygen, nitrate, phosphate, silicate, total dissolved inorganic carbon (TCO2), total alkalinity (TAlk), pH, and CaCO3 saturation states using the Data-Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVA) mapping method. title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description: First defined in 1988 by scientist Norman Myers, biodiversity hotspots are areas characterized by high levels of endemic plants coupled with significant habitat loss. Endemism is the ecological state of a species being unique to a defined geographic location, such as an island, nation, country or other defined zone, or habitat type. Specifically, a region must meet the following criteria to achieve the hotspot classification formulated by Conservation International (CI): (1) at least 1,500 species of vascular plants (>0.5% of the world’s total) are endemic; and (2) at least 70% of the original natural vegetation has been lost. When Myers first defined the term, he identified 10 tropical forest hotspots. The need to pinpoint priority conservation regions led CI to adopt the term and reassess the hotspot concept. In this process, CI introduced quantitative thresholds (see above) and added additional regions. At that time, there were 25 hotspots. Because of the constant change in environmental threats and the improved understanding of biodiversity, CI has since revisited the hotspots to refine boundaries, update information, and add new regions to create this global data set. This process produced an additional 10 hotspots, bringing the total to 35. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Electricity Installed Capacity
description: ### Overview Electricity installed capacity measures the [maximum electric output](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3) an electricity generator can produce under specific conditions. This dataset reveals the amount of electricity all the power plants in a country can produce within a year and helps quantify the [growth of energy resources](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/what-generation-capacity). However, considering many generators do not operate at their full capacity all the time, a generator's actual electric output [varies based on conditions at the power plant, fuel costs, and/or as instructed by the electric power grid operator](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3). Therefore, this dataset represents the theoretical electricity output that is possible, rather than the actual electricity generation. The Electricity Installed Capacity dataset was released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). This data was reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is available for the years 1980-2019, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. ### Methodology EIA compiled data from a list of external sources including - International Energy Agency (IEA) - Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) - Platts World Power Plants Database - International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) - International Hydropower Association (IHA) - United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database - BP Statistical Review of World Energy - Other government agencies, research institutes, and companies Electricity data shows the capacity as of December 31 each year. Data from both utility and non-utility sources was used. EIA is in the process of creating specific country-level metadata for this dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Total Energy Consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/67cf410f-4cdf-4437-aa09-187e5fa590ae) dataset and [Electricity Consumption] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/eef10736-8d8b-4ac9-a715-ef0653a83196) dataset by EIA. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the electricity installed capacity of different energy resources from 1980 through 2018 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_eia_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: CO₂ Concentrations
description: This monthly midtropospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) Level 3 Monthly Gridded Retrieval, from the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) instrument onboard the Aqua satellite, is aboard the second Earth Observing System (EOS) polar-orbiting platform. In combination with the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit (AMSU) and the Humidity Sounder for Brazil (HSB), AIRS constitutes an innovative atmospheric sounding group of visible, infrared, and microwave sensors. The data are in mole fraction units (data x 10^6 = ppm in volume). Each file covers a calendar month and the mean values provided are simply the arithmetic means of the individual CO₂ retrievals which fall within that grid box over the month. The midtropospheric CO₂ retrievals have been averaged and binned into 2.5 x 2 degree grid cells, from -180.0 to +180.0 degrees longitude and from -60.0 to +90.0 degrees latitude. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

Annual Internal Displacement from Conflict
description: ### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to conflict worldwide each year. Internal displacement refers to the forced movement of people within the country they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from conflict can include, but are not limited to - families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats; and - families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs. Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis. ### Methodology After IDMC learns that displacement due to conflict has occurred, it conducts situational monitoring within certain countries. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Tsunami Tide Gauges -- U.S.
description: CO-OPS has been involved with tsunami warning and mitigation since the Coast & Geodetic Survey started the Tsunami Warning System in 1948 to provide warnings to the Hawaiian Islands. After the December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, CO-OPS was tasked to coordinate with the NOAA Tsunami Warning Centers in upgrading existing stations with new Data Collection Platform (DCP) and communications technology and with expanding the tsunami warning capabilities of the NWLON. Work began in 2005 to upgrade 33 existing water level sand install 16 new stations from the Pacific Ocean to the Caribbean Sea by October 2006. As of September 2006, all 33 upgrades are complete, as well as 15 of the 16 new installations. As of October 2006 the NWLON consist of 196 long-term water level stations along all U.S. coasts, including the Great Lakes, Alaska, Hawaii, the Pacific Ocean Island Territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC) serves as the archive center for this data and provides the historical data to users.

Saltmarshes
description: ### Overview The Saltmarshes dataset displays the distribution of saltmarshes globally, drawing from occurrence data (surveyed and/or remotely sensed). The dataset captures location data for saltmarsh in 99 countries worldwide. The data were collected from 1973 to 2015, with most occurring after 2005. Saltmarshes are highly productive ecosystems that are rich in biodiversity and underpin the estuarine food web. In particular, saltmarshes serve as nesting, nursery and feeding grounds for numerous species of birds, fish, molluscs and crustaceans. Saltmarshes are extremely valuable but often overlooked ecosystems, contributing to livelihoods locally and globally through the associated ecosystem services they provide, including fish production, carbon storage, and coastal protection. Despite their importance, saltmarsh areas are declining around the world, having lost between 25% and 50% of their global historical coverage ([Crooks et al. 2011](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/18318/605780REPLACEM10of0Coastal0Wetlands.pdf), [Duarte et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12237-008-9038-7)). Vast areas have been lost through conversion to agriculture, urban and industrial land, while remaining saltmarshes face many other current and potential threats ([Gedan et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163930)). In light of increasing anthropogenic and environmental pressures on coastal ecosystems, global data on the occurrence and extent of saltmarshes are needed to draw attention to these critical ecosystems and the benefits they generate for people. The dataset was developed to establish a mapped baseline inventory of the extent of the global distribution of saltmarshes. The data aim to support resource management, strengthen decision-making, and facilitate tracking of progress towards global conservation targets set by multilateral environmental agreements. The UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) collated and integrated the dataset with support from Conservation International and The Nature Conservancy. ### Methodology The Saltmarshes dataset consists of data derived from peer-reviewed articles and [grey literature](https://www.greylit.org/about), including reports and databases created by governmental and non-governmental organisations, universities, institutes and researchers globally. Data in the original source materials were collected using remote sensing and field-based survey methods. Data quality ranges from high-resolution maps to low-resolution representations, with the scale varying from 1:10,000 to 1:4,000,000, with most falling within the 1:10,000 to 1:100,000 range. Data contributors were asked to submit metadata with each dataset to provide the contextual information important for informing analyses. Saltmarshes were identified in accordance with definitions provided by data sources, where available, or were determined using expert opinion (available in the supplementary material).The precautionary principle was applied to ensure consistency across designations: if the authors were uncertain about the classification of the habitat, it was not included. Please refer to the supplementary material and associated [metadata](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/pdfs/43/WCMC_027_Global_Distribution_of_Saltmarsh.pdf?1617122640) from the authors for more information regarding each data source presented. For the full documentation, please see the source [publication](https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.5.e11764). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional point data is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) as a replacement.**_ This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss. In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. Historical Coral Bleaching Stress Frequency
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the frequency and intensity of heat stress events. Heat stress events can be detected using sea surface temperature (SST), which is the water temperature close to the ocean's surface. A heat stress event occurs when the SST near coral reefs exceeds the historical baseline for that area. This dataset describes the number of heat stress events and the average period of time between them during 1985-2018 at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. Stress events are defined by applying Coral Reef Watch's [Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/education/tutorial/crw24_dhw_product.php) at coral reef-containing and adjacent satellite pixel locations worldwide. The DHW attempts to capture both the level of abnormal heating and its duration: 1 DHW is equivalent to 1 week of SST 1°C above the expected summertime maximum at a given location. The three thresholds for heat stress in this dataset correspond to occurrence (DHW>0), significant coral bleaching (DHW≥4), and widespread bleaching and significant mortality (DHW≥8). SST and its fluctuations are critical to ecosystem dynamics and health, as many marine organisms can thrive only within certain temperature ranges. In particular, research indicates that a coral reef’s “thermal history” is among the most important factors influencing its ability to withstand heat stress events. Accordingly, with support from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [Coral Reef Conservation Program](http://coralreef.noaa.gov/), [Coral Reef Watch (CRW)] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php) developed a variety of thermal history metrics for coral reef management, initially released in July 2014. The metrics were derived from CRW's Version 3.1 [CoralTemp daily global 5 km (1/20°) satellite SST data product] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), for the period 1985-2018. Coral reef sites that have experienced fewer heat stress events may have natural protection from exposure to conditions conducive to bleaching (e.g., strong mixing, upwelling). However, corals at those sites may also be more sensitive to heat stress, resulting in higher impacts if a stress event does occur. Alternatively, sites that have been regularly exposed to heat stress can have a reduced sensitivity, and therefore lower impact from the stress. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Stress events are defined for 1985-2018 by applying CRW's Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology at pixel locations worldwide that either contained coral reefs or were adjacent to pixels that did. SST input data were drawn from the [CoralTemp daily global 5 km satellite SST data product (Version 3.1)](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), which represents the nighttime ocean temperature measured at the surface. The source data for CoralTemp are a combination of the: 1. NOAA/National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) operational near real-time daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar-orbiting (Geo-Polar) Blended Night-only SST Analysis; 2. NOAA/NESDIS 2002-2016 reprocessed daily global 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analysis; and the 3. 1985-2002 daily global 5 km night-only SST reanalysis produced by the United Kingdom Met Office, on the Operational SST and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system. NOAA's daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analyses (both the near real-time and reprocessed products) utilize sensors from multiple geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites to derive a global SST data field at a resolution of 5 km (1/20°). The few remaining gaps are filled using optimal interpolation through space and time. Heat stress will build up if the temperature around corals rises and stays above the bleaching threshold (1°C above the highest summertime mean SST). The DHW is the product of the deviation above this threshold and the length of time it persists. This captures not only how far the temperature is above the threshold, but how long it has stayed above that point. Thus the DHW shows how much heat stress has accumulated in an area over the past 12 weeks. It is a running sum: as time advances one half-week (a timestep), a half-week timestep "falls off" the back end of the 12-week window. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency, heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. title: Total Suspended Matter
description: ### Overview The Total Suspended Matter (TSM) dataset shows the concentration of inorganic particulate matter in seawater in grams per cubic meter (g/m³). The specific data products shown on Resource Watch originate with the [Ocean Land Color Instrument](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/user-guides/sentinel-3-olci) B (OLCI B), a sensor carried by the [Sentinel-3B satellite](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/missions/sentinel-3). An equivalent product for Sentinel-3A is available from the provider. This monthly and 8-day global products have a resolution of 1/24 degrees (°) at the equator (about 4.63 kilometers); between the two satellites, the time series run back to 2016. Like all similar [GlobColour datasets](https://www.globcolour.info/products_description.html), monthly and 8-day "Level-3" TSM is derived from the accumulated data of the daily [Level-2 product](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) across that month. In the case of TSM, the monthly values represent a simple average of the daily values. TSM is a measure of turbidity: the haziness of a liquid due to suspended particles. Runoff water can carry clay, silt, and other matter from land into the ocean. As the turbidity of water increases, it becomes denser and less clear due to a higher concentration of these light-blocking particles. This in turn can have a wide variety of effects including: reduced sunlight reaching plants and animals, affecting the growth of plankton; increased water temperatures and altered transportation of heat through the water column; and decreased visibility. Ocean color is an "essential climate variable" needed to support the carbon cycle monitoring requirements of the [UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change)](http://unfccc.int/2860.php). It is also a climate variable that cannot be globally monitored without using satellite observations. In order to cover the long time span necessary for climate monitoring purposes, the required ocean color dataset can only be built by merging together observations made with different satellite systems. The GlobColour project started in 2005 to provide a continuous dataset of merged [Level-3 Ocean Colour](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf) products. Merging outputs from different sensors ensures data continuity, improves spatial and temporal coverage, and reduces data noise. ### Methodology The monthly, Level-3 TSM product represents an average of the constituent Level-2 inputs, as is the 8-day TSM product. The [ocean processing](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) component of OLCI Level-2 processing is dedicated to handling water pixels. It is divided into two main tasks: atmospheric correction and ocean color processing. Atmospheric correction follows two approaches; the "standard" or "baseline" approach, further split into atmosphere characterisation and correction, and an "alternative" approach in which atmospheric parameters and water-leaving reflectances are inverted through dedicated neural networks. TSM is produced via the latter. One output of the ocean color processing is a set of bio-geophysical products, including TSM, derived from the water-leaving reflectance (and associated error) using a neural net; these products are particularly focused on more complex Case 2 waters (typically along coasts) in which additional constituents must be considered (scattering by total suspended matter as well as absorption by detrital and Gelbstoff material). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing), as well as the [Product User Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. In addition to monthly TSM, GlobColour also offers daily and 8-day versions. GlobColour generates similar Level-3 (merged Level-2) products for a large number of biological parameters, such as particulate inorganic carbon and primary production, as well as atmospheric and ocean optical parameters. Collectively these are too numerous to list here. The full set can be found in the [Product User's Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_011_nrt_rw0_total_suspended_matter). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Maritime Boundaries
description: ### Overview The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2019 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries. ### Methodology The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries. The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Extreme Precipitation Days
description: Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Estimated Emissions
description: ### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of black carbon in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning, and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.” Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution. Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic. Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: India Projected Change in Precipitation
description: This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in precipitation over the Indian subcontinent. These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp). Projected change in precipitation is computed using daily precipitation in kilograms per square meter per second for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average. The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.
